item.title: Epic 改了 UE 的 EULA：现在你可以合法地拿 UE 与 MetaHuman 项目训练自己的 AI 模型 ｜ UE devs can now choose to train AI Models on their projects
item.description:
一句话：删掉两条禁令，且不授予 Epic 任何权利；Fab 的 NoAI 标签与 UEFN 不受影响。

要点：

  • 删掉的两条禁令：① 禁止把 UE（含源码）当生成式 AI 的训练输入或 prompt 输入；② 禁止用 MetaHuman 角色、动画曲线或复刻 MetaHuman 的渲染输出去训练/测试 AI 与神经网络——对所有 UE 版本生效
  • 边界很清楚：不授予 Epic 训练你内容或代码的权利；Fab 资产仍由卖家通过 NoAI 标签决定；UEFN、Verse 与 Fortnite 岛屿不适用本 EULA；有自定义协议的以协议为准
  • 接受方式：新用户自动提示，老用户可在 EULA 接受页随时接受

为什么值得看：这是许可层面的解锁：此前「用自家 UE 项目训模型」在法律上是灰区，现在放开了，风格/资产微调、MetaHuman 数据驱动的神经渲染都变得可行。副作用是「引擎侧数据治理」（NoAI 标签、资产来源、训练数据可审计）会变成管线里新增的一层。

中文摘要：Epic 于 10 月 29 日更新虚幻引擎 EULA，允许开发者选择用虚幻引擎与 MetaHuman 项目训练 AI 模型，并强调这不授予 Epic 对开发者内容或代码的任何权利。具体是删除了 Section 6e 里的两条通用限制：一是禁止把 UE（含源码）用作生成式 AI 的训练输入或会被训练的 prompt 输入；二是禁止用 MetaHuman 数字角色、动画曲线或复刻 MetaHuman 功能的渲染输出去构建数据库或训练测试 AI/ML/深度学习/神经网络。新用户会被自动提示接受，老用户可在接受页手动接受。边界上：Fab 卖家仍可用 NoAI 标签控制；UEFN、Verse 与 Fortnite 岛屿内容不适用；自定义授权协议优先。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：Unreal Engine（中文）

原文发布：2026-10-29

本期推送：2026-10-31

Epic 在 10 月 29 日更新了虚幻引擎最终用户许可协议（EULA），允许开发者选择用 UE 与 MetaHuman 项目来训练 AI 模型。官方措辞很明确：这项改动不会授予 Epic 对你的内容或代码的任何权利。

具体删掉了哪两条限制

新版 EULA 从 Section 6e（General Restrictions）里删除了两条、且对所有 UE 版本生效：

  1. 禁止把虚幻引擎（含源码）作为生成式 AI 程序的训练输入、或作为会被训练的 prompt 输入；
  2. 禁止用 MetaHuman 数字角色、动画曲线，或用于复刻 MetaHuman 功能的渲染输出，来构建/增强数据库，或训练、测试 AI / 机器学习 / 深度学习 / 神经网络技术。

怎么接受、以及几条关键边界

  • 新用户会被自动提示接受新 EULA；老用户可随时在 EULA 接受页手动接受；
  • 不授予 Epic 训练你的游戏或资产的权利——改动只解除了「对被许可方的限制」；
  • Fab 上的资产不受影响：卖家仍可用 NoAI 标签选择是否允许 AI 训练；
  • UEFN 不适用：Fortnite 岛屿、Verse 代码与岛屿内容仍归 Fortnite 开发者规则与条款管；
  • 有自定义授权协议的，以你的协议为准。

为什么这条比任何一篇技术论文都重要

此前「用 UE 项目训 AI」这件事在法律上是灰的——很多团队不敢把自家 UE 资产喂给模型微调。现在许可层面放开了，直接结果是三条路变得可行：

  • 用自家项目数据做风格/资产微调（而不是只能用公开数据集）；
  • 用 MetaHuman 数据训练角色相关的神经渲染或动画模型（此前明确禁止）；
  • 把「引擎内数据」当成训练基础设施的一部分，而不是只能用来自外部采集的数据。

反过来，这也会推高「引擎侧数据治理」的重要性：NoAI 标签、资产来源追踪、以及训练数据的可审计性，都会成为管线里新增的一层。

（正文为编辑整理的官方页面要点。）

item.title: Wizard：把「动作控制」交给 agent、把画面交给世界模型，零样本换场景换角色也能精确操控 ｜ Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control
item.description:
一句话：显式游戏逻辑 + 可控世界表示与视觉生成解耦，角色动作实时可控、跨场景角色零样本泛化。

要点：

  • 定位是「agentic 游戏世界模型」：把显式游戏逻辑与可控的世界表示从视觉生成里拆出来，由 agent 侧承担操控，视觉部分只负责出画面
  • 解决的是现有 agentic 框架的三个硬伤：只支持简单游戏设定与预定义动作模式、对未见环境与角色泛化差、实时交互能力有限
  • 目标是实时、精确地控制角色动作，并对全新场景、角色与动作做到零样本泛化

为什么值得看：这条和昨天的 BoxWorld、今天的 Fight World Model 指向同一个结论：把「规则/状态」放在引擎侧、把「像素」交给生成模型，是让交互可控的唯一现实路径。Wizard 的增量在「agent 侧控制精度」——这正是玩家手感所在。

中文摘要：视频世界模型已经能生成越来越真实的交互环境，为「玩家自定义玩法」打开空间；agentic 框架进一步把显式游戏逻辑与可控世界表示从视觉生成中解耦。但现有做法只支持简单游戏设定与预定义动作模式，对未见环境与角色泛化差，实时交互也有限。Wizard 提出一种 agentic 游戏世界模型：在解耦的基础上，用 agent 侧承担对角色动作的精确控制，从而做到实时、精确操控，并对全新场景、角色与动作零样本泛化。它把「谁来决定动作、谁来画画面」这件事分得比此前更彻底，也正是玩家手感与生成质量之间那条线的位置所在。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-29

本期推送：2026-10-31

Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control

Abstract

Recent advances in video world models have enabled the generation of increasingly realistic and interactive virtual environments, opening new possibilities for player-customizable gameplay. Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured representations. We leverage these representations as intermediate proxies to condition a video generation model, together with an adaptive masking mechanism that improves alignment between the conditioning signals and generated video rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce an agentic framework that explicitly maintains and updates game states, allowing players to freely configure their virtual worlds and exercise fine-grained control over character motions while preserving visual quality and gameplay consistency. By combining agentic control with structured proxy-based generation, our framework unlocks new possibilities for player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.

00footnotetext: Equal Contribution.00footnotetext: Corresponding Author and Project Leader.

1 Introduction

World models aim to predict future observations from visual histories and current actions, attracting growing interest in gaming applications [33, 2, 11, 27, 10]. By conditioning video generation on players’ mouse and keyboard inputs, video world models offer a natural foundation for interactive and personalized gameplay [14, 42, 48, 40, 22].

Despite recent progress, existing game world models face limitations in control flexibility, generalization, and real-time interaction. Action-conditioned models [38, 35, 13] typically restrict players to predefined action sets, while prompt-conditioned models [49, 7, 4] often depend on motion and skill patterns seen during training, limiting their ability to follow unseen instructions. To improve state consistency and spatial controllability, recent agentic frameworks maintain explicit world states [21, 7] and translate them into structured proxies, such as depth maps [28], semantic maps [5], blockouts [23] or oriented 3D bounding boxes [15], to guide video generation. However, their demonstrations largely focus on basic movement, such as vehicle driving [26, 18] and character locomotion [39, 45], with limited support for articulated character actions. Engine-based approaches [16, 43] offer another route to structured control, but their reliance on predefined scenes and extra processing introduces constraints on scene flexibility and interaction latency.

To address this gap, we introduce Wizard (Fig. 1), an agentic game world model that combines fine-grained character control, zero-shot generalization, real-time interaction and mechanically consistent gameplay, enabling players to customize their game worlds with novel scenes, characters, and motions specified through reference images or free-form language. At its core, Wizard employs an agentic framework to decouple scene construction, character animation, and gameplay logic from visual generation through structured spatial conditioning.

For fine-grained control over camera movement and character animation, our method represents scenes with geometric proxies encoding depth and height, and characters with articulated skeletons. Given any user-provided scene image, we estimate monocular geometry to construct an approximate traversable 2.5D environment and render view-dependent geometric control maps. Character references are converted into 3D meshes and automatically rigged into controllable skeletons, with channel coding distinguishing character instances and their camera-relative orientations. These representations form a unified visual proxy.

Building on the unified visual proxy shown in Fig. 1, the agentic framework then updates scene geometry according to camera inputs and animates character skeletons according to action inputs, providing precise spatial and motion control for the causal video generator. To enable diverse motions for novel characters, a vision-language model retrieves compatible skeletons and animations from a motion library based on character morphology and intended motion style. The selected motions are retargeted to the character’s skeleton, enabling natural movement and player-defined actions. Beyond visual control, the agent further maintains explicit combat states, including health, relative distance, and orientation, to enforce gameplay rules and adapt boss behavior to evolving combat situations.

To train the video model to faithfully follow these structured proxies and generalize across scenes, characters, and motions, we construct 50.3 hours of aligned proxy–video pairs from diverse sources, including data specifically designed for skeletal control. We further introduce an adaptive masking mechanism that restricts reference-image attention to the corresponding character regions, strengthening appearance alignment and preserving character identity during motion. Finally, we apply causal adaptation and few-step distillation [47] to enable real-time video generation, bringing detailed proxy control and consistent visual rendering into an interactive gameplay loop.

In summary, our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We propose Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, zero-shot generalization across unseen scenes, characters, and motions with precise control, substantially expanding the possibilities for player-driven game creation.

  • •

    We build a diverse dataset covering 750 scenes and 178 characters from public videos, game footage, and synthetic sources, with aligned character skeleton and scene geometry to enhance model generalization.

  • •

    We introduce an agentic video-to-video framework that leverages structured proxies to enable fine-grained player control and mechanics-consistent gameplay.

  • •

    We leverage the character positions provided by visual proxies during both training and inference to construct adaptive attention masks, improving character identity preservation and alignment between reference images and generated videos.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Video World Model

    Recent advances in video generation have enabled action-conditioned world models that allow users to interactively explore generated environments. In games, these models translate keyboard and mouse inputs into dynamic gameplay, with emerging capabilities including NPC control in ReactiveGWM [38], fine-grained FPS interactions in SCOPE [35], and multiplayer experiences in WorldCast [40] and Multics [14]. However, relying primarily on pixel-level supervision makes it difficult to maintain persistent game states, retain long-term history, and preserve spatial consistency [15]. To address these limitations, agentic frameworks such as WorldMind [7] and Marionette [28] decouple explicit state management and gameplay logic from visual generation. Despite these advances, existing methods often remain constrained to the game settings seen during training. In contrast, Wizard combines fine-grained skeletal control with a diverse training dataset to enable zero-shot generalization to unseen scenes, characters, and motions.

    2.2 Agentic World Model

    Agentic world models decouple world-state management and action planning from visual generation, enabling explicit control over world dynamics while video models focus on rendering. Related simulation-guided approaches, such as PhysDreamer [46], RealWonder [24], and RoboRender [12], leverage explicit physical dynamics to guide video generation. Moving beyond simulator-defined dynamics, GameDirector [21] maintains combat states and enforces gameplay rules to support player-configurable game settings, while Code World Model [5] and Programmable World Model [15] employ agent-generated programs to maintain persistent world states and guide visual generation through structured proxies. However, these methods primarily emphasize state consistency and entity-level control [39, 45], leaving fine-grained character animation underexplored. Concurrent work, SolarRenderer [8], enables real-time video rendering from diverse proxies, yet seamlessly integrating this capability into a closed-loop gameplay experience remains a challenge. To bridge this gap, Wizard extends agentic control to scene geometry and articulated skeletons, enabling flexible scene manipulation and precise character animation. A diverse, multi-source training dataset enhances generalization, while causal adaptation and few-step distillation enable real-time video generation for responsive gameplay.

    3 Data

    Training a video world model with fine-grained control and zero-shot generalization requires diverse visual data paired with complementary proxies tailored to characters and backgrounds, namely articulated skeletons for character motion and geometry maps for scene structure. Existing public datasets for video world models either lack these complementary conditions [3, 41] or provide them within a single game with limited gameplay diversity [19].

    To this end, we construct 50.3 hours of aligned proxy–video pairs, covering 750 scenes and 178 characters across diverse environments, character morphologies, and motion patterns. Our dataset combines real gameplay recordings, synthetic data, Unreal Engine simulations, and public datasets to achieve broad coverage of scenes, characters, and motions while supporting scalable data production and high visual quality (Sec. 3.1). All sources are converted into a unified representation of scene geometry and articulated character skeletons, enabling the video generator to learn consistent control across different scenes and characters (Sec. 3.2). Fig. 2 illustrates the dataset composition, diversity and processing pipeline.

    3.1 Diverse Data Sources

    Gameplay Recordings.

    We collect 8.8 hours of third-person combat and exploration footage from Elden Ring  [9] to capture authentic AAA-game appearance, combat dynamics, and visual effects. Combat sequences feature six bosses with diverse body structures, capturing articulated attacks, hit reactions, and combat effects. Exploration sequences span 11 regions and more than 20 player outfits, covering varied environments, camera trajectories, and character locomotion. We record RGB frames alongside camera parameters, scene depth, and character skeletons directly from the game, ensuring accurate temporal alignment between visual observations and control signals.

    Synthetic Data.

    While gameplay recordings provide realistic visual dynamics, their character appearances, motion patterns, and interactions remain constrained by the original games. To broaden this coverage, we develop a procedural rendering pipeline that generates 11.6 hours of data using 133 boss and 29 player assets from Sketchfab [32], Quaternius [30], and KayKit [25], with diverse skeletons and animation libraries. We construct varied environments using 842 Poly Haven [29] assets, populate each scene with 15–30 randomly placed props, and randomize character colors, enabling scalable generation of diverse character–scene combinations. Beyond appearance diversity, we design four scenarios to strengthen control robustness: (i) novel-character entry; (ii) multi-character coexistence; (iii) camera-induced disappearance and reappearance; and (iv) rapid turns under a following camera. These scenarios encourage the model to associate each character with its corresponding skeleton and reference image, rather than a fixed appearance or screen position. Camera motion is applied to 95% of generated samples to further diversify viewpoints. Finally, we use a vision-language model to filter out invalid renders and physically implausible placements to ensure data quality.

    Unreal Engine Simulations.

    Furthermore, we use Unreal Engine to generate 3.3 hours of gameplay footage featuring reconstructed characters and weapons [34], scripted opponents, and bot-controlled players. Rendering RGB frames and geometric proxies from the same simulated state ensures precise alignment, while configurable scenes enable scalable collection of varied combat interactions and camera viewpoints.

    Public Datasets.

    We incorporate 26.6 hours of high-quality gameplay footage from WildWorld [19], complementing our collected data with diverse creature morphologies and motion patterns. Its synchronized camera, skeletal, and depth annotations are converted into our unified proxy representation, preserving control–video alignment while broadening the coverage of articulated interactions.

    3.2 Dataset Processing Pipeline

    Data Acquisition.

    We first obtain camera parameters, character skeletons, and scene depth for each video to construct proxies aligned with the video frames. For real gameplay, we extract camera poses, intrinsics, and skeletal states directly from the game process. We also capture scene depth at one frame per second and use it to reconstruct scene geometry, from which depth maps are rendered at each frame’s camera pose. For synthetic and Unreal Engine data, we obtain these quantities directly from the underlying assets and simulation states. For public datasets, we use the provided annotations.

    Unified Proxy Encoding.

    We construct a unified geometric conditioning video that represents character poses and scene structure under a shared camera. At each frame, character skeletons and scene geometry are jointly rendered to preserve their spatial relationships and mutual occlusion. For the scene branch, we remove characters and sky from depth maps, fuse temporally neighboring observations into 3D scene geometry, and re-render it under each frame’s camera pose. For the character branch, we project 3D joints into the camera view and render bones as rounded segments with joint markers, adapting their thickness to character scale and camera distance. Following the geometric channel encoding of Marionette [28], the RGB channels represent geometric attributes rather than appearance colors. R encodes height, with character and scene values mapped to [0,0.2] and [0.5,1], respectively, while B encodes camera-forward depth, with brighter values indicating closer surfaces. At each pixel, the renderer retains the surface closest to the camera.

    To support reference-conditioned character control, we use G to jointly encode a character’s slot and facing direction, while assigning scene geometry G=0. All parts of a character share the same value within each frame, and the facing component helps distinguish otherwise similar front- and back-facing skeletal configurations. Slots are assigned to the player and bosses present in the current scene, with each slot linked to its corresponding reference image. This scene-specific assignment decouples slot codes from fixed character appearances, encouraging the generator to recover appearance from the associated references and supporting generalization to unseen characters.

    Filtering and Annotation.

    We filter out synthetic samples with implausible configurations, such as floating players, or rendering failures. For each training sample, we use Qwen3-VL-8B [1] to generate structured captions from the first frame and character references, describing the conditioning signals, player, boss, and background. Each training sample consists of an aligned proxy video, an RGB clip, character reference images, and a textual description.

    4 Method

    As illustrated in Fig. 3, Wizard combines an agentic framework for explicit world-state control with a video generator that renders the evolving state through structured visual proxies. Before each gameplay session, an initialization stage taking less than five minutes reconstructs the scene and characters, rigs character skeletons, and builds a target-specific motion set through motion retrieval and retargeting. Once initialized, the framework supports real-time gameplay by updating character motions, scene geometry, and combat states in response to player inputs and boss decisions, while the video generator renders the corresponding visual observations. We first describe the agentic framework for character animation, scene manipulation, boss control and mechanics-consistent combat (Sec. 4.1), then introduce character-aware adaptive masking and the training pipeline for real-time video generation (Sec. 4.2).

    4.1 Agentic Framework

    Character Animation via Skeletal Control.

    Given a user-provided character image, Qwen3-VL [1] detects characters and infers their body structures, including posture (upright or horizontal), the number and arrangement of legs, arms, wings, tails, and heads, and their anatomical left–right assignments. We use the predicted bounding boxes to guide SAM2 [31] in segmenting each character, then reconstruct its mesh with TripoSG [17]. UniRig [44] and our medial-axis fitting procedure generate candidate skeletons, from which we select the one that best matches the inferred body structure. We assign semantic labels to its joints and limb chains, identifying body parts such as the left arm or right leg. These labels allow corresponding body parts to be matched across characters with different joint counts and proportions, providing a shared interface for motion retargeting and control.

    To enable realistic combat movements for novel characters, we build a reference motion library from CombatMotion [20], WildWorld [19], and animation assets from Elden Ring [9]. For each target character, we retrieve motions from source skeletons with compatible body structures and use a VLM to assess whether the source characters’ movement styles, such as aggression, grace, or power, suit the target’s appearance. The selected motions can come from multiple sources, allowing each target to inherit a varied moveset. We retarget these motions by matching corresponding limb chains, adapting motion to the target’s limb lengths, and applying inverse kinematics to maintain ground contact. We then filter out clips with poor ground contact, body penetration, or unnatural limb crossing. The remaining clips form a motion library tailored to the target character, enabling the controller to retrieve and execute motions in real time without custom animation scripts.

    Scene Manipulation via Geometry Control.

    As with character control, users can customize and manipulate scenes according to their preferences. Given a scene image, we use MoGe-2 [37] to recover a 3D point map and camera parameters, remove character regions, and construct a background mesh supplemented by a height field. An OpenGL-based offscreen renderer, implemented with ModernGL and EGL, renders this geometry from the current camera viewpoint using the same proxy encoding as in training: the R and B channels encode world height and inverse depth, respectively, while the G channel is set to zero. As the camera moves, the world agent re-renders the persistent scene geometry to produce a spatially consistent visual proxy. To support exploration beyond the input view, the agent extends the height field with smoothly blended terrain variations based on the observed scene’s roughness.

    During gameplay, the world agent, powered by Qwen3-VL-8B, translates users’ natural-language instructions into executable programs that compose predefined geometric operators and specify their locations, scales, and deformation parameters. These programs modify the underlying scene geometry, enabling transformations such as raising a platform from the ground or turning the world upside down. The modified geometry is then re-rendered into the proxy video, supporting creative, interactive scene manipulation while maintaining consistent camera projection and spatial structure.

    State-Aware Combat Control.

    Our framework maintains a shared world state that tracks both characters’ positions, poses, health, action phases, and skill cooldowns. Based on this state, a behavior planner selects movements and attacks from the previously constructed target-specific motion set. When the player is out of reach, the planner selects a motion that moves the boss toward the player. Within attack range, it evaluates candidate attacks by simulating their swings against the player’s current geometry and prioritizes those likely to connect, subject to action-phase and cooldown constraints. This state-aware planning enables the boss to respond to the player’s movements and the evolving combat situation.

    The selected motion is then executed in the simulation, where a rule-based controller enforces gameplay constraints and resolves combat outcomes for both characters. It detects hits by checking each attack’s swept hitbox against the target’s geometry while accounting for invulnerability windows. Valid hits reduce the target’s health, update its health bar, and trigger hit reactions. Skills become available only after their cooldowns expire, and combat ends when either character’s health reaches zero. The updated world state informs the planner’s next decision and is rendered into visual proxies that condition the video generator. Together, state-aware planning and rule-based execution support responsive, mechanics-consistent combat independently of video generation.

    4.2 Model Training

    We build our video generator on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [36], which renders the evolving visual proxies into video conditioned on the initial scene image and character references:

    X̂_t:t+L-1=G_θ (P_t:t+L-1,I₀,{Rᵏ}ₖ₌₁^K;H_

    		(1)

    where P_t:t+L-1, I₀, and Rᵏ denote the visual proxy sequence, the initial scene image, and the reference image for character k, respectively. H_

    As shown in Fig. 4, the first frame is encoded as a clean latent prefix to establish scene appearance. Proxy frames are encoded by the same VAE and concatenated with noisy video latents along channels, using a zero-initialized condition embedding to introduce spatial control while preserving the pretrained model’s initial behavior. Character references are appended as additional tokens to specify appearance. We bind these references to their corresponding characters through adaptive attention masking, then distill the conditioned generator for real-time autoregressive inference.

    Character-Aware Adaptive Masking.

    Character skeletons provide explicit spatial information during both training and inference: training data include ground-truth skeletons, while our agentic framework maintains and updates them at runtime. We leverage this shared structure to bind each reference image to its intended character. Each character reference image is VAE-encoded and appended as tokens with a distinct temporal positional offset. For each frame, we derive a bounding region from each character’s skeleton and expand it by 25% to include the character and its surrounding context. In every DiT self-attention layer, we gate attention from video token i to reference token j using an additive mask:

    Aᵢⱼ=Softmaxⱼ ((qᵢ^⊤kⱼ)/(√d)+Mᵢⱼ), Mᵢⱼ=\begincases0,&uᵢ∈Ω_k(j),τ(i), -∞,&otherwise,\endcases

    		(2)

    where k(j) identifies the character associated with reference token j, uᵢ and τ(i) denote the spatial position and frame index of video token i, and Ω_k,τ is character k’s expanded region on the token grid at frame τ. The softmax also includes video keys permitted by the temporal attention mask, allowing tokens outside character regions to attend to these keys.

    These spatial masks are updated from the explicit character states maintained by our agentic framework, allowing players to control when and where bosses appear or disappear while directing reference guidance to the corresponding regions. As characters move, the masks follow their positions, reducing cross-character appearance leakage. During character transformation, we additionally block attention to cached tokens associated with the previous identity while preserving access to background history and the first-frame sink. By linking appearance guidance to agent-controlled character states, this strategy supports flexible summoning, removal, transformation, and multi-character gameplay while maintaining scene continuity.

    Causal Adaptation and Few-Step Distillation.

    Following Causal Forcing++ [47], we adopt a three-stage training pipeline for real-time autoregressive generation. First, we adapt the bidirectional model to autoregressive generation through teacher forcing. Second, we perform consistency distillation with a guided causal teacher and an exponential moving average (EMA) target, training the student with a sliding window of 20 latent frames and the first frame as a persistent attention sink. Third, we apply distribution matching distillation (DMD) to the student’s own autoregressive rollouts, using the frozen bidirectional model as the target score network and a learned critic to estimate the student’s score. Our visual proxy conditions and character-gated reference attention remain active throughout all three stages, preserving spatial and appearance control during adaptation and distillation. The resulting model generates real-time rollouts at 24 FPS with only 2 denoising steps.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Experimental Setup

    Data.

    We partition the aligned RGB and proxy sequences into non-overlapping windows of 121 frames at 30 fps, each spanning approximately four seconds. Frames are resized to a height of 480 pixels and center-cropped to 832×480, with identical transformations applied to both modalities to preserve spatial alignment. Character reference images are resized to 480×480. For efficient training, we pre-encode the RGB and proxy clips using the Wan2.2 VAE, yielding latent representations with 31 temporal steps and a spatial resolution of 30×52.

    Implementation Details.

    We initialize our model from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [36], keeping its VAE and UMT5 text encoder [6] frozen. We train on 44,075 clips, paired with geometry-and-skeleton conditions, a text description, and up to two character appearance references. Training comprises 30K steps of bidirectional fine-tuning, 10K steps of causal adaptation, and subsequent distillation for efficient inference. We deploy the student’s exponential moving average (EMA) checkpoint after 500 distillation steps. At inference, the model uses two denoising steps and a KV cache that retains 20 recent latent frames and one persistent sink frame, enabling continuous, bounded-memory streaming for real-time interaction.

    Evaluation Setup.

    We qualitatively evaluate Wizard’s zero-shot generalization in Fig. 5 and its support for open-ended creative gameplay in Fig. 6. Each example presents user-provided scene or character references on the left, followed by paired agent-controlled visual proxies and generated gameplay frames on the right. The references are unseen during training, and all examples use the same trained model without additional fine-tuning. This presentation allows direct inspection of how user inputs are translated into structured controls and reflected in the generated videos.

    5.2 Zero-shot Generalization

    As shown in Fig. 5(a), Wizard generalizes to novel scenes, characters, and motions. Given user-provided inputs, the agent controls visual proxies to generate real-time combat rollouts that follow the specified scene structure and character motions. The paired visualizations show how character poses and spatial arrangements in the proxies are reflected in the generated frames, while reference images specify the desired appearance. These examples illustrate the model’s ability to accommodate new combinations of environments, character appearances, and motion controls without additional training. Diverse training data and character-aware adaptive masking support visual consistency throughout the rollouts.

    Furthermore, Fig. 5(b) illustrates how Wizard’s agentic framework maintains and updates game states and enforces combat rules. We showcase a core rule: when either character’s health reaches zero, the controller resolves the character’s death, ends combat, and displays the outcome. The framework also allows additional gameplay rules to be flexibly incorporated.

    5.3 Open-ended Creative Gameplay

    Wizard’s generalization capabilities enable diverse, open-ended gameplay, giving players control over both characters and their surroundings. As shown in Fig. 6(a), players can transform characters during gameplay by providing a reference image of the desired appearance. This allows character appearance to become an interactive part of the gameplay experience rather than a fixed initial choice.

    Fig. 6(b) demonstrates scene manipulation, including inverting the environment and introducing new scene elements through agent-controlled visual proxies. These examples extend user control from character animation to the geometry and layout of the game world. Character transformation and scene manipulation can also be combined within a single gameplay scenario, as illustrated in Fig. 6(c). Together, these capabilities allow players to create scenarios by composing character and environment changes, extending the range of experiences supported by the same underlying framework.

    6 Conclusions and Discussions

    In this paper, we introduce Wizard, the first agentic game world model to enable fine-grained control of characters and scenes through articulated skeletons and geometry maps, respectively, while maintaining mechanics-consistent, real-time interaction. Trained on our constructed diverse dataset111 WildWorld is used under its non-commercial research license; no WildWorld-derived data is redistributed. Elden Ring footage was recorded by the authors and is used solely for research. , Wizard demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to unseen characters, scenes, and motions, enabling players to create and manipulate customized game worlds.

    However, Wizard still has some limitations. First, its reliance on a motion library makes it difficult to find compatible motions for characters with uncommon body structures. Second, consistency between the scene proxies and the generated video may decline over longer rollouts. Future work will focus on supporting more flexible, realistic character motions that better reflect actual gameplay and maintaining consistent scene appearance over long rollouts. These improvements will bring agentic video generation closer to fully playable, closed-loop game worlds with greater player freedom and more precise, nuanced control.

    Acknowledgements

    We would like to express our sincere gratitude to Ruidong Wang and Murphy Zhao for their invaluable support throughout this project.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：显式游戏逻辑 + 可控世界表示与视觉生成解耦，角色动作实时可控、跨场景角色零样本泛化。

要点：

  • 定位是「agentic 游戏世界模型」：把显式游戏逻辑与可控的世界表示从视觉生成里拆出来，由 agent 侧承担操控，视觉部分只负责出画面
  • 解决的是现有 agentic 框架的三个硬伤：只支持简单游戏设定与预定义动作模式、对未见环境与角色泛化差、实时交互能力有限
  • 目标是实时、精确地控制角色动作，并对全新场景、角色与动作做到零样本泛化

为什么值得看：这条和昨天的 BoxWorld、今天的 Fight World Model 指向同一个结论：把「规则/状态」放在引擎侧、把「像素」交给生成模型，是让交互可控的唯一现实路径。Wizard 的增量在「agent 侧控制精度」——这正是玩家手感所在。

中文摘要：视频世界模型已经能生成越来越真实的交互环境，为「玩家自定义玩法」打开空间；agentic 框架进一步把显式游戏逻辑与可控世界表示从视觉生成中解耦。但现有做法只支持简单游戏设定与预定义动作模式，对未见环境与角色泛化差，实时交互也有限。Wizard 提出一种 agentic 游戏世界模型：在解耦的基础上，用 agent 侧承担对角色动作的精确控制，从而做到实时、精确操控，并对全新场景、角色与动作零样本泛化。它把「谁来决定动作、谁来画画面」这件事分得比此前更彻底，也正是玩家手感与生成质量之间那条线的位置所在。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-29

本期推送：2026-10-31

Wizard: Manipulate Any World in Real Time via Agentic Control

Abstract

Recent advances in video world models have enabled the generation of increasingly realistic and interactive virtual environments, opening new possibilities for player-customizable gameplay. Agentic frameworks further advance this direction by decoupling explicit game logic and controllable world representations from visual generation. However, existing approaches support only simple game settings and predefined motion patterns, generalize poorly to unseen environments and characters, and offer limited real-time interactivity. In this paper, we introduce Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, precise control over character motions while generalizing zero-shot across novel scenes, characters, and actions. To achieve this, we construct a diverse dataset spanning 750 scenes and 178 characters, incorporating skeleton and geometry information as structured representations. We leverage these representations as intermediate proxies to condition a video generation model, together with an adaptive masking mechanism that improves alignment between the conditioning signals and generated video rollouts. Furthermore, we introduce an agentic framework that explicitly maintains and updates game states, allowing players to freely configure their virtual worlds and exercise fine-grained control over character motions while preserving visual quality and gameplay consistency. By combining agentic control with structured proxy-based generation, our framework unlocks new possibilities for player-driven game creation with real-time, generalizable, and mechanically consistent world simulation.

00footnotetext: Equal Contribution.00footnotetext: Corresponding Author and Project Leader.

1 Introduction

World models aim to predict future observations from visual histories and current actions, attracting growing interest in gaming applications [33, 2, 11, 27, 10]. By conditioning video generation on players’ mouse and keyboard inputs, video world models offer a natural foundation for interactive and personalized gameplay [14, 42, 48, 40, 22].

Despite recent progress, existing game world models face limitations in control flexibility, generalization, and real-time interaction. Action-conditioned models [38, 35, 13] typically restrict players to predefined action sets, while prompt-conditioned models [49, 7, 4] often depend on motion and skill patterns seen during training, limiting their ability to follow unseen instructions. To improve state consistency and spatial controllability, recent agentic frameworks maintain explicit world states [21, 7] and translate them into structured proxies, such as depth maps [28], semantic maps [5], blockouts [23] or oriented 3D bounding boxes [15], to guide video generation. However, their demonstrations largely focus on basic movement, such as vehicle driving [26, 18] and character locomotion [39, 45], with limited support for articulated character actions. Engine-based approaches [16, 43] offer another route to structured control, but their reliance on predefined scenes and extra processing introduces constraints on scene flexibility and interaction latency.

To address this gap, we introduce Wizard (Fig. 1), an agentic game world model that combines fine-grained character control, zero-shot generalization, real-time interaction and mechanically consistent gameplay, enabling players to customize their game worlds with novel scenes, characters, and motions specified through reference images or free-form language. At its core, Wizard employs an agentic framework to decouple scene construction, character animation, and gameplay logic from visual generation through structured spatial conditioning.

For fine-grained control over camera movement and character animation, our method represents scenes with geometric proxies encoding depth and height, and characters with articulated skeletons. Given any user-provided scene image, we estimate monocular geometry to construct an approximate traversable 2.5D environment and render view-dependent geometric control maps. Character references are converted into 3D meshes and automatically rigged into controllable skeletons, with channel coding distinguishing character instances and their camera-relative orientations. These representations form a unified visual proxy.

Building on the unified visual proxy shown in Fig. 1, the agentic framework then updates scene geometry according to camera inputs and animates character skeletons according to action inputs, providing precise spatial and motion control for the causal video generator. To enable diverse motions for novel characters, a vision-language model retrieves compatible skeletons and animations from a motion library based on character morphology and intended motion style. The selected motions are retargeted to the character’s skeleton, enabling natural movement and player-defined actions. Beyond visual control, the agent further maintains explicit combat states, including health, relative distance, and orientation, to enforce gameplay rules and adapt boss behavior to evolving combat situations.

To train the video model to faithfully follow these structured proxies and generalize across scenes, characters, and motions, we construct 50.3 hours of aligned proxy–video pairs from diverse sources, including data specifically designed for skeletal control. We further introduce an adaptive masking mechanism that restricts reference-image attention to the corresponding character regions, strengthening appearance alignment and preserving character identity during motion. Finally, we apply causal adaptation and few-step distillation [47] to enable real-time video generation, bringing detailed proxy control and consistent visual rendering into an interactive gameplay loop.

In summary, our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We propose Wizard, an agentic game world model that enables real-time, zero-shot generalization across unseen scenes, characters, and motions with precise control, substantially expanding the possibilities for player-driven game creation.

  • •

    We build a diverse dataset covering 750 scenes and 178 characters from public videos, game footage, and synthetic sources, with aligned character skeleton and scene geometry to enhance model generalization.

  • •

    We introduce an agentic video-to-video framework that leverages structured proxies to enable fine-grained player control and mechanics-consistent gameplay.

  • •

    We leverage the character positions provided by visual proxies during both training and inference to construct adaptive attention masks, improving character identity preservation and alignment between reference images and generated videos.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Video World Model

    Recent advances in video generation have enabled action-conditioned world models that allow users to interactively explore generated environments. In games, these models translate keyboard and mouse inputs into dynamic gameplay, with emerging capabilities including NPC control in ReactiveGWM [38], fine-grained FPS interactions in SCOPE [35], and multiplayer experiences in WorldCast [40] and Multics [14]. However, relying primarily on pixel-level supervision makes it difficult to maintain persistent game states, retain long-term history, and preserve spatial consistency [15]. To address these limitations, agentic frameworks such as WorldMind [7] and Marionette [28] decouple explicit state management and gameplay logic from visual generation. Despite these advances, existing methods often remain constrained to the game settings seen during training. In contrast, Wizard combines fine-grained skeletal control with a diverse training dataset to enable zero-shot generalization to unseen scenes, characters, and motions.

    2.2 Agentic World Model

    Agentic world models decouple world-state management and action planning from visual generation, enabling explicit control over world dynamics while video models focus on rendering. Related simulation-guided approaches, such as PhysDreamer [46], RealWonder [24], and RoboRender [12], leverage explicit physical dynamics to guide video generation. Moving beyond simulator-defined dynamics, GameDirector [21] maintains combat states and enforces gameplay rules to support player-configurable game settings, while Code World Model [5] and Programmable World Model [15] employ agent-generated programs to maintain persistent world states and guide visual generation through structured proxies. However, these methods primarily emphasize state consistency and entity-level control [39, 45], leaving fine-grained character animation underexplored. Concurrent work, SolarRenderer [8], enables real-time video rendering from diverse proxies, yet seamlessly integrating this capability into a closed-loop gameplay experience remains a challenge. To bridge this gap, Wizard extends agentic control to scene geometry and articulated skeletons, enabling flexible scene manipulation and precise character animation. A diverse, multi-source training dataset enhances generalization, while causal adaptation and few-step distillation enable real-time video generation for responsive gameplay.

    3 Data

    Training a video world model with fine-grained control and zero-shot generalization requires diverse visual data paired with complementary proxies tailored to characters and backgrounds, namely articulated skeletons for character motion and geometry maps for scene structure. Existing public datasets for video world models either lack these complementary conditions [3, 41] or provide them within a single game with limited gameplay diversity [19].

    To this end, we construct 50.3 hours of aligned proxy–video pairs, covering 750 scenes and 178 characters across diverse environments, character morphologies, and motion patterns. Our dataset combines real gameplay recordings, synthetic data, Unreal Engine simulations, and public datasets to achieve broad coverage of scenes, characters, and motions while supporting scalable data production and high visual quality (Sec. 3.1). All sources are converted into a unified representation of scene geometry and articulated character skeletons, enabling the video generator to learn consistent control across different scenes and characters (Sec. 3.2). Fig. 2 illustrates the dataset composition, diversity and processing pipeline.

    3.1 Diverse Data Sources

    Gameplay Recordings.

    We collect 8.8 hours of third-person combat and exploration footage from Elden Ring  [9] to capture authentic AAA-game appearance, combat dynamics, and visual effects. Combat sequences feature six bosses with diverse body structures, capturing articulated attacks, hit reactions, and combat effects. Exploration sequences span 11 regions and more than 20 player outfits, covering varied environments, camera trajectories, and character locomotion. We record RGB frames alongside camera parameters, scene depth, and character skeletons directly from the game, ensuring accurate temporal alignment between visual observations and control signals.

    Synthetic Data.

    While gameplay recordings provide realistic visual dynamics, their character appearances, motion patterns, and interactions remain constrained by the original games. To broaden this coverage, we develop a procedural rendering pipeline that generates 11.6 hours of data using 133 boss and 29 player assets from Sketchfab [32], Quaternius [30], and KayKit [25], with diverse skeletons and animation libraries. We construct varied environments using 842 Poly Haven [29] assets, populate each scene with 15–30 randomly placed props, and randomize character colors, enabling scalable generation of diverse character–scene combinations. Beyond appearance diversity, we design four scenarios to strengthen control robustness: (i) novel-character entry; (ii) multi-character coexistence; (iii) camera-induced disappearance and reappearance; and (iv) rapid turns under a following camera. These scenarios encourage the model to associate each character with its corresponding skeleton and reference image, rather than a fixed appearance or screen position. Camera motion is applied to 95% of generated samples to further diversify viewpoints. Finally, we use a vision-language model to filter out invalid renders and physically implausible placements to ensure data quality.

    Unreal Engine Simulations.

    Furthermore, we use Unreal Engine to generate 3.3 hours of gameplay footage featuring reconstructed characters and weapons [34], scripted opponents, and bot-controlled players. Rendering RGB frames and geometric proxies from the same simulated state ensures precise alignment, while configurable scenes enable scalable collection of varied combat interactions and camera viewpoints.

    Public Datasets.

    We incorporate 26.6 hours of high-quality gameplay footage from WildWorld [19], complementing our collected data with diverse creature morphologies and motion patterns. Its synchronized camera, skeletal, and depth annotations are converted into our unified proxy representation, preserving control–video alignment while broadening the coverage of articulated interactions.

    3.2 Dataset Processing Pipeline

    Data Acquisition.

    We first obtain camera parameters, character skeletons, and scene depth for each video to construct proxies aligned with the video frames. For real gameplay, we extract camera poses, intrinsics, and skeletal states directly from the game process. We also capture scene depth at one frame per second and use it to reconstruct scene geometry, from which depth maps are rendered at each frame’s camera pose. For synthetic and Unreal Engine data, we obtain these quantities directly from the underlying assets and simulation states. For public datasets, we use the provided annotations.

    Unified Proxy Encoding.

    We construct a unified geometric conditioning video that represents character poses and scene structure under a shared camera. At each frame, character skeletons and scene geometry are jointly rendered to preserve their spatial relationships and mutual occlusion. For the scene branch, we remove characters and sky from depth maps, fuse temporally neighboring observations into 3D scene geometry, and re-render it under each frame’s camera pose. For the character branch, we project 3D joints into the camera view and render bones as rounded segments with joint markers, adapting their thickness to character scale and camera distance. Following the geometric channel encoding of Marionette [28], the RGB channels represent geometric attributes rather than appearance colors. R encodes height, with character and scene values mapped to [0,0.2] and [0.5,1], respectively, while B encodes camera-forward depth, with brighter values indicating closer surfaces. At each pixel, the renderer retains the surface closest to the camera.

    To support reference-conditioned character control, we use G to jointly encode a character’s slot and facing direction, while assigning scene geometry G=0. All parts of a character share the same value within each frame, and the facing component helps distinguish otherwise similar front- and back-facing skeletal configurations. Slots are assigned to the player and bosses present in the current scene, with each slot linked to its corresponding reference image. This scene-specific assignment decouples slot codes from fixed character appearances, encouraging the generator to recover appearance from the associated references and supporting generalization to unseen characters.

    Filtering and Annotation.

    We filter out synthetic samples with implausible configurations, such as floating players, or rendering failures. For each training sample, we use Qwen3-VL-8B [1] to generate structured captions from the first frame and character references, describing the conditioning signals, player, boss, and background. Each training sample consists of an aligned proxy video, an RGB clip, character reference images, and a textual description.

    4 Method

    As illustrated in Fig. 3, Wizard combines an agentic framework for explicit world-state control with a video generator that renders the evolving state through structured visual proxies. Before each gameplay session, an initialization stage taking less than five minutes reconstructs the scene and characters, rigs character skeletons, and builds a target-specific motion set through motion retrieval and retargeting. Once initialized, the framework supports real-time gameplay by updating character motions, scene geometry, and combat states in response to player inputs and boss decisions, while the video generator renders the corresponding visual observations. We first describe the agentic framework for character animation, scene manipulation, boss control and mechanics-consistent combat (Sec. 4.1), then introduce character-aware adaptive masking and the training pipeline for real-time video generation (Sec. 4.2).

    4.1 Agentic Framework

    Character Animation via Skeletal Control.

    Given a user-provided character image, Qwen3-VL [1] detects characters and infers their body structures, including posture (upright or horizontal), the number and arrangement of legs, arms, wings, tails, and heads, and their anatomical left–right assignments. We use the predicted bounding boxes to guide SAM2 [31] in segmenting each character, then reconstruct its mesh with TripoSG [17]. UniRig [44] and our medial-axis fitting procedure generate candidate skeletons, from which we select the one that best matches the inferred body structure. We assign semantic labels to its joints and limb chains, identifying body parts such as the left arm or right leg. These labels allow corresponding body parts to be matched across characters with different joint counts and proportions, providing a shared interface for motion retargeting and control.

    To enable realistic combat movements for novel characters, we build a reference motion library from CombatMotion [20], WildWorld [19], and animation assets from Elden Ring [9]. For each target character, we retrieve motions from source skeletons with compatible body structures and use a VLM to assess whether the source characters’ movement styles, such as aggression, grace, or power, suit the target’s appearance. The selected motions can come from multiple sources, allowing each target to inherit a varied moveset. We retarget these motions by matching corresponding limb chains, adapting motion to the target’s limb lengths, and applying inverse kinematics to maintain ground contact. We then filter out clips with poor ground contact, body penetration, or unnatural limb crossing. The remaining clips form a motion library tailored to the target character, enabling the controller to retrieve and execute motions in real time without custom animation scripts.

    Scene Manipulation via Geometry Control.

    As with character control, users can customize and manipulate scenes according to their preferences. Given a scene image, we use MoGe-2 [37] to recover a 3D point map and camera parameters, remove character regions, and construct a background mesh supplemented by a height field. An OpenGL-based offscreen renderer, implemented with ModernGL and EGL, renders this geometry from the current camera viewpoint using the same proxy encoding as in training: the R and B channels encode world height and inverse depth, respectively, while the G channel is set to zero. As the camera moves, the world agent re-renders the persistent scene geometry to produce a spatially consistent visual proxy. To support exploration beyond the input view, the agent extends the height field with smoothly blended terrain variations based on the observed scene’s roughness.

    During gameplay, the world agent, powered by Qwen3-VL-8B, translates users’ natural-language instructions into executable programs that compose predefined geometric operators and specify their locations, scales, and deformation parameters. These programs modify the underlying scene geometry, enabling transformations such as raising a platform from the ground or turning the world upside down. The modified geometry is then re-rendered into the proxy video, supporting creative, interactive scene manipulation while maintaining consistent camera projection and spatial structure.

    State-Aware Combat Control.

    Our framework maintains a shared world state that tracks both characters’ positions, poses, health, action phases, and skill cooldowns. Based on this state, a behavior planner selects movements and attacks from the previously constructed target-specific motion set. When the player is out of reach, the planner selects a motion that moves the boss toward the player. Within attack range, it evaluates candidate attacks by simulating their swings against the player’s current geometry and prioritizes those likely to connect, subject to action-phase and cooldown constraints. This state-aware planning enables the boss to respond to the player’s movements and the evolving combat situation.

    The selected motion is then executed in the simulation, where a rule-based controller enforces gameplay constraints and resolves combat outcomes for both characters. It detects hits by checking each attack’s swept hitbox against the target’s geometry while accounting for invulnerability windows. Valid hits reduce the target’s health, update its health bar, and trigger hit reactions. Skills become available only after their cooldowns expire, and combat ends when either character’s health reaches zero. The updated world state informs the planner’s next decision and is rendered into visual proxies that condition the video generator. Together, state-aware planning and rule-based execution support responsive, mechanics-consistent combat independently of video generation.

    4.2 Model Training

    We build our video generator on Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [36], which renders the evolving visual proxies into video conditioned on the initial scene image and character references:

    X̂_t:t+L-1=G_θ (P_t:t+L-1,I₀,{Rᵏ}ₖ₌₁^K;H_

    		(1)

    where P_t:t+L-1, I₀, and Rᵏ denote the visual proxy sequence, the initial scene image, and the reference image for character k, respectively. H_

    As shown in Fig. 4, the first frame is encoded as a clean latent prefix to establish scene appearance. Proxy frames are encoded by the same VAE and concatenated with noisy video latents along channels, using a zero-initialized condition embedding to introduce spatial control while preserving the pretrained model’s initial behavior. Character references are appended as additional tokens to specify appearance. We bind these references to their corresponding characters through adaptive attention masking, then distill the conditioned generator for real-time autoregressive inference.

    Character-Aware Adaptive Masking.

    Character skeletons provide explicit spatial information during both training and inference: training data include ground-truth skeletons, while our agentic framework maintains and updates them at runtime. We leverage this shared structure to bind each reference image to its intended character. Each character reference image is VAE-encoded and appended as tokens with a distinct temporal positional offset. For each frame, we derive a bounding region from each character’s skeleton and expand it by 25% to include the character and its surrounding context. In every DiT self-attention layer, we gate attention from video token i to reference token j using an additive mask:

    Aᵢⱼ=Softmaxⱼ ((qᵢ^⊤kⱼ)/(√d)+Mᵢⱼ), Mᵢⱼ=\begincases0,&uᵢ∈Ω_k(j),τ(i), -∞,&otherwise,\endcases

    		(2)

    where k(j) identifies the character associated with reference token j, uᵢ and τ(i) denote the spatial position and frame index of video token i, and Ω_k,τ is character k’s expanded region on the token grid at frame τ. The softmax also includes video keys permitted by the temporal attention mask, allowing tokens outside character regions to attend to these keys.

    These spatial masks are updated from the explicit character states maintained by our agentic framework, allowing players to control when and where bosses appear or disappear while directing reference guidance to the corresponding regions. As characters move, the masks follow their positions, reducing cross-character appearance leakage. During character transformation, we additionally block attention to cached tokens associated with the previous identity while preserving access to background history and the first-frame sink. By linking appearance guidance to agent-controlled character states, this strategy supports flexible summoning, removal, transformation, and multi-character gameplay while maintaining scene continuity.

    Causal Adaptation and Few-Step Distillation.

    Following Causal Forcing++ [47], we adopt a three-stage training pipeline for real-time autoregressive generation. First, we adapt the bidirectional model to autoregressive generation through teacher forcing. Second, we perform consistency distillation with a guided causal teacher and an exponential moving average (EMA) target, training the student with a sliding window of 20 latent frames and the first frame as a persistent attention sink. Third, we apply distribution matching distillation (DMD) to the student’s own autoregressive rollouts, using the frozen bidirectional model as the target score network and a learned critic to estimate the student’s score. Our visual proxy conditions and character-gated reference attention remain active throughout all three stages, preserving spatial and appearance control during adaptation and distillation. The resulting model generates real-time rollouts at 24 FPS with only 2 denoising steps.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Experimental Setup

    Data.

    We partition the aligned RGB and proxy sequences into non-overlapping windows of 121 frames at 30 fps, each spanning approximately four seconds. Frames are resized to a height of 480 pixels and center-cropped to 832×480, with identical transformations applied to both modalities to preserve spatial alignment. Character reference images are resized to 480×480. For efficient training, we pre-encode the RGB and proxy clips using the Wan2.2 VAE, yielding latent representations with 31 temporal steps and a spatial resolution of 30×52.

    Implementation Details.

    We initialize our model from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [36], keeping its VAE and UMT5 text encoder [6] frozen. We train on 44,075 clips, paired with geometry-and-skeleton conditions, a text description, and up to two character appearance references. Training comprises 30K steps of bidirectional fine-tuning, 10K steps of causal adaptation, and subsequent distillation for efficient inference. We deploy the student’s exponential moving average (EMA) checkpoint after 500 distillation steps. At inference, the model uses two denoising steps and a KV cache that retains 20 recent latent frames and one persistent sink frame, enabling continuous, bounded-memory streaming for real-time interaction.

    Evaluation Setup.

    We qualitatively evaluate Wizard’s zero-shot generalization in Fig. 5 and its support for open-ended creative gameplay in Fig. 6. Each example presents user-provided scene or character references on the left, followed by paired agent-controlled visual proxies and generated gameplay frames on the right. The references are unseen during training, and all examples use the same trained model without additional fine-tuning. This presentation allows direct inspection of how user inputs are translated into structured controls and reflected in the generated videos.

    5.2 Zero-shot Generalization

    As shown in Fig. 5(a), Wizard generalizes to novel scenes, characters, and motions. Given user-provided inputs, the agent controls visual proxies to generate real-time combat rollouts that follow the specified scene structure and character motions. The paired visualizations show how character poses and spatial arrangements in the proxies are reflected in the generated frames, while reference images specify the desired appearance. These examples illustrate the model’s ability to accommodate new combinations of environments, character appearances, and motion controls without additional training. Diverse training data and character-aware adaptive masking support visual consistency throughout the rollouts.

    Furthermore, Fig. 5(b) illustrates how Wizard’s agentic framework maintains and updates game states and enforces combat rules. We showcase a core rule: when either character’s health reaches zero, the controller resolves the character’s death, ends combat, and displays the outcome. The framework also allows additional gameplay rules to be flexibly incorporated.

    5.3 Open-ended Creative Gameplay

    Wizard’s generalization capabilities enable diverse, open-ended gameplay, giving players control over both characters and their surroundings. As shown in Fig. 6(a), players can transform characters during gameplay by providing a reference image of the desired appearance. This allows character appearance to become an interactive part of the gameplay experience rather than a fixed initial choice.

    Fig. 6(b) demonstrates scene manipulation, including inverting the environment and introducing new scene elements through agent-controlled visual proxies. These examples extend user control from character animation to the geometry and layout of the game world. Character transformation and scene manipulation can also be combined within a single gameplay scenario, as illustrated in Fig. 6(c). Together, these capabilities allow players to create scenarios by composing character and environment changes, extending the range of experiences supported by the same underlying framework.

    6 Conclusions and Discussions

    In this paper, we introduce Wizard, the first agentic game world model to enable fine-grained control of characters and scenes through articulated skeletons and geometry maps, respectively, while maintaining mechanics-consistent, real-time interaction. Trained on our constructed diverse dataset111 WildWorld is used under its non-commercial research license; no WildWorld-derived data is redistributed. Elden Ring footage was recorded by the authors and is used solely for research. , Wizard demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to unseen characters, scenes, and motions, enabling players to create and manipulate customized game worlds.

    However, Wizard still has some limitations. First, its reliance on a motion library makes it difficult to find compatible motions for characters with uncommon body structures. Second, consistency between the scene proxies and the generated video may decline over longer rollouts. Future work will focus on supporting more flexible, realistic character motions that better reflect actual gameplay and maintaining consistent scene appearance over long rollouts. These improvements will bring agentic video generation closer to fully playable, closed-loop game worlds with greater player freedom and more precise, nuanced control.

    Acknowledgements

    We would like to express our sincere gratitude to Ruidong Wang and Murphy Zhao for their invaluable support throughout this project.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 格斗游戏不能只画得像：Fight World Model 用可执行引擎算胜负，再把结果编译成「交互代理」喂给渲染 ｜ Fight World Model: Customizable Combat through Visual Interaction Proxies
item.description:
一句话：受击反应与血量必须跟规则一致；把规则执行与视频渲染分开，代理里对齐动作/技能窗口与血量。

要点：

  • 问题很具体：视频世界模型能生成「看着像」的战斗，但受击反应与血量更新常常和游戏规则对不上——可玩的战斗必须是状态一致、规则可执行、机制可扩展的
  • FWM 把规则驱动的战斗执行与视频渲染分开：一个可执行引擎维护状态并判定交互，再由确定性编译器把这些结果与尝试的动作编码成空间、时间都对齐的「交互代理」
  • 代理按角色身份与时间对齐三类线索：动作与技能窗口、短暂受击反应、持续血量；三类线索可以分别控制，用来渲染不同的交互结果

为什么值得看：这是「AI 原生引擎」里最难也最该做的一块：判定逻辑必须是确定性的代码，不是采样出来的像素。FWM 的「交互代理」等于给渲染层的接口契约——引擎只需输出少量结构化线索，生成器负责表现。

中文摘要：可玩、可编程的游戏世界必须维持持久状态、执行规则并支持可扩展玩法。现有视频世界模型能生成像样的战斗画面，却很难让受击反应与血量更新和游戏规则保持一致。Fight World Model（FWM）把规则驱动的战斗执行与视频渲染分开：一个可执行引擎维护状态、判定交互结果，再由确定性编译器把这些结果连同尝试动作编码成一个在空间与时间上都对齐的「交互代理」。该代理按角色身份与时间对齐三类线索——动作与技能窗口、短暂受击反应、持续血量——并且这三类线索可以分别控制，从而渲染出不同的交互结果。这让「判定」回到确定性代码，「表现」交给生成模型。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-29

本期推送：2026-10-31

Fight World Model: Customizable Combat through Visual Interaction Proxies

Abstract

A playable, programmable game world must maintain persistent state, enforce executable rules, and support extensible gameplay mechanics. Existing video world models can generate plausible combat, yet struggle to keep hit reactions and health updates consistent with game rules. We introduce Fight World Model (FWM), which separates rule-governed combat execution from video rendering. An executable engine maintains state and resolves interactions. A deterministic compiler encodes these outcomes and attempted actions in a spatially and temporally aligned interaction proxy. The proxy aligns action and skill windows, brief hit reactions, and persistent health by fighter identity and timing. These cues can be controlled separately to render interactions under modified rules. Identity-bound references preserve character appearance across side switches. We train FWM on FightWorld Corpus, spanning 52 skill effects, 187 character-appearance variants, and 15 arenas. Without retraining the renderer, FWM supports damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, lifesteal, and multi-stage skill mechanisms beyond the native game. It also allows character and arena customization. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FWM, which outperforms existing game world models in action fidelity, hit reactions, health-state consistency, and character appearance preservation. Our project is available at fight-world-model.github.io.

1 Introduction

Interactive world models aim to simulate how environments evolve under user actions [10, 2, 27, 47, 46]. Recent video world models learn from gameplay recordings to generate playable sequences from controller or text inputs [33, 7, 43, 39, 30, 15]. Customizing such worlds requires changing both gameplay rules and visual appearances. In multi-fighter combat, the same attack may cause different health loss under different rules. A protected fighter may react to a hit without losing health, while lifesteal may restore the attacker’s health. When only character or arena appearance changes, the specified interactions should remain the same. As illustrated in Fight World Model: Customizable Combat through Visual Interaction Proxies, a customizable system must allow interaction outcomes to follow edited rules while preserving those interactions across appearance changes.

These requirements are difficult to meet when state transitions are inferred within the video generator [33, 7, 39, 15, 5, 37]. The model learns how actions relate to reactions and state changes from recorded gameplay. StatePlay further predicts game-state variables, such as health, alongside video frames [21], but predicting state does not itself provide an editable rule for updating it. Multi-entity action binding, identity-aware instructions, and NPC planning extend control over characters [51, 28, 8, 37, 36]. They do not by themselves determine how interaction outcomes should change under a new rule configuration. When rules change, a generator may retain familiar action–consequence associations from training and deviate from the externally specified outcomes.

Code-driven world models offer a way to execute world-state transitions outside the video generator and render the resulting spatial proxies [6, 16, 44, 42]. Correct state execution alone, however, does not ensure that the generated interaction follows those results. The renderer must identify the acting and affected fighters, depict each event at the intended time, and preserve the resulting state across subsequent exchanges. Spatial layouts alone do not specify action windows, hit reactions, or persistent health changes. Text and state tokens can carry these quantities, but the renderer must map them to the appropriate body regions, heads-up display (HUD) elements, and video frames. Appearance customization adds a related difficulty: actions and consequences must remain associated with the intended fighters as their appearances change or they exchange positions. The interface must therefore convey attempted actions, events, and persistent state with consistent identity and timing.

We introduce Fight World Model (FWM), a customizable world-model framework that connects executable combat rules to video generation through a visual interaction proxy. As shown in Fig.2, an executable engine resolves interactions and maintains state. A deterministic compiler rasterizes fighter states, action and skill windows, and transient hit-reaction cues onto a shared canvas and timeline. Reactions and health updates are encoded separately, allowing a hit to trigger a visible response without necessarily reducing health. Rule edits change the executed records and the resulting proxy, while the proxy format and renderer remain unchanged. Character and arena references specify appearance, with identity binding associating character references with the intended fighters across side switches. This design lets the same trained renderer depict interactions under different rules and visual appearances.

We instantiate and evaluate FWM in a fixed-view two-fighter combat setting. FightWorld Corpus pairs gameplay videos with interaction proxies across 52 skill effects, 187 character-appearance variants, and 15 arenas. FWM outperforms adapted game world models in action fidelity, hit reactions, persistent health accuracy, and character appearance preservation. Under matched executed records, reference binding, and training budgets, the interaction proxy also achieves higher joint fidelity than spatial proxies augmented with text or state tokens. Without retraining the renderer, FWM supports damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, lifesteal, and multi-stage skill mechanisms beyond native Street Fighter II/III. Appearance and side-switch evaluations test whether specified interactions and reference-to-entity associations are preserved under visual changes. We make the following contributions:

  • •

    We present FWM, a customizable combat world-model system that supports editable interaction rules and character or arena appearances without retraining the renderer.

  • •

    We design a visual interaction proxy that separately encodes action windows, hit reactions, and persistent health with consistent identity and timing. Identity binding connects appearance references to the fighters participating in these interactions.

  • •

    We construct FightWorld Corpus and evaluate the system through comparisons with existing methods, controlled encoding studies, rule interventions, and appearance customization.

    • 2 Related Work

    Game World Models. Action-conditioned video world models predict future frames from user inputs [2, 33, 1]. Recent systems extend this approach toward real-time streaming, longer horizons, and broader environments [7, 43, 48, 11, 39, 30, 9, 5]. Beyond navigation and player-centric interaction, multi-entity control introduces the need to associate each input with the intended character. Per-player keyboard streams can be paired with character references [15], while language conditions, persistent subject tokens, and synchronized inputs support multiple subjects or players [51, 28, 31]. Compact state representations also support NPC planning [8]. ReactiveGWM v1 separates player keyboard control from NPC strategy conditioning [37], and ReactiveGWM v2 uses identity handles to direct action and rule text to either fighter [36]. StatePlay additionally predicts health and skill meters alongside video through a dedicated state branch [21]. These methods improve action specification, entity control, and state prediction, but interaction outcomes remain largely governed by learned video dynamics. We focus on rendered reactions and persistent state under externally edited rules.

    World State and Visual Proxies. Spatial and trajectory conditioning provides explicit control over object placement and motion in video generation [45, 35, 25, 38]. Recent world models separate state execution or maintenance from video rendering [6, 16, 44, 42, 3]. MASS maintains a learned authoritative state shared across players [3], while Magpie translates white-box engine frames into generated video [44]. Oneira represents geometry and coarse interaction states through colored 3D boxes [42]. Code World Model compiles depth, semantic-ID, and instance maps from executable code [6], and Programmable World Model projects 3D boxes into identity, semantic-category, and motion-direction maps [16]. These methods establish explicit interfaces between world state and visual generation. Our focus is on the interaction information needed when edited rules change the relationship between attempted actions, hit reactions, and persistent health.

    Reference-Guided Video Generation. Reference-guided video generators condition diffusion models on reference images to preserve subject appearance across frames [23, 17, 49, 40, 13]. Multi-subject methods use spatial masks, semantic alignment from vision-language models, or binding slots to distinguish appearances across entities [20, 50, 41]. Character animation and motion-transfer methods drive reference subjects through explicit pose sequences [14] or in-context spatiotemporal tokens aligned with the output video [26, 41]. In our setting, appearance references must remain associated with the fighters performing each action and receiving each consequence, including through side switches. We study this association jointly with rule-controlled interaction outcomes.

    3 Method

    FWM supports rule and appearance customization by coupling executable state updates with conditional video generation. As shown in Fig.2, an engine executes the active rules, and a deterministic compiler converts the resulting states and events into a visual interaction proxy. Rule edits change the executed interaction and proxy, while appearance edits retain the proxy and change the references. Both use the same trained renderer.

    3.1 Rule Execution and Customization

    Let Sₖ be the executable state at engine update k, uₖ the available action inputs, and R the rule configuration. The engine computes

    (Sₖ₊₁,eₖ₊₁)=F_R(Sₖ,uₖ),

    		(1)

    where eₖ₊₁ contains the events produced together with the updated state Sₖ₊₁. The engine computes entity motion, resolves hit events, and applies the configured state updates. Sₖ includes persistent entity attributes and the counters or timers needed to execute the rules. The configuration R can be edited in code [6, 16].

    We reserve t for output video frames. Engine states and event records are aligned to this frame timeline before compilation. Let S̄ₜ denote the aligned state and sₜ=P(S̄ₜ) its visible projection. From the aligned event history, we form active records Eₜ that specify entity identities, onsets, and durations for action windows and reaction events. An event onset is paired with the state update it produces. The compiler then generates each proxy frame as πₜ=D(sₜ,Eₜ).

    A rule edit replaces R with R^′ and reruns the engine from the same initial state and submitted action sequence. Entity trajectories, hit times, and rule-dependent state are recomputed under R^′. Multi-stage skill mechanisms are expressed through rules that schedule displacement, impacts, and status windows. The resulting records are compiled and rendered without changing the renderer parameters. For damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, and lifesteal, the appearance references and text conditions also remain fixed. Changes in executed outcomes reach the renderer only through the recomputed proxy.

    An appearance edit changes the character or arena references while keeping the executed records and proxy fixed. Character references retain their target entity identities. Rule and appearance edits can also be combined by rendering recomputed records with new appearance conditions. For successive action intervals, the engine carries its state forward, while visual context supports continuity between generated segments.

    3.2 Interaction Proxy

    The proxy separates attempted actions, transient reactions, and persistent state because editable rules can change their relationship. These signals share entity identities and frame indices, allowing their values and durations to vary without changing the conditioning format. We describe the concrete combat encoding used in our experiments below.

    For this instantiation, the visible state at video frame t is

    sₜ={(i,bₜⁱ,fₜⁱ,qₜⁱ,aₜⁱ,hₜⁱ)}ᵢ₌₁²,

    		(2)
