    where i is a persistent fighter identity, and b, f, q, a, and h denote its bounding box, facing direction, stance, coarse action label, and health. Each fighter’s box and HUD health bar share an identity color. Facing and stance marks encode orientation and posture, and a separate band encodes the coarse action label, including an unknown value for unannotated actions.

    Action and Skill Windows. For the fighter with logged inputs, six attack classes combine punches and kicks with light, medium, and heavy strengths. Horizontal stripes encode punches and vertical stripes encode kicks, with coverage indicating strength. The marks remain active during the command window and supplement the coarse labels available for both fighters. They encode attempted actions, with hit outcomes specified separately. At inference, the engine can assign command windows to either fighter through its persistent identity.

    A magenta block in front of the caster follows its position and facing direction to mark a skill’s casting window. Text describes the effect’s type and appearance, so the corpus’s 52 visual skill effects share the same casting marker.

    Reactions and Persistent State. Reaction onset is marked by briefly inverting the affected fighter’s box fill and health-bar color. Bar length independently encodes health. This supports a protected hit with a reaction cue but no health decrease, or lifesteal with an additional update to the attacker’s health. Identity colors associate each reaction and state update with the affected fighter across side switches.

    The same compiler processes video-derived annotations during training and engine-generated records at inference. Training reaction onsets are inferred from observed health decreases, while the engine specifies reaction events and health under the edited rules. The shared format therefore permits rule-dependent cue combinations beyond those implied by the training annotations. Rule-intervention experiments test whether the trained renderer realizes these combinations. Broad command stripes and four-frame inversions are designed to retain cues through spatial and temporal compression by the video variational autoencoder (VAE) [18, 19]. Detailed motion, textures, and effect appearance are supplied by the renderer.

    3.3 Video Rendering and Identity Binding

    We condition a pretrained video diffusion transformer on the proxy and appearance inputs. Video, reference, and proxy inputs share a VAE and patch embedding. Their tokens are concatenated in video–reference–proxy order, with learned channel-wise gates on the reference and proxy streams. The initial video context, proxy, and references remain clean, while future video latents are denoised. Text descriptions are encoded by the text encoder and supplied through cross-attention. Only video tokens are decoded.

    Let xⁱⁿⁱᵗ=x₀ be the initial context frame and T the number of future video frames. The renderer samples

    x̂_1:T∼p_θ( ·|xⁱⁿⁱᵗ,π_0:T,r,c),

    		(3)

    where r contains the available character or arena references and the target identity associated with each character reference. The text condition c describes appearance and skill-effect type. The proxy supplies executed interaction states and event schedules.

    Proxy tokens share spatiotemporal rotary positions with the corresponding video tokens [32]. Reference tokens use positions outside the video grid, distinguishing appearance conditions from video-aligned interaction cues.

    As illustrated in Fig.2, shared identity embeddings bind character references to persistent entity identities. For each training sample, we assign the fighters distinct slots sampled without replacement from a learned codebook. Each fighter’s slot embedding is added to its corresponding tokens in the first video latent and throughout the proxy sequence, weighted by soft bounding-box coverage. The same embedding is added to all tokens of that fighter’s reference. Random slot assignment discourages a fixed mapping between codebook entries and appearances. At inference, the target identity attached to a character reference selects its slot embedding. Arena references do not use an entity slot. A training sample for character appearance editing contains a source initial image, a reference crop, and an edited target video. The source image establishes the scene and entity locations, while the reference specifies the target appearance in the continuation.

    3.4 Training

    We optimize the diffusion transformer, conditioning gates, and identity codebook with flow matching [22, 24]. The objective in Eq.5 supervises only future video latents, while the VAE and text encoder remain frozen. We apply condition dropout [12] to proxy, reference, and text inputs. For reference-conditioned samples, appearance-description dropout encourages reliance on the reference image.

    3.5 FightWorld Corpus

    We construct FightWorld Corpus by pairing Street Fighter II [4] gameplay videos with interaction proxies and optional appearance references. A frozen video editor augments native recordings with edits to skill effects, character appearances, and arenas, yielding 112,618 training samples. As summarized in Fig.3, the corpus spans 52 skill effects, 187 character-appearance variants, and 15 arenas.

    Character and arena edits vary visual appearance while retaining the source interaction. We reuse source state annotations only after checking consistency in fighter trajectories, event timing, and health. Each accepted video is paired with a character crop or an arena reference, as illustrated for scene edits in Fig.4.

    Skill edits change the visual effect associated with a casting event and may also alter the visible interaction. We therefore extract state and event annotations from both native and skill-edited videos, retaining only clips that pass quality screening.

    Native and edited videos share the same training format, with interaction proxies, text descriptions, and optional character or arena references as conditions. We use these samples to train a shared renderer across skill effects and appearances.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate appearance control, interaction fidelity, and rule customization. We compare FWM with adapted game world models and conduct controlled studies to examine the contributions of interaction encoding and identity binding.

    4.1 Evaluation Setup

    Implementation. We evaluate FWM on two-fighter interactions in the fixed 2D view of Street Fighter II [4]. Our renderer uses Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [34] as its backbone and is trained on FightWorld Corpus.

    Evaluation Protocol. For recorded interactions, held-out video annotations specify the target interactions. For rule interventions, we fix the initial state and submitted actions, then rerun the engine under each rule configuration to compute trajectories, hit events, and state updates. FWM’s reference images and text condition c remain unchanged for damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, and lifesteal. Appearance evaluations change the references while retaining the executed interaction. Each controlled encoding comparison supplies identical interaction records to all variants.

    Action and Reaction Metrics. Move Accuracy (MoveAcc) measures agreement between fighter motion and directional commands. Attack Accuracy (AttackAcc) is the fraction of detected punch or kick events supported by the corresponding input commands within their temporal windows. Skill Accuracy (SkillAcc) requires the correct skill class and an onset within the command-relative evaluation window. Reaction measures the fraction of expected hit responses visibly performed by the designated fighter. Qwen judges these responses from body motion in nearby frames, with the HUD excluded.

    Health and Persistence. Health MAE measures the mean absolute error between generated and target HUD health, normalized by maximum health and reported in percentage points. The joint health check requires correct updates for both fighters and persistence of the resulting health values between events.

    Joint Interaction Fidelity. Joint interaction fidelity (J) treats an attempt as successful only if all applicable action, entity, timing, reaction, and health checks pass. We average attempt-level results within each episode and give episodes equal weight. For rule interventions, Jᵣᵤₗₑ requires the applicable reaction and health checks to pass together.

    Appearance and Entity Assignment. Adherence uses a VLM to judge whether the requested appearance is applied to the designated character or arena. The judge receives the target reference and a source-frame identity guide. DINO measures cosine similarity between reference and generated features for characters and arenas separately. Both metrics exclude the fixed initial context.

    Baselines. We compare FWM with H3-WORLD [5], ReactiveGWM v1 [37], and ReactiveGWM v2 [36]. We adapt all three methods to FightWorld Corpus and its 52 skill effects. For skill control, we add a dedicated trigger to v1 and v2 and specify activation in H3-WORLD’s interval action text. The +Ref variants use our reference-conditioning branch for appearance editing.

    4.2 Character and Scene Customization

    As illustrated in Fig.5, FWM renders the same prescribed interaction with different character and arena references. We retain the executed records and proxy while changing appearance, testing whether the specified actions and consequences are preserved.

    Identity Association across Side Switches. We further test whether character references remain associated with their intended fighters across side switches. This requires preserving identity independently of the fighters’ screen positions. The variants in Table1 share reference inputs and training budgets, differing only in whether identity binding is enabled. Binding improves character adherence and DINO similarity, with an adherence gain of approximately 45 percentage points on side-switch clips.

    4.3 Control Representation Comparisons

    From Commands to Executed Outcomes. Adding rule text to action commands improves joint fidelity, but the generated interactions remain inconsistent. Spatial Proxy Only accurately controls movement while showing low joint fidelity in Table2. These conditions leave the renderer to infer hit events and health updates. The results motivate supplying executed outcomes alongside attempted actions.

    Holding Executed Information Fixed. To isolate the effect of encoding, we compare Spatial Proxy + Text, Spatial Proxy + State Tokens, and FWM under identical executed interaction records. The records specify fighter identities, action classes, affected fighters, event onsets and durations, and frame-wise health trajectories. All variants share geometry, initial context, reference binding, backbone initialization, and training budgets.

    Effect of Interaction Encoding. With identical executed information, FWM improves joint fidelity by approximately 22 percentage points over Spatial Proxy + Text, the stronger symbolic baseline in Table2. State Tokens have lower average health error than Text but poorer joint fidelity, showing that average health accuracy does not fully capture interaction correctness.

    Text misassigns damage to the attacker or misses the recipient’s health update in Fig.6. State Tokens track health more closely on average but lag at impact onset and show local limb blur during contact. Both baselines supply events and health as symbolic records that must be associated with body regions, HUD bars, and video frames. FWM places these cues in the corresponding proxy regions and frames.

    4.4 Comparison with Existing Methods

    Action Control and State Consistency. ReactiveGWM v1 [37] achieves higher player movement and attack precision than H3-WORLD [5] in Table3. It uses keyboard inputs for the player and coarser strategy text for the NPC. ReactiveGWM v2 [36] directs action instructions to either fighter, but still infers hit outcomes and health updates within video generation. The baselines miss actions and reactions in Fig.7, and v2 shows spurious health recovery.

    Multi-Phase Skills. The baselines struggle to synchronize skill effects with their consequences. In Fig.8, ReactiveGWM v1 and v2 deduct health before projectile impact, while H3-WORLD shows insufficient health loss after contact. ReactiveGWM v2 also renders a malformed projectile effect.

    Appearance and Interaction Fidelity. Adding appearance references improves v2’s movement and skill accuracy by approximately 22 and 18 percentage points, respectively. The +Ref baselines achieve high character adherence in Table3, yet their hit reactions and health updates remain inconsistent. Garment blur and identity drift during rapid contact and side switches further indicate that overall adherence does not guarantee stable visual identity throughout an interaction.

    Executed Outcomes as Visual Conditions. FWM improves action accuracy, hit reactions, health consistency, and character adherence over the adapted baselines in Table3. Its Reaction score exceeds the best +Ref result by approximately 43 percentage points. The rollouts in Figs.7 and 8 follow the prescribed action and reaction timing while preserving the resulting health across subsequent frames.

    4.5 Rule Interventions

    Rule and Skill Customization. We test whether generated interactions follow edited rules and newly composed skill mechanisms without retraining the renderer. For attack-level interventions, the initial state, submitted actions, appearance references, and FWM text condition c remain fixed. The engine recomputes motion, hit timing, and state updates, and the changed outcomes reach FWM only through the proxy. FWM maintains high joint fidelity across the revised rules in Table5, while symbolic encodings degrade particularly under immunity and lifesteal.

    Damage Magnitude. Damage scaling changes the health loss associated with a valid hit. FWM tracks the resulting health changes under both reduced and amplified damage, with low health error and high joint fidelity.

    Limited-Hit Immunity. Limited-hit immunity blocks health loss for a specified number of hits while retaining reaction events. FWM renders the corresponding body responses with unchanged health during protection, then shows the prescribed health loss once protection is exhausted.

    Lifesteal. Under lifesteal, a hit reduces the recipient’s health and restores the attacker’s health. FWM renders these coupled updates for the correct fighters and preserves the resulting health values after the hit.

    Multi-Stage Skill Mechanisms. We extend the rule interventions to skills that combine displacement, repeated impacts, and state constraints. In Fig.9, Earthshatter couples knockback with staged health loss and lingering ground damage. Other mechanisms cover per-projectile hits, staggered area impacts, action locks, and spatial confinement. FWM renders these combinations through the shared proxy without additional skill-specific conditioning channels or renderer retraining.

    4.6 Proxy Ablations

    Attempted Actions and Their Consequences. We retrain each variant with one cue family removed, keeping the training setting unchanged. In Table4, removing command marks lowers attack precision while leaving Reaction largely unchanged. Removing the skill trigger reduces skill accuracy by approximately 20 percentage points. These results support encoding attempted actions separately from their consequences.

    Events and Persistent State. Removing damage-event cues lowers the Reaction score while health error remains low. Removing health bars largely preserves reactions but degrades health accuracy and joint fidelity. These complementary effects support separate conditioning for transient reactions and persistent state. More details, comparisons and visualizations are provided in the appendix.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented Fight World Model (FWM), which connects executable gameplay rules to video generation through a visual interaction proxy. Experiments in a combat setting demonstrate improved interaction and appearance fidelity over adapted game world models. FWM supports edited rules and multi-stage skill mechanisms without retraining the renderer. Character and arena customization preserves the prescribed interactions, with identity binding maintaining character associations across side switches.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Implementation Details

    A.1 Engine and Timeline

    The combat engine exposes damage magnitude, the number of protected hits, and the lifesteal rate as editable parameters. Its state retains protection counts and active skill windows across action intervals.

    Engine updates indexed by k are mapped to output video frames t before proxy compilation. State samples and event windows use the same frame mapping, so an event onset is paired with its resulting state update. Frame index zero denotes the initial context, and x̂_1:T denotes the continuation. The engine carries executable state between action intervals, while visual context conditions the next generated segment.

    A.2 Proxy Encoding Parameters

    For light, medium, and heavy attacks, stripes cover the top one third, top two thirds, or full box interior below the coarse action band. They remain active over the command window. The skill-trigger block follows the caster for 30 output video frames, and reaction color inversions last four frames. Both durations are defined at the output video rate and resampled together with the state and event records.

    A.3 Renderer and Binding Parameters

    We initialize the renderer from the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B checkpoint [34]. For F video latent frames, character references use temporal coordinate τ_ref=F+2, and arena references use τ_ref=F+3. Their spatial coordinates lie outside the video grid. Video and proxy inputs use matched temporal indices and the same resize and center-crop transform.

    The identity codebook contains six learned slots. Each embedding is normalized to unit root-mean-square magnitude and scaled by 0.25 at all three injection sites. For the first video latent and proxy sequence, soft bounding-box coverage weights the corresponding entity’s embedding, with weights normalized where boxes overlap. The target entity’s embedding is added to all character-reference tokens without a spatial box mask. Persistent entity IDs in the proxy identify the reference targets. Arena references receive no identity embedding.

    A.4 Training Objective and Configuration

    Let z denote clean video latents and ε∼ℕ(0,I). We construct noisy latents with flow matching [22, 24]:

    z_τ=(1-τ)z+τε, τ=5v/1+4v, v∼U(0,1).

    		(4)

    Here τ is flow time, distinct from engine index k and video-frame index t. The first latent is replaced with the clean source-image encoding at noise level zero. Future video tokens receive noise level τ. With conditions ℂ=(xⁱⁿⁱᵗ,π,r,c), the loss is

    L=𝔼 [(1)/(|Ω₊|)∑_j∈Ω₊∥v_θ(z_τ,τ;ℂ)ⱼ-(ε-z)ⱼ∥₂²],

    		(5)

    where Ω₊ contains future video latent elements. Initial-context, proxy, and reference tokens are excluded from the loss. At inference, future video latents start from noise.

    We use AdamW with a constant learning rate of 8×10⁻⁵, weight decay of 0.01, and no learning-rate warmup. Training uses bfloat16 autocast with fp32 master parameters and an effective batch size of 128 on 128 H200 GPUs. The budget is 35 epochs, corresponding to 30,765 optimizer steps.

    Each clip contains 89 frames at 928×704 resolution. Dropout probabilities for proxy, reference, text, and appearance descriptions are 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, and 0.2, respectively. The controlled encoding variants in Table2 share initialization, training data, and optimization budget. Only the representation and its required input layers differ.

    Appendix B Data Construction Details

    B.1 Video Editing and Quality Control

    A frozen MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA editor produces appearance and skill-effect variants using edit-specific prompts. Screening checks the requested content, temporal coherence, and interaction consistency.

    Appearance-only variants are checked against the source video for fighter trajectories, event timing, and health traces. Only edits that pass these checks reuse the source state annotations. Skill-effect edits are annotated from the edited videos.

    B.2 State and Event Annotation

    Gemma-4-31B-it localizes fighters at regularly spaced keyframes to initialize SAM 2 video propagation [29]. Semantic descriptions help distinguish fighters from similar background characters. At each keyframe, the tracker checks the two identity assignments against appearance and trajectory continuity, retaining or swapping them to correct drift and bridge short gaps. Bounding boxes specify spatial state. Facing direction follows relative fighter positions and retains its previous value while the boxes overlap.

    Health traces are estimated from HUD bar lengths and cleaned within each round. Nearby decreases are merged into damage events, each recording the affected fighter and event time. Gemma also supplies coarse action and stance labels at selected frames, including frames near damage events. Unannotated action frames use the unknown label. Logged inputs provide fine attack commands and scheduled skill triggers for the controlled fighter. The compiler converts these annotations into interaction proxies.

    Appendix C Evaluation Protocols

    C.1 Controlled Interactions

    Recorded-interaction tests use held-out video annotations, with source episodes separated between training and testing. Rule interventions rerun the engine from the same initial state and submitted actions under each configuration, recomputing motion trajectories, hit events, and state outcomes. These records define the target interactions for the compared encodings. In FWM’s damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, and lifesteal tests, reference images and text condition c remain fixed. Changed outcomes reach FWM only through the proxy.

    Appearance interventions retain the executed records and proxy while changing the references. Evaluation cases include no-hit attempts, repeated attacks, overlap, and side switches.

    Complete-Information Encodings. The encodings use matched event-free intervals, sampled values, and temporal indices, with shared resolution and sampling settings. Each uses the input layers required by its representation, and text inputs are checked for truncation.

    C.2 Action Recognition and Timing

    Movement. MoveAcc compares tracked fighter motion with directional commands over valid command windows and averages across the four movement keys. Jump positives require an actual airborne jump. Grounded hurt recovery is excluded from jump positives.

    Attack and Skill Recognition. We train ResNet-18-based temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) for attack and skill recognition. Attack detections are grouped into temporally contiguous events. AttackAcc measures the fraction of detected punch or kick events supported by the corresponding input command within its temporal window.

    The skill classifier uses a 256-channel temporal trunk with dilation rates 1, 2, 4, and 8. It predicts onset and class, with a no-skill outcome in the onset prediction. Class logits are pooled over the predicted effect interval. SkillAcc requires the correct class and onset within the command-relative window. The same timing rule applies across methods and accommodates skill startup, release, and recovery.

    An attempted attack may hit or miss, so AttackAcc and Reaction assess command-grounded action execution and received-hit consequences, respectively.

    C.3 Reaction and Health

    Visible Reactions. Reaction measures the fraction of expected hit responses visibly performed by the designated fighter within the evaluation window. Qwen judges body motion in surrounding gameplay frames, using a source-frame identity guide and excluding the HUD.

    Brief reactions can resemble ordinary motion across appearances and effects, so we judge them using local temporal context around expected events. Computing reaction precision would additionally require locating every visible received-hit onset throughout the generated video, a dense detection task that is difficult for current VLMs.

    Health and Persistence. Let V contain readable fighter-frame observations and H denote maximum health. Health MAE is the normalized mean absolute error, expressed in percentage points:

    MAEₕ=(100)/(|V|H)∑_(i,t)∈V|ĥₜⁱ-hₜⁱ|.

    		(6)

    Observed and target health values are obtained from HUD bar lengths. The joint health check uses a one-pixel tolerance and requires correct updates for both fighters, with the resulting values preserved between events. This includes unchanged health under immunity and the attacker’s restored health under lifesteal.

    C.4 Joint Interaction Fidelity

    An attempt succeeds only when all applicable action, entity, timing, reaction, and health checks pass. The score J averages attempts within each episode and weights episodes equally:

    q_ℓe=∏_k∈K_ℓec_ℓe,k, J=1/L∑_ℓ=1^L(1)/(N_ℓ)∑ₑ₌₁^N_ℓq_ℓe.

    		(7)

    Here L counts episodes, N_ℓ counts attempts in episode ℓ, and c_ℓe,k are binary checks indexed by K_ℓe. The applicable set follows the registered interaction. Its checks cover command-grounded actions and timing, the identities of acting and affected fighters, visible body responses, and correct health updates with persistence. For rule interventions, Jᵣᵤₗₑ combines the required reaction and health checks. Both rates are expressed as percentages in the results.

    C.5 Appearance and Entity Assignment

    Adherence assesses appearance-edit success for the designated character or arena. A VLM judges sampled continuation frames using the target reference and a source-frame identity guide. Frame judgments are combined into a clip-level decision.

    DINO measures reference-to-generation feature cosine similarity separately for characters and arenas. Proxy boxes localize fighter crops, while fighter and HUD regions are suppressed for arena scoring. The fixed initial context is excluded from both appearance metrics.

    Appendix D Reference-Augmented Baselines

    We augment H3-WORLD [5], ReactiveGWM v1 [37], and ReactiveGWM v2 [36] with our reference-conditioning branch. Variants are evaluated on the same clips and frame indices as FWM, using explicit appearance references. The comparisons in Figs.12, 12, 14 and 14 show character drift or garment blur during rapid contact and side switches, together with missed (), premature (), or incomplete () health updates. FWM preserves appearance and the prescribed health updates more consistently in these examples.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：受击反应与血量必须跟规则一致；把规则执行与视频渲染分开，代理里对齐动作/技能窗口与血量。

要点：

  • 问题很具体：视频世界模型能生成「看着像」的战斗，但受击反应与血量更新常常和游戏规则对不上——可玩的战斗必须是状态一致、规则可执行、机制可扩展的
  • FWM 把规则驱动的战斗执行与视频渲染分开：一个可执行引擎维护状态并判定交互，再由确定性编译器把这些结果与尝试的动作编码成空间、时间都对齐的「交互代理」
  • 代理按角色身份与时间对齐三类线索：动作与技能窗口、短暂受击反应、持续血量；三类线索可以分别控制，用来渲染不同的交互结果

为什么值得看：这是「AI 原生引擎」里最难也最该做的一块：判定逻辑必须是确定性的代码，不是采样出来的像素。FWM 的「交互代理」等于给渲染层的接口契约——引擎只需输出少量结构化线索，生成器负责表现。

中文摘要：可玩、可编程的游戏世界必须维持持久状态、执行规则并支持可扩展玩法。现有视频世界模型能生成像样的战斗画面，却很难让受击反应与血量更新和游戏规则保持一致。Fight World Model（FWM）把规则驱动的战斗执行与视频渲染分开：一个可执行引擎维护状态、判定交互结果，再由确定性编译器把这些结果连同尝试动作编码成一个在空间与时间上都对齐的「交互代理」。该代理按角色身份与时间对齐三类线索——动作与技能窗口、短暂受击反应、持续血量——并且这三类线索可以分别控制，从而渲染出不同的交互结果。这让「判定」回到确定性代码，「表现」交给生成模型。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-29

本期推送：2026-10-31

Fight World Model: Customizable Combat through Visual Interaction Proxies

Abstract

A playable, programmable game world must maintain persistent state, enforce executable rules, and support extensible gameplay mechanics. Existing video world models can generate plausible combat, yet struggle to keep hit reactions and health updates consistent with game rules. We introduce Fight World Model (FWM), which separates rule-governed combat execution from video rendering. An executable engine maintains state and resolves interactions. A deterministic compiler encodes these outcomes and attempted actions in a spatially and temporally aligned interaction proxy. The proxy aligns action and skill windows, brief hit reactions, and persistent health by fighter identity and timing. These cues can be controlled separately to render interactions under modified rules. Identity-bound references preserve character appearance across side switches. We train FWM on FightWorld Corpus, spanning 52 skill effects, 187 character-appearance variants, and 15 arenas. Without retraining the renderer, FWM supports damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, lifesteal, and multi-stage skill mechanisms beyond the native game. It also allows character and arena customization. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of FWM, which outperforms existing game world models in action fidelity, hit reactions, health-state consistency, and character appearance preservation. Our project is available at fight-world-model.github.io.

1 Introduction

Interactive world models aim to simulate how environments evolve under user actions [10, 2, 27, 47, 46]. Recent video world models learn from gameplay recordings to generate playable sequences from controller or text inputs [33, 7, 43, 39, 30, 15]. Customizing such worlds requires changing both gameplay rules and visual appearances. In multi-fighter combat, the same attack may cause different health loss under different rules. A protected fighter may react to a hit without losing health, while lifesteal may restore the attacker’s health. When only character or arena appearance changes, the specified interactions should remain the same. As illustrated in Fight World Model: Customizable Combat through Visual Interaction Proxies, a customizable system must allow interaction outcomes to follow edited rules while preserving those interactions across appearance changes.

These requirements are difficult to meet when state transitions are inferred within the video generator [33, 7, 39, 15, 5, 37]. The model learns how actions relate to reactions and state changes from recorded gameplay. StatePlay further predicts game-state variables, such as health, alongside video frames [21], but predicting state does not itself provide an editable rule for updating it. Multi-entity action binding, identity-aware instructions, and NPC planning extend control over characters [51, 28, 8, 37, 36]. They do not by themselves determine how interaction outcomes should change under a new rule configuration. When rules change, a generator may retain familiar action–consequence associations from training and deviate from the externally specified outcomes.

Code-driven world models offer a way to execute world-state transitions outside the video generator and render the resulting spatial proxies [6, 16, 44, 42]. Correct state execution alone, however, does not ensure that the generated interaction follows those results. The renderer must identify the acting and affected fighters, depict each event at the intended time, and preserve the resulting state across subsequent exchanges. Spatial layouts alone do not specify action windows, hit reactions, or persistent health changes. Text and state tokens can carry these quantities, but the renderer must map them to the appropriate body regions, heads-up display (HUD) elements, and video frames. Appearance customization adds a related difficulty: actions and consequences must remain associated with the intended fighters as their appearances change or they exchange positions. The interface must therefore convey attempted actions, events, and persistent state with consistent identity and timing.

We introduce Fight World Model (FWM), a customizable world-model framework that connects executable combat rules to video generation through a visual interaction proxy. As shown in Fig.2, an executable engine resolves interactions and maintains state. A deterministic compiler rasterizes fighter states, action and skill windows, and transient hit-reaction cues onto a shared canvas and timeline. Reactions and health updates are encoded separately, allowing a hit to trigger a visible response without necessarily reducing health. Rule edits change the executed records and the resulting proxy, while the proxy format and renderer remain unchanged. Character and arena references specify appearance, with identity binding associating character references with the intended fighters across side switches. This design lets the same trained renderer depict interactions under different rules and visual appearances.

We instantiate and evaluate FWM in a fixed-view two-fighter combat setting. FightWorld Corpus pairs gameplay videos with interaction proxies across 52 skill effects, 187 character-appearance variants, and 15 arenas. FWM outperforms adapted game world models in action fidelity, hit reactions, persistent health accuracy, and character appearance preservation. Under matched executed records, reference binding, and training budgets, the interaction proxy also achieves higher joint fidelity than spatial proxies augmented with text or state tokens. Without retraining the renderer, FWM supports damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, lifesteal, and multi-stage skill mechanisms beyond native Street Fighter II/III. Appearance and side-switch evaluations test whether specified interactions and reference-to-entity associations are preserved under visual changes. We make the following contributions:

  • •

    We present FWM, a customizable combat world-model system that supports editable interaction rules and character or arena appearances without retraining the renderer.

  • •

    We design a visual interaction proxy that separately encodes action windows, hit reactions, and persistent health with consistent identity and timing. Identity binding connects appearance references to the fighters participating in these interactions.

  • •

    We construct FightWorld Corpus and evaluate the system through comparisons with existing methods, controlled encoding studies, rule interventions, and appearance customization.

    • 2 Related Work

    Game World Models. Action-conditioned video world models predict future frames from user inputs [2, 33, 1]. Recent systems extend this approach toward real-time streaming, longer horizons, and broader environments [7, 43, 48, 11, 39, 30, 9, 5]. Beyond navigation and player-centric interaction, multi-entity control introduces the need to associate each input with the intended character. Per-player keyboard streams can be paired with character references [15], while language conditions, persistent subject tokens, and synchronized inputs support multiple subjects or players [51, 28, 31]. Compact state representations also support NPC planning [8]. ReactiveGWM v1 separates player keyboard control from NPC strategy conditioning [37], and ReactiveGWM v2 uses identity handles to direct action and rule text to either fighter [36]. StatePlay additionally predicts health and skill meters alongside video through a dedicated state branch [21]. These methods improve action specification, entity control, and state prediction, but interaction outcomes remain largely governed by learned video dynamics. We focus on rendered reactions and persistent state under externally edited rules.

    World State and Visual Proxies. Spatial and trajectory conditioning provides explicit control over object placement and motion in video generation [45, 35, 25, 38]. Recent world models separate state execution or maintenance from video rendering [6, 16, 44, 42, 3]. MASS maintains a learned authoritative state shared across players [3], while Magpie translates white-box engine frames into generated video [44]. Oneira represents geometry and coarse interaction states through colored 3D boxes [42]. Code World Model compiles depth, semantic-ID, and instance maps from executable code [6], and Programmable World Model projects 3D boxes into identity, semantic-category, and motion-direction maps [16]. These methods establish explicit interfaces between world state and visual generation. Our focus is on the interaction information needed when edited rules change the relationship between attempted actions, hit reactions, and persistent health.

    Reference-Guided Video Generation. Reference-guided video generators condition diffusion models on reference images to preserve subject appearance across frames [23, 17, 49, 40, 13]. Multi-subject methods use spatial masks, semantic alignment from vision-language models, or binding slots to distinguish appearances across entities [20, 50, 41]. Character animation and motion-transfer methods drive reference subjects through explicit pose sequences [14] or in-context spatiotemporal tokens aligned with the output video [26, 41]. In our setting, appearance references must remain associated with the fighters performing each action and receiving each consequence, including through side switches. We study this association jointly with rule-controlled interaction outcomes.

    3 Method

    FWM supports rule and appearance customization by coupling executable state updates with conditional video generation. As shown in Fig.2, an engine executes the active rules, and a deterministic compiler converts the resulting states and events into a visual interaction proxy. Rule edits change the executed interaction and proxy, while appearance edits retain the proxy and change the references. Both use the same trained renderer.

    3.1 Rule Execution and Customization

    Let Sₖ be the executable state at engine update k, uₖ the available action inputs, and R the rule configuration. The engine computes

    (Sₖ₊₁,eₖ₊₁)=F_R(Sₖ,uₖ),

    		(1)

    where eₖ₊₁ contains the events produced together with the updated state Sₖ₊₁. The engine computes entity motion, resolves hit events, and applies the configured state updates. Sₖ includes persistent entity attributes and the counters or timers needed to execute the rules. The configuration R can be edited in code [6, 16].

    We reserve t for output video frames. Engine states and event records are aligned to this frame timeline before compilation. Let S̄ₜ denote the aligned state and sₜ=P(S̄ₜ) its visible projection. From the aligned event history, we form active records Eₜ that specify entity identities, onsets, and durations for action windows and reaction events. An event onset is paired with the state update it produces. The compiler then generates each proxy frame as πₜ=D(sₜ,Eₜ).

    A rule edit replaces R with R^′ and reruns the engine from the same initial state and submitted action sequence. Entity trajectories, hit times, and rule-dependent state are recomputed under R^′. Multi-stage skill mechanisms are expressed through rules that schedule displacement, impacts, and status windows. The resulting records are compiled and rendered without changing the renderer parameters. For damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, and lifesteal, the appearance references and text conditions also remain fixed. Changes in executed outcomes reach the renderer only through the recomputed proxy.

    An appearance edit changes the character or arena references while keeping the executed records and proxy fixed. Character references retain their target entity identities. Rule and appearance edits can also be combined by rendering recomputed records with new appearance conditions. For successive action intervals, the engine carries its state forward, while visual context supports continuity between generated segments.

    3.2 Interaction Proxy

    The proxy separates attempted actions, transient reactions, and persistent state because editable rules can change their relationship. These signals share entity identities and frame indices, allowing their values and durations to vary without changing the conditioning format. We describe the concrete combat encoding used in our experiments below.

    For this instantiation, the visible state at video frame t is

    sₜ={(i,bₜⁱ,fₜⁱ,qₜⁱ,aₜⁱ,hₜⁱ)}ᵢ₌₁²,

    		(2)

    where i is a persistent fighter identity, and b, f, q, a, and h denote its bounding box, facing direction, stance, coarse action label, and health. Each fighter’s box and HUD health bar share an identity color. Facing and stance marks encode orientation and posture, and a separate band encodes the coarse action label, including an unknown value for unannotated actions.

    Action and Skill Windows. For the fighter with logged inputs, six attack classes combine punches and kicks with light, medium, and heavy strengths. Horizontal stripes encode punches and vertical stripes encode kicks, with coverage indicating strength. The marks remain active during the command window and supplement the coarse labels available for both fighters. They encode attempted actions, with hit outcomes specified separately. At inference, the engine can assign command windows to either fighter through its persistent identity.

    A magenta block in front of the caster follows its position and facing direction to mark a skill’s casting window. Text describes the effect’s type and appearance, so the corpus’s 52 visual skill effects share the same casting marker.

    Reactions and Persistent State. Reaction onset is marked by briefly inverting the affected fighter’s box fill and health-bar color. Bar length independently encodes health. This supports a protected hit with a reaction cue but no health decrease, or lifesteal with an additional update to the attacker’s health. Identity colors associate each reaction and state update with the affected fighter across side switches.

    The same compiler processes video-derived annotations during training and engine-generated records at inference. Training reaction onsets are inferred from observed health decreases, while the engine specifies reaction events and health under the edited rules. The shared format therefore permits rule-dependent cue combinations beyond those implied by the training annotations. Rule-intervention experiments test whether the trained renderer realizes these combinations. Broad command stripes and four-frame inversions are designed to retain cues through spatial and temporal compression by the video variational autoencoder (VAE) [18, 19]. Detailed motion, textures, and effect appearance are supplied by the renderer.

    3.3 Video Rendering and Identity Binding

    We condition a pretrained video diffusion transformer on the proxy and appearance inputs. Video, reference, and proxy inputs share a VAE and patch embedding. Their tokens are concatenated in video–reference–proxy order, with learned channel-wise gates on the reference and proxy streams. The initial video context, proxy, and references remain clean, while future video latents are denoised. Text descriptions are encoded by the text encoder and supplied through cross-attention. Only video tokens are decoded.

    Let xⁱⁿⁱᵗ=x₀ be the initial context frame and T the number of future video frames. The renderer samples

    x̂_1:T∼p_θ( ·|xⁱⁿⁱᵗ,π_0:T,r,c),

    		(3)

    where r contains the available character or arena references and the target identity associated with each character reference. The text condition c describes appearance and skill-effect type. The proxy supplies executed interaction states and event schedules.

    Proxy tokens share spatiotemporal rotary positions with the corresponding video tokens [32]. Reference tokens use positions outside the video grid, distinguishing appearance conditions from video-aligned interaction cues.

    As illustrated in Fig.2, shared identity embeddings bind character references to persistent entity identities. For each training sample, we assign the fighters distinct slots sampled without replacement from a learned codebook. Each fighter’s slot embedding is added to its corresponding tokens in the first video latent and throughout the proxy sequence, weighted by soft bounding-box coverage. The same embedding is added to all tokens of that fighter’s reference. Random slot assignment discourages a fixed mapping between codebook entries and appearances. At inference, the target identity attached to a character reference selects its slot embedding. Arena references do not use an entity slot. A training sample for character appearance editing contains a source initial image, a reference crop, and an edited target video. The source image establishes the scene and entity locations, while the reference specifies the target appearance in the continuation.

    3.4 Training

    We optimize the diffusion transformer, conditioning gates, and identity codebook with flow matching [22, 24]. The objective in Eq.5 supervises only future video latents, while the VAE and text encoder remain frozen. We apply condition dropout [12] to proxy, reference, and text inputs. For reference-conditioned samples, appearance-description dropout encourages reliance on the reference image.

    3.5 FightWorld Corpus

    We construct FightWorld Corpus by pairing Street Fighter II [4] gameplay videos with interaction proxies and optional appearance references. A frozen video editor augments native recordings with edits to skill effects, character appearances, and arenas, yielding 112,618 training samples. As summarized in Fig.3, the corpus spans 52 skill effects, 187 character-appearance variants, and 15 arenas.

    Character and arena edits vary visual appearance while retaining the source interaction. We reuse source state annotations only after checking consistency in fighter trajectories, event timing, and health. Each accepted video is paired with a character crop or an arena reference, as illustrated for scene edits in Fig.4.

    Skill edits change the visual effect associated with a casting event and may also alter the visible interaction. We therefore extract state and event annotations from both native and skill-edited videos, retaining only clips that pass quality screening.

    Native and edited videos share the same training format, with interaction proxies, text descriptions, and optional character or arena references as conditions. We use these samples to train a shared renderer across skill effects and appearances.

    4 Experiments

    We evaluate appearance control, interaction fidelity, and rule customization. We compare FWM with adapted game world models and conduct controlled studies to examine the contributions of interaction encoding and identity binding.

    4.1 Evaluation Setup

    Implementation. We evaluate FWM on two-fighter interactions in the fixed 2D view of Street Fighter II [4]. Our renderer uses Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [34] as its backbone and is trained on FightWorld Corpus.

    Evaluation Protocol. For recorded interactions, held-out video annotations specify the target interactions. For rule interventions, we fix the initial state and submitted actions, then rerun the engine under each rule configuration to compute trajectories, hit events, and state updates. FWM’s reference images and text condition c remain unchanged for damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, and lifesteal. Appearance evaluations change the references while retaining the executed interaction. Each controlled encoding comparison supplies identical interaction records to all variants.

    Action and Reaction Metrics. Move Accuracy (MoveAcc) measures agreement between fighter motion and directional commands. Attack Accuracy (AttackAcc) is the fraction of detected punch or kick events supported by the corresponding input commands within their temporal windows. Skill Accuracy (SkillAcc) requires the correct skill class and an onset within the command-relative evaluation window. Reaction measures the fraction of expected hit responses visibly performed by the designated fighter. Qwen judges these responses from body motion in nearby frames, with the HUD excluded.

    Health and Persistence. Health MAE measures the mean absolute error between generated and target HUD health, normalized by maximum health and reported in percentage points. The joint health check requires correct updates for both fighters and persistence of the resulting health values between events.

    Joint Interaction Fidelity. Joint interaction fidelity (J) treats an attempt as successful only if all applicable action, entity, timing, reaction, and health checks pass. We average attempt-level results within each episode and give episodes equal weight. For rule interventions, Jᵣᵤₗₑ requires the applicable reaction and health checks to pass together.

    Appearance and Entity Assignment. Adherence uses a VLM to judge whether the requested appearance is applied to the designated character or arena. The judge receives the target reference and a source-frame identity guide. DINO measures cosine similarity between reference and generated features for characters and arenas separately. Both metrics exclude the fixed initial context.

    Baselines. We compare FWM with H3-WORLD [5], ReactiveGWM v1 [37], and ReactiveGWM v2 [36]. We adapt all three methods to FightWorld Corpus and its 52 skill effects. For skill control, we add a dedicated trigger to v1 and v2 and specify activation in H3-WORLD’s interval action text. The +Ref variants use our reference-conditioning branch for appearance editing.

    4.2 Character and Scene Customization

    As illustrated in Fig.5, FWM renders the same prescribed interaction with different character and arena references. We retain the executed records and proxy while changing appearance, testing whether the specified actions and consequences are preserved.

    Identity Association across Side Switches. We further test whether character references remain associated with their intended fighters across side switches. This requires preserving identity independently of the fighters’ screen positions. The variants in Table1 share reference inputs and training budgets, differing only in whether identity binding is enabled. Binding improves character adherence and DINO similarity, with an adherence gain of approximately 45 percentage points on side-switch clips.

    4.3 Control Representation Comparisons

    From Commands to Executed Outcomes. Adding rule text to action commands improves joint fidelity, but the generated interactions remain inconsistent. Spatial Proxy Only accurately controls movement while showing low joint fidelity in Table2. These conditions leave the renderer to infer hit events and health updates. The results motivate supplying executed outcomes alongside attempted actions.

    Holding Executed Information Fixed. To isolate the effect of encoding, we compare Spatial Proxy + Text, Spatial Proxy + State Tokens, and FWM under identical executed interaction records. The records specify fighter identities, action classes, affected fighters, event onsets and durations, and frame-wise health trajectories. All variants share geometry, initial context, reference binding, backbone initialization, and training budgets.

    Effect of Interaction Encoding. With identical executed information, FWM improves joint fidelity by approximately 22 percentage points over Spatial Proxy + Text, the stronger symbolic baseline in Table2. State Tokens have lower average health error than Text but poorer joint fidelity, showing that average health accuracy does not fully capture interaction correctness.

    Text misassigns damage to the attacker or misses the recipient’s health update in Fig.6. State Tokens track health more closely on average but lag at impact onset and show local limb blur during contact. Both baselines supply events and health as symbolic records that must be associated with body regions, HUD bars, and video frames. FWM places these cues in the corresponding proxy regions and frames.

    4.4 Comparison with Existing Methods

    Action Control and State Consistency. ReactiveGWM v1 [37] achieves higher player movement and attack precision than H3-WORLD [5] in Table3. It uses keyboard inputs for the player and coarser strategy text for the NPC. ReactiveGWM v2 [36] directs action instructions to either fighter, but still infers hit outcomes and health updates within video generation. The baselines miss actions and reactions in Fig.7, and v2 shows spurious health recovery.

    Multi-Phase Skills. The baselines struggle to synchronize skill effects with their consequences. In Fig.8, ReactiveGWM v1 and v2 deduct health before projectile impact, while H3-WORLD shows insufficient health loss after contact. ReactiveGWM v2 also renders a malformed projectile effect.

    Appearance and Interaction Fidelity. Adding appearance references improves v2’s movement and skill accuracy by approximately 22 and 18 percentage points, respectively. The +Ref baselines achieve high character adherence in Table3, yet their hit reactions and health updates remain inconsistent. Garment blur and identity drift during rapid contact and side switches further indicate that overall adherence does not guarantee stable visual identity throughout an interaction.

    Executed Outcomes as Visual Conditions. FWM improves action accuracy, hit reactions, health consistency, and character adherence over the adapted baselines in Table3. Its Reaction score exceeds the best +Ref result by approximately 43 percentage points. The rollouts in Figs.7 and 8 follow the prescribed action and reaction timing while preserving the resulting health across subsequent frames.

    4.5 Rule Interventions

    Rule and Skill Customization. We test whether generated interactions follow edited rules and newly composed skill mechanisms without retraining the renderer. For attack-level interventions, the initial state, submitted actions, appearance references, and FWM text condition c remain fixed. The engine recomputes motion, hit timing, and state updates, and the changed outcomes reach FWM only through the proxy. FWM maintains high joint fidelity across the revised rules in Table5, while symbolic encodings degrade particularly under immunity and lifesteal.

    Damage Magnitude. Damage scaling changes the health loss associated with a valid hit. FWM tracks the resulting health changes under both reduced and amplified damage, with low health error and high joint fidelity.

    Limited-Hit Immunity. Limited-hit immunity blocks health loss for a specified number of hits while retaining reaction events. FWM renders the corresponding body responses with unchanged health during protection, then shows the prescribed health loss once protection is exhausted.

    Lifesteal. Under lifesteal, a hit reduces the recipient’s health and restores the attacker’s health. FWM renders these coupled updates for the correct fighters and preserves the resulting health values after the hit.

    Multi-Stage Skill Mechanisms. We extend the rule interventions to skills that combine displacement, repeated impacts, and state constraints. In Fig.9, Earthshatter couples knockback with staged health loss and lingering ground damage. Other mechanisms cover per-projectile hits, staggered area impacts, action locks, and spatial confinement. FWM renders these combinations through the shared proxy without additional skill-specific conditioning channels or renderer retraining.

    4.6 Proxy Ablations

    Attempted Actions and Their Consequences. We retrain each variant with one cue family removed, keeping the training setting unchanged. In Table4, removing command marks lowers attack precision while leaving Reaction largely unchanged. Removing the skill trigger reduces skill accuracy by approximately 20 percentage points. These results support encoding attempted actions separately from their consequences.

    Events and Persistent State. Removing damage-event cues lowers the Reaction score while health error remains low. Removing health bars largely preserves reactions but degrades health accuracy and joint fidelity. These complementary effects support separate conditioning for transient reactions and persistent state. More details, comparisons and visualizations are provided in the appendix.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented Fight World Model (FWM), which connects executable gameplay rules to video generation through a visual interaction proxy. Experiments in a combat setting demonstrate improved interaction and appearance fidelity over adapted game world models. FWM supports edited rules and multi-stage skill mechanisms without retraining the renderer. Character and arena customization preserves the prescribed interactions, with identity binding maintaining character associations across side switches.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Implementation Details

    A.1 Engine and Timeline

    The combat engine exposes damage magnitude, the number of protected hits, and the lifesteal rate as editable parameters. Its state retains protection counts and active skill windows across action intervals.

    Engine updates indexed by k are mapped to output video frames t before proxy compilation. State samples and event windows use the same frame mapping, so an event onset is paired with its resulting state update. Frame index zero denotes the initial context, and x̂_1:T denotes the continuation. The engine carries executable state between action intervals, while visual context conditions the next generated segment.

    A.2 Proxy Encoding Parameters

    For light, medium, and heavy attacks, stripes cover the top one third, top two thirds, or full box interior below the coarse action band. They remain active over the command window. The skill-trigger block follows the caster for 30 output video frames, and reaction color inversions last four frames. Both durations are defined at the output video rate and resampled together with the state and event records.

    A.3 Renderer and Binding Parameters

    We initialize the renderer from the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B checkpoint [34]. For F video latent frames, character references use temporal coordinate τ_ref=F+2, and arena references use τ_ref=F+3. Their spatial coordinates lie outside the video grid. Video and proxy inputs use matched temporal indices and the same resize and center-crop transform.

    The identity codebook contains six learned slots. Each embedding is normalized to unit root-mean-square magnitude and scaled by 0.25 at all three injection sites. For the first video latent and proxy sequence, soft bounding-box coverage weights the corresponding entity’s embedding, with weights normalized where boxes overlap. The target entity’s embedding is added to all character-reference tokens without a spatial box mask. Persistent entity IDs in the proxy identify the reference targets. Arena references receive no identity embedding.

    A.4 Training Objective and Configuration

    Let z denote clean video latents and ε∼ℕ(0,I). We construct noisy latents with flow matching [22, 24]:

    z_τ=(1-τ)z+τε, τ=5v/1+4v, v∼U(0,1).

    		(4)

    Here τ is flow time, distinct from engine index k and video-frame index t. The first latent is replaced with the clean source-image encoding at noise level zero. Future video tokens receive noise level τ. With conditions ℂ=(xⁱⁿⁱᵗ,π,r,c), the loss is

    L=𝔼 [(1)/(|Ω₊|)∑_j∈Ω₊∥v_θ(z_τ,τ;ℂ)ⱼ-(ε-z)ⱼ∥₂²],

    		(5)

    where Ω₊ contains future video latent elements. Initial-context, proxy, and reference tokens are excluded from the loss. At inference, future video latents start from noise.

    We use AdamW with a constant learning rate of 8×10⁻⁵, weight decay of 0.01, and no learning-rate warmup. Training uses bfloat16 autocast with fp32 master parameters and an effective batch size of 128 on 128 H200 GPUs. The budget is 35 epochs, corresponding to 30,765 optimizer steps.

    Each clip contains 89 frames at 928×704 resolution. Dropout probabilities for proxy, reference, text, and appearance descriptions are 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, and 0.2, respectively. The controlled encoding variants in Table2 share initialization, training data, and optimization budget. Only the representation and its required input layers differ.

    Appendix B Data Construction Details

    B.1 Video Editing and Quality Control

    A frozen MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA editor produces appearance and skill-effect variants using edit-specific prompts. Screening checks the requested content, temporal coherence, and interaction consistency.

    Appearance-only variants are checked against the source video for fighter trajectories, event timing, and health traces. Only edits that pass these checks reuse the source state annotations. Skill-effect edits are annotated from the edited videos.

    B.2 State and Event Annotation

    Gemma-4-31B-it localizes fighters at regularly spaced keyframes to initialize SAM 2 video propagation [29]. Semantic descriptions help distinguish fighters from similar background characters. At each keyframe, the tracker checks the two identity assignments against appearance and trajectory continuity, retaining or swapping them to correct drift and bridge short gaps. Bounding boxes specify spatial state. Facing direction follows relative fighter positions and retains its previous value while the boxes overlap.

    Health traces are estimated from HUD bar lengths and cleaned within each round. Nearby decreases are merged into damage events, each recording the affected fighter and event time. Gemma also supplies coarse action and stance labels at selected frames, including frames near damage events. Unannotated action frames use the unknown label. Logged inputs provide fine attack commands and scheduled skill triggers for the controlled fighter. The compiler converts these annotations into interaction proxies.

    Appendix C Evaluation Protocols

    C.1 Controlled Interactions

    Recorded-interaction tests use held-out video annotations, with source episodes separated between training and testing. Rule interventions rerun the engine from the same initial state and submitted actions under each configuration, recomputing motion trajectories, hit events, and state outcomes. These records define the target interactions for the compared encodings. In FWM’s damage scaling, limited-hit immunity, and lifesteal tests, reference images and text condition c remain fixed. Changed outcomes reach FWM only through the proxy.

    Appearance interventions retain the executed records and proxy while changing the references. Evaluation cases include no-hit attempts, repeated attacks, overlap, and side switches.

    Complete-Information Encodings. The encodings use matched event-free intervals, sampled values, and temporal indices, with shared resolution and sampling settings. Each uses the input layers required by its representation, and text inputs are checked for truncation.

    C.2 Action Recognition and Timing

    Movement. MoveAcc compares tracked fighter motion with directional commands over valid command windows and averages across the four movement keys. Jump positives require an actual airborne jump. Grounded hurt recovery is excluded from jump positives.

    Attack and Skill Recognition. We train ResNet-18-based temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) for attack and skill recognition. Attack detections are grouped into temporally contiguous events. AttackAcc measures the fraction of detected punch or kick events supported by the corresponding input command within its temporal window.

    The skill classifier uses a 256-channel temporal trunk with dilation rates 1, 2, 4, and 8. It predicts onset and class, with a no-skill outcome in the onset prediction. Class logits are pooled over the predicted effect interval. SkillAcc requires the correct class and onset within the command-relative window. The same timing rule applies across methods and accommodates skill startup, release, and recovery.

    An attempted attack may hit or miss, so AttackAcc and Reaction assess command-grounded action execution and received-hit consequences, respectively.

    C.3 Reaction and Health

    Visible Reactions. Reaction measures the fraction of expected hit responses visibly performed by the designated fighter within the evaluation window. Qwen judges body motion in surrounding gameplay frames, using a source-frame identity guide and excluding the HUD.

    Brief reactions can resemble ordinary motion across appearances and effects, so we judge them using local temporal context around expected events. Computing reaction precision would additionally require locating every visible received-hit onset throughout the generated video, a dense detection task that is difficult for current VLMs.

    Health and Persistence. Let V contain readable fighter-frame observations and H denote maximum health. Health MAE is the normalized mean absolute error, expressed in percentage points:

    MAEₕ=(100)/(|V|H)∑_(i,t)∈V|ĥₜⁱ-hₜⁱ|.

    		(6)

    Observed and target health values are obtained from HUD bar lengths. The joint health check uses a one-pixel tolerance and requires correct updates for both fighters, with the resulting values preserved between events. This includes unchanged health under immunity and the attacker’s restored health under lifesteal.

    C.4 Joint Interaction Fidelity

    An attempt succeeds only when all applicable action, entity, timing, reaction, and health checks pass. The score J averages attempts within each episode and weights episodes equally:

    q_ℓe=∏_k∈K_ℓec_ℓe,k, J=1/L∑_ℓ=1^L(1)/(N_ℓ)∑ₑ₌₁^N_ℓq_ℓe.

    		(7)

    Here L counts episodes, N_ℓ counts attempts in episode ℓ, and c_ℓe,k are binary checks indexed by K_ℓe. The applicable set follows the registered interaction. Its checks cover command-grounded actions and timing, the identities of acting and affected fighters, visible body responses, and correct health updates with persistence. For rule interventions, Jᵣᵤₗₑ combines the required reaction and health checks. Both rates are expressed as percentages in the results.

    C.5 Appearance and Entity Assignment

    Adherence assesses appearance-edit success for the designated character or arena. A VLM judges sampled continuation frames using the target reference and a source-frame identity guide. Frame judgments are combined into a clip-level decision.

    DINO measures reference-to-generation feature cosine similarity separately for characters and arenas. Proxy boxes localize fighter crops, while fighter and HUD regions are suppressed for arena scoring. The fixed initial context is excluded from both appearance metrics.

    Appendix D Reference-Augmented Baselines

    We augment H3-WORLD [5], ReactiveGWM v1 [37], and ReactiveGWM v2 [36] with our reference-conditioning branch. Variants are evaluated on the same clips and frame indices as FWM, using explicit appearance references. The comparisons in Figs.12, 12, 14 and 14 show character drift or garment blur during rapid contact and side switches, together with missed (), premature (), or incomplete () health updates. FWM preserves appearance and the prescribed health updates more consistently in these examples.

item.title: Agent Harness 才是主角：视频生成正在变成「可执行运行时」，规划、工具、状态、预算都在这一层 ｜ Video Generation Meets Agent Harness: Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Beyond
item.description:
一句话：把 agent harness 定义为模型外面的可执行运行时：构造上下文、暴露工具、维护状态、路由反馈、执行预算。

要点：

  • 报告的核心概念是 agent harness：包在视频生成器等模型之外的那层「可执行运行时」，负责构造 agent 上下文、暴露工具、维护状态、路由反馈并执行预算约束
  • 三个方向之一：agentic 视频生成——由 harness 协调剧本与分镜规划、资产管理、镜头生产与剪辑，产出多镜头一致的视频
  • 另两个方向把「视频世界模型」当作 agent 的交互环境：世界模型提供动作条件观测与预测未来，harness 则在上面驱动 agent 反复试错

为什么值得看：这篇把「引擎该长什么样」换了个说法讲：未来引擎的一部分职责就是 harness——上下文、工具、状态与预算。对做 agent 接入的团队，它给出的是可对照的职责清单，而不是又一个模型。

中文摘要：视频生成正从端到端合成走向 agentic 生成：规划、工具使用与反馈共同产出可控的多镜头视频；与此同时，视频世界模型为 agent 提供动作条件观测与未来预测，可以充当交互环境。这篇报告用「agent harness」把两者串起来：harness 是围绕模型（如视频生成器）的可执行运行时，负责构造 agent 上下文、暴露工具、维护状态、路由反馈与执行预算。报告按三个方向展开：agentic 视频生成（剧本与分镜规划、资产管理与剪辑的协调）、agentic 世界建模（世界模型当环境）、以及两者的组合与边界。它的价值在于把「模型外面那层工程」定义清楚——这层恰好是引擎的主场。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-29

本期推送：2026-10-31

Video Generation Meets Agent Harness
Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement

Abstract

Abstract: Video generation is evolving from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, in which planning, tool use, and feedback produce coherent multi-shot videos with greater control. Meanwhile, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures and can serve as interactive environments for agents. We study this intersection through the agent harness: the executable runtime that constructs an agent’s context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces budgets around models such as video generators. The report is organized around three directions. First, we study agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate script and shot planning, asset management, shot production, and editing, and we discuss what the evaluation of such systems must separate. Second, we examine agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state, including designs in which a game engine or a program written by a coding agent holds the world state while the video model renders it, and where agents and world models test and improve one another. Third, we examine recursive self-improvement (RSI) for video model development: we separate revisions of a current output from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and from changes to the procedure that produces later updates, and we identify the channels through which an improvement could re-enter development. Across these directions, we analyze the agent capabilities that video imposes, from audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, and memory to interaction through code and computer use, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent organization. We conclude with open challenges, including autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance and cost accounting, and evaluation that links video quality and task performance to sustained improvement of models and harnesses.

Keywords: Video Generation, Agent, Harness Engineering, World Models, Recursive Self-Improvement
Webpage: https://agentic-videogen.github.io/
GitHub: https://github.com/agentic-videogen/awesome-agentic-videogen

1 Introduction

1.1 Motivation

Video generators produce increasingly realistic, controllable, and temporally coherent clips [kong2024hunyuanvideo]. A generator alone, however, does not organize the decisions needed to complete a video task. A creative brief must become coherent shots; references must persist across scenes; takes must be inspected; edits must preserve what is correct [huang2026vimax, vista2025]. Interactive video must also support continuing actions grounded in observations, not just a finished clip [gao2026lingbotworld2]. These requirements motivate a transition from video generation to agentic video generation: a goal-directed process in which generated results inform subsequent decisions. An agent can revise a plan, retrieve a reference, select a tool, or localize a failure in response to actual outcomes [li2026videogenagent]. Agentic video generation denotes a system-level perspective, not a new generator architecture: the video model provides synthesis or predicted transitions, while the agent makes consequential choices around those capabilities. Video couples these choices over time. References affect later shots [chen2026cinecrew], actions change subsequent observations, and local repairs can disrupt temporal consistency elsewhere. Plausible footage may still violate a narrative requirement or fail to realize an intended action, so a quality score alone rarely specifies what to do next [liu2024videogenerationevaluation, ding2026playworld]. Effective control requires connecting observations to localized decisions while maintaining project or interaction state and accounting for generation cost.

The development from large language models (LLMs) to agents offers a foundation for this control. Rather than only generating a response, an LLM can operate within a cycle of reasoning, tool use, and observation, as demonstrated by ReAct [yao2023react]. Planning and memory extend this cycle to tasks requiring multiple decisions [weng2023agents]. Making these capabilities operational requires an agent harness: the executable runtime around the model that constructs its context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces permissions and budgets [weng2026harness, ning2026code] (Section ). For video generation, the harness is where a creative brief or an interactive goal becomes executable operations on generators, editors, and world models. The central question shifts from generating a good clip to reliably completing a video task through feedback. Agentic video generation and video world-model interaction are two concrete settings. A further question is whether experience from these tasks can improve the system that will perform future tasks.

Feedback changes different objects at different timescales. Prompt revision or take replacement targets the current artifact [vista2025]; retaining a skill targets subsequent tasks [wei2026videoweaver]; updating a dataset, critic, or generator targets later model versions [liu2025videoalign]. These outcomes should not be conflated: effective repair of a current video does not by itself establish improvement in future capability. Beyond repairing individual outputs, context engineering considers how instructions, retrieved evidence, memory, and execution records are selected and organized for subsequent decisions [weng2026harness]. Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), for example, accumulates and revises a structured context from execution feedback rather than updating model weights [zhang2025ace]. Such work shifts attention from a current response toward reusable knowledge, while leaving open whether the mechanisms that construct and update that knowledge can themselves improve.

Recent work on automated research extends these ideas to model development. The AI Scientist links idea generation, coding, experiments, and reporting [lu2024aiscientist]; autoresearch runs a bounded loop of training code modification, experimentation, and validation-based acceptance [karpathy2026autoresearch]. These workflows connect proposals to empirical feedback, but automating a fixed experiment loop is not the same as improving the loop itself. Research on self-improving agents, exemplified by the Darwin Gödel Machine and Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement (RRSI), explores changes to the agent’s own code or harness [zhang2025dgm, xia2026rrsi]. Such work motivates examining the processes that generate and validate subsequent improvements.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) asks whether a system can improve the procedures that produce further improvements [chen2026surveyr04, duan2026surveyn21]. Video-specific targets include failure diagnosis, data collection, supervision construction, update selection, and candidate validation. Repeating a fixed collection-and-training pipeline is iterative improvement. The recursive direction additionally allows evidence to revise that pipeline, changing how a later round discovers and addresses weaknesses. An agent harness provides an executable surface for this direction. Its context construction, tool orchestration, memory, testing workflow, and update-selection rules can be inspected and, where authorized, revised [weng2026harness]. This does not make every harness self-improving: a revision must be retained and independently evaluated on later tasks or improvement rounds under stated resource constraints [xia2026rrsi].

Existing video research supplies parts of this connection: feedback can revise reusable production skills [wei2026videoweaver], uncertainty can guide data acquisition for adaptation [savov2025autoexplore], and validation can govern critic renewal for later training [yang2026dualipo]. These are building blocks rather than evidence that one system has completed the full RSI loop. Our survey therefore connects three questions: how harnesses organize agentic video generation, how they support video world-model interaction, and how they may drive video-generation development toward RSI. The first two establish task execution and sources of experience; the third examines persistent capability and the procedures used to improve it. Figure 2 maps representative work from a shared video generation foundation into the three directions corresponding to the questions below.

1.2 Contributions and Positioning

The survey addresses three questions about the influence of the agent harness on video generation (Figure 1), each corresponding to one core chapter.

How does the agent harness enable agentic video generation? Agentic Video Generation (Section ) studies how harnesses coordinate planning, execution, tool use, memory, editing, and watermarking around shared project state, and what the evaluation of such systems must separate. We examine how feedback changes generation and editing decisions and how those changes affect video quality, consistency, and efficiency.

How can the agent harness be integrated into video world models? Agentic World Modeling (Section ) locates where a harness can intervene in observation, control, execution, event organization, and state management, and examines designs in which an engine holds the world state while the video model renders it. We examine how these interventions support sustained interaction, control fidelity, state continuity, and agent-driven evaluation. The focus of this question is how a harness enables reliable interaction with a video world model.

How can video generation systems move toward recursive self-improvement? Toward RSI in Video Generation (Section ) examines how advances in video generators and the agent harness can feed back into the process that produces subsequent model improvements. We review foundation model improvement, agent harness improvement, and evaluation, and identify the channels through which gains in these components can strengthen failure diagnosis, data curation, training, and validation in later development rounds. The goal is to identify mechanisms and evidence needed for recursively improving development processes that can support next-generation video generation models.

These questions connect through feedback: agentic video generation and world interaction can expose failures, while development can turn selected evidence into changes deployed in later tasks. Section compares the shared agent capabilities that support all three settings.

Differentiating Our Work from Existing Surveys

Existing surveys provide complementary accounts of video generation. Work on spatiotemporal consistency examines generation models, representations, training strategies, and evaluation, emphasizing the mechanisms that maintain coherent video sequences [yin2025spatiotemporal]. Post-training and alignment surveys organize methods for adapting video generators to human intent, including supervised fine-tuning, distillation, preference optimization, and inference-time adaptation [li2026videoposttraining]. Evaluation surveys examine perceptual quality, semantic fidelity, and alignment with user instructions [liu2024videogenerationevaluation]. Together, these accounts explain how video models are built, improved, and assessed.
