More directly related to our system perspective, agentic visual generation surveys organize the conditioning, execution, and adaptation decisions available to a controller across visual modalities [huang2026agenticvisual], or study autonomous multimodal content creation and the construction of stateful artifacts [xu2026ags, wang2026artifactcreation]. Wu et al. place agentic generation and world-modeling generation on a single capability ladder of visual generation [wu2026visualnewera]. World model surveys characterize predictive and simulation capabilities across domains, focus on action conditioning, memory, and responsiveness in sustained interaction [chu2026agenticworldmodel, liu2026interactiveworldmodel], or treat world models as interactive proxies that supply feedback to continually improving agents [yang2026quovadis]. Harness surveys analyze the execution layer around text and coding agents [ning2026code, guo2026harnessdesign]. Surveys of self-evolving agents and RSI examine evolutionary targets, adaptation stages, and feedback loops across general AI systems [gao2025surveyr02, chen2026surveyr04, wu2026rsisurvey]. These perspectives share concepts such as feedback, memory, and agent control, but none of them takes the harness around a video generator as the unit of analysis across production, interaction, and model development.

Table 1.2 compares related surveys and adjacent studies by scope, thematic coverage (including RSI), and agent design. Our survey complements these perspectives with a framework centered on video generation that covers three settings in which a harness meets a video model: as a synthesizer in production, as an interactive environment, and as the object of development. The settings are linked through the harness: agents organize generation and refinement, while video models provide interactive experience that can inform agent decisions and further model development. Where capability ladders treat agentic generation and world modeling as successive stages of the generator [wu2026visualnewera], we take the agent harness around the generator as the unit of analysis, so that one framework covers production, interaction, and development.

Our contributions are threefold.

  • •

    A harness-centered framework. We define a common agent–harness execution loop (Section ) and apply it to production, organized by workflow function (Section ), and to world-model interaction, organized by the interfaces through which a harness intervenes, including designs in which an engine or a program holds the world state (Section ).

  • •

    An account of improvement. We separate revisions of the current output from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and from changes to the development procedure. We identify four channels through which an improvement could re-enter video development. No surveyed system yet revises the procedure that trains and validates the generator (Section ).

  • •

    Evaluation requirements and open problems. We state how the agent harness supports active testing and reciprocal evaluation of agents and world models (Section ), what the evaluation of agentic production must separate (Section ), which capabilities video imposes on agents (Section ), and which challenges remain (Section ).

一句话：把 agent harness 定义为模型外面的可执行运行时：构造上下文、暴露工具、维护状态、路由反馈、执行预算。

要点：

  • 报告的核心概念是 agent harness：包在视频生成器等模型之外的那层「可执行运行时」，负责构造 agent 上下文、暴露工具、维护状态、路由反馈并执行预算约束
  • 三个方向之一：agentic 视频生成——由 harness 协调剧本与分镜规划、资产管理、镜头生产与剪辑，产出多镜头一致的视频
  • 另两个方向把「视频世界模型」当作 agent 的交互环境：世界模型提供动作条件观测与预测未来，harness 则在上面驱动 agent 反复试错

为什么值得看：这篇把「引擎该长什么样」换了个说法讲：未来引擎的一部分职责就是 harness——上下文、工具、状态与预算。对做 agent 接入的团队，它给出的是可对照的职责清单，而不是又一个模型。

中文摘要：视频生成正从端到端合成走向 agentic 生成：规划、工具使用与反馈共同产出可控的多镜头视频；与此同时，视频世界模型为 agent 提供动作条件观测与未来预测，可以充当交互环境。这篇报告用「agent harness」把两者串起来：harness 是围绕模型（如视频生成器）的可执行运行时，负责构造 agent 上下文、暴露工具、维护状态、路由反馈与执行预算。报告按三个方向展开：agentic 视频生成（剧本与分镜规划、资产管理与剪辑的协调）、agentic 世界建模（世界模型当环境）、以及两者的组合与边界。它的价值在于把「模型外面那层工程」定义清楚——这层恰好是引擎的主场。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-29

本期推送：2026-10-31

Video Generation Meets Agent Harness
Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement

Abstract

Abstract: Video generation is evolving from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, in which planning, tool use, and feedback produce coherent multi-shot videos with greater control. Meanwhile, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures and can serve as interactive environments for agents. We study this intersection through the agent harness: the executable runtime that constructs an agent’s context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces budgets around models such as video generators. The report is organized around three directions. First, we study agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate script and shot planning, asset management, shot production, and editing, and we discuss what the evaluation of such systems must separate. Second, we examine agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state, including designs in which a game engine or a program written by a coding agent holds the world state while the video model renders it, and where agents and world models test and improve one another. Third, we examine recursive self-improvement (RSI) for video model development: we separate revisions of a current output from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and from changes to the procedure that produces later updates, and we identify the channels through which an improvement could re-enter development. Across these directions, we analyze the agent capabilities that video imposes, from audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, and memory to interaction through code and computer use, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent organization. We conclude with open challenges, including autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance and cost accounting, and evaluation that links video quality and task performance to sustained improvement of models and harnesses.

Keywords: Video Generation, Agent, Harness Engineering, World Models, Recursive Self-Improvement
Webpage: https://agentic-videogen.github.io/
GitHub: https://github.com/agentic-videogen/awesome-agentic-videogen

1 Introduction

1.1 Motivation

Video generators produce increasingly realistic, controllable, and temporally coherent clips [kong2024hunyuanvideo]. A generator alone, however, does not organize the decisions needed to complete a video task. A creative brief must become coherent shots; references must persist across scenes; takes must be inspected; edits must preserve what is correct [huang2026vimax, vista2025]. Interactive video must also support continuing actions grounded in observations, not just a finished clip [gao2026lingbotworld2]. These requirements motivate a transition from video generation to agentic video generation: a goal-directed process in which generated results inform subsequent decisions. An agent can revise a plan, retrieve a reference, select a tool, or localize a failure in response to actual outcomes [li2026videogenagent]. Agentic video generation denotes a system-level perspective, not a new generator architecture: the video model provides synthesis or predicted transitions, while the agent makes consequential choices around those capabilities. Video couples these choices over time. References affect later shots [chen2026cinecrew], actions change subsequent observations, and local repairs can disrupt temporal consistency elsewhere. Plausible footage may still violate a narrative requirement or fail to realize an intended action, so a quality score alone rarely specifies what to do next [liu2024videogenerationevaluation, ding2026playworld]. Effective control requires connecting observations to localized decisions while maintaining project or interaction state and accounting for generation cost.

The development from large language models (LLMs) to agents offers a foundation for this control. Rather than only generating a response, an LLM can operate within a cycle of reasoning, tool use, and observation, as demonstrated by ReAct [yao2023react]. Planning and memory extend this cycle to tasks requiring multiple decisions [weng2023agents]. Making these capabilities operational requires an agent harness: the executable runtime around the model that constructs its context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces permissions and budgets [weng2026harness, ning2026code] (Section ). For video generation, the harness is where a creative brief or an interactive goal becomes executable operations on generators, editors, and world models. The central question shifts from generating a good clip to reliably completing a video task through feedback. Agentic video generation and video world-model interaction are two concrete settings. A further question is whether experience from these tasks can improve the system that will perform future tasks.

Feedback changes different objects at different timescales. Prompt revision or take replacement targets the current artifact [vista2025]; retaining a skill targets subsequent tasks [wei2026videoweaver]; updating a dataset, critic, or generator targets later model versions [liu2025videoalign]. These outcomes should not be conflated: effective repair of a current video does not by itself establish improvement in future capability. Beyond repairing individual outputs, context engineering considers how instructions, retrieved evidence, memory, and execution records are selected and organized for subsequent decisions [weng2026harness]. Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), for example, accumulates and revises a structured context from execution feedback rather than updating model weights [zhang2025ace]. Such work shifts attention from a current response toward reusable knowledge, while leaving open whether the mechanisms that construct and update that knowledge can themselves improve.

Recent work on automated research extends these ideas to model development. The AI Scientist links idea generation, coding, experiments, and reporting [lu2024aiscientist]; autoresearch runs a bounded loop of training code modification, experimentation, and validation-based acceptance [karpathy2026autoresearch]. These workflows connect proposals to empirical feedback, but automating a fixed experiment loop is not the same as improving the loop itself. Research on self-improving agents, exemplified by the Darwin Gödel Machine and Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement (RRSI), explores changes to the agent’s own code or harness [zhang2025dgm, xia2026rrsi]. Such work motivates examining the processes that generate and validate subsequent improvements.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) asks whether a system can improve the procedures that produce further improvements [chen2026surveyr04, duan2026surveyn21]. Video-specific targets include failure diagnosis, data collection, supervision construction, update selection, and candidate validation. Repeating a fixed collection-and-training pipeline is iterative improvement. The recursive direction additionally allows evidence to revise that pipeline, changing how a later round discovers and addresses weaknesses. An agent harness provides an executable surface for this direction. Its context construction, tool orchestration, memory, testing workflow, and update-selection rules can be inspected and, where authorized, revised [weng2026harness]. This does not make every harness self-improving: a revision must be retained and independently evaluated on later tasks or improvement rounds under stated resource constraints [xia2026rrsi].

Existing video research supplies parts of this connection: feedback can revise reusable production skills [wei2026videoweaver], uncertainty can guide data acquisition for adaptation [savov2025autoexplore], and validation can govern critic renewal for later training [yang2026dualipo]. These are building blocks rather than evidence that one system has completed the full RSI loop. Our survey therefore connects three questions: how harnesses organize agentic video generation, how they support video world-model interaction, and how they may drive video-generation development toward RSI. The first two establish task execution and sources of experience; the third examines persistent capability and the procedures used to improve it. Figure 2 maps representative work from a shared video generation foundation into the three directions corresponding to the questions below.

1.2 Contributions and Positioning

The survey addresses three questions about the influence of the agent harness on video generation (Figure 1), each corresponding to one core chapter.

How does the agent harness enable agentic video generation? Agentic Video Generation (Section ) studies how harnesses coordinate planning, execution, tool use, memory, editing, and watermarking around shared project state, and what the evaluation of such systems must separate. We examine how feedback changes generation and editing decisions and how those changes affect video quality, consistency, and efficiency.

How can the agent harness be integrated into video world models? Agentic World Modeling (Section ) locates where a harness can intervene in observation, control, execution, event organization, and state management, and examines designs in which an engine holds the world state while the video model renders it. We examine how these interventions support sustained interaction, control fidelity, state continuity, and agent-driven evaluation. The focus of this question is how a harness enables reliable interaction with a video world model.

How can video generation systems move toward recursive self-improvement? Toward RSI in Video Generation (Section ) examines how advances in video generators and the agent harness can feed back into the process that produces subsequent model improvements. We review foundation model improvement, agent harness improvement, and evaluation, and identify the channels through which gains in these components can strengthen failure diagnosis, data curation, training, and validation in later development rounds. The goal is to identify mechanisms and evidence needed for recursively improving development processes that can support next-generation video generation models.

These questions connect through feedback: agentic video generation and world interaction can expose failures, while development can turn selected evidence into changes deployed in later tasks. Section compares the shared agent capabilities that support all three settings.

Differentiating Our Work from Existing Surveys

Existing surveys provide complementary accounts of video generation. Work on spatiotemporal consistency examines generation models, representations, training strategies, and evaluation, emphasizing the mechanisms that maintain coherent video sequences [yin2025spatiotemporal]. Post-training and alignment surveys organize methods for adapting video generators to human intent, including supervised fine-tuning, distillation, preference optimization, and inference-time adaptation [li2026videoposttraining]. Evaluation surveys examine perceptual quality, semantic fidelity, and alignment with user instructions [liu2024videogenerationevaluation]. Together, these accounts explain how video models are built, improved, and assessed.

More directly related to our system perspective, agentic visual generation surveys organize the conditioning, execution, and adaptation decisions available to a controller across visual modalities [huang2026agenticvisual], or study autonomous multimodal content creation and the construction of stateful artifacts [xu2026ags, wang2026artifactcreation]. Wu et al. place agentic generation and world-modeling generation on a single capability ladder of visual generation [wu2026visualnewera]. World model surveys characterize predictive and simulation capabilities across domains, focus on action conditioning, memory, and responsiveness in sustained interaction [chu2026agenticworldmodel, liu2026interactiveworldmodel], or treat world models as interactive proxies that supply feedback to continually improving agents [yang2026quovadis]. Harness surveys analyze the execution layer around text and coding agents [ning2026code, guo2026harnessdesign]. Surveys of self-evolving agents and RSI examine evolutionary targets, adaptation stages, and feedback loops across general AI systems [gao2025surveyr02, chen2026surveyr04, wu2026rsisurvey]. These perspectives share concepts such as feedback, memory, and agent control, but none of them takes the harness around a video generator as the unit of analysis across production, interaction, and model development.

Table 1.2 compares related surveys and adjacent studies by scope, thematic coverage (including RSI), and agent design. Our survey complements these perspectives with a framework centered on video generation that covers three settings in which a harness meets a video model: as a synthesizer in production, as an interactive environment, and as the object of development. The settings are linked through the harness: agents organize generation and refinement, while video models provide interactive experience that can inform agent decisions and further model development. Where capability ladders treat agentic generation and world modeling as successive stages of the generator [wu2026visualnewera], we take the agent harness around the generator as the unit of analysis, so that one framework covers production, interaction, and development.

Our contributions are threefold.

  • •

    A harness-centered framework. We define a common agent–harness execution loop (Section ) and apply it to production, organized by workflow function (Section ), and to world-model interaction, organized by the interfaces through which a harness intervenes, including designs in which an engine or a program holds the world state (Section ).

  • •

    An account of improvement. We separate revisions of the current output from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and from changes to the development procedure. We identify four channels through which an improvement could re-enter video development. No surveyed system yet revises the procedure that trains and validates the generator (Section ).

  • •

    Evaluation requirements and open problems. We state how the agent harness supports active testing and reciprocal evaluation of agents and world models (Section ), what the evaluation of agentic production must separate (Section ), which capabilities video imposes on agents (Section ), and which challenges remain (Section ).

item.title: Unity Industry 让 agent 自己搭流程：说一句「把这个 STEP 处理好」，它跑完导入/修模/优化/QA 渲染/发布 ｜ 2026 Industry releases and what’s coming in Q4
item.description:
一句话：Industry AI Workflows（实验）：把自家 agent 接到 Asset Manager / Asset Transformer / Pipeline 上。

要点：

  • Industry AI Workflows（10 月实验性发布）：把你的 agent 接到 Asset Manager、Asset Transformer 与 Pipeline Automation 上，描述想要的结果，由 agent 自己把整条工作流搭出来
  • 给出的例子就是硬流程：指向一个 STEP 文件 → 导入、修模、优化、QA 渲染、导出、发布、打标签，一句话触发全链路
  • 配套还有 Unity Pipeline 内测：统一 API 把 DCC、IDE、CLI 与「受支持的 AI agent」都接进来，且**不需要 Editor 席位**；另外 UI Toolkit 的 Figma 连接器把设计稿变成可编辑 UI

为什么值得看：这是「引擎管线为 agent 重做接口」的又一例，而且是工业向（CAD/数字孪生）先落地——因为那里的流程最标准化、最适合被描述成任务。游戏侧的同构问题（资产导入、LOD、烘焙、QA）几乎一样，值得直接对照。

中文摘要：Unity Industry 的年度回顾里，最值得记的是 10 月上线的 Industry AI Workflows（实验性）：开发者可以把自己的 AI agent 接到 Asset Manager、Asset Transformer 与 Pipeline Automation 上，用自然语言描述目标，由 agent 自行搭建整条工作流——官方给的例子是「指向一个 STEP 文件」，随后自动完成导入、修模、优化、QA 渲染、导出、发布与打标签。同期还有两项相关更新：Unity Pipeline 进入内测，用统一 API 把 DCC、IDE、CLI 与受支持的 AI agent 接入，且无需 Editor 席位；UI Toolkit 的 Figma 连接器把 Figma 画板转成可编辑的 Unity UI。整体方向是把「引擎 + 资产管线」变成 agent 可调用的接口集合。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：Unity Blog（English）

原文发布：2026-10-30

本期推送：2026-10-31

2026 Industry releases and what’s coming in Q4

Oct 30, 2026|7 Min

Avery Vernon-Moore - Unity Technologies

Product Marketing Manager

Asset managementEngineAsset managementEngineAI

2026 has been a big year for Unity Industry, so we're looking back at the major Unity Industry releases and updates, plus a preview on what’s coming in Q4.

In March, Unity Studio made it possible to create interactive 3D experiences directly in a web browser. By September, robotics teams could prototype and validate systems in simulation before deploying them to physical hardware. In between, Unity Industry shipped 15+ releases.

Those releases span every part of the Unity Industry product suite. They serve teams building digital twins, simulations, HMI and embedded systems, robotics, XR training, and product configurators.

TL;DR: Unity Industry's 2026 releases at a glance

Short on time? Here's what Unity Industry shipped this year:

  • AI agents joined the 3D data pipeline:Industry AI Workflows launched in October as an experimental release, so your own AI agent can prep, optimize, and publish CAD data across Asset Manager, Asset Transformer, and Pipeline Automation.
  • Design and simulation tools connected to Unity: The experimental UI Toolkit Connector for Figma turns Figma frames into editable Unity UI, and the Unity USD Toolkit round-trips USD between Unity and NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
  • 3D creation moved into the browser:Unity Studio went GA in March, then added annotations, Editor export, and live co-editing.
  • Collaboration opened up beyond the Editor:Unity Pipeline entered closed beta, giving every role one API into a Unity production.
  • Enterprise security got independent proof: Unity's creator services are now SOC 2 Type 2 certified, and Asset Manager deploys in your own cloud.
  • Robotics and embedded got purpose-built tools: Simulation Pro entered early access. Automotive teams got multi-window control and a shared Android render service.
  • The Editor kept getting faster: Unity 6.4, 6.5, and 6.6 shipped, with Unity 6.7 LTS coming soon.

    • Below, we break down every Unity Industry release from 2026 by quarter and product, then preview what's coming in Q4.

    Q1 2026: 3D creation opens up

    Unity Studio is generally available

    Bring 3D ideas to life, fast: Unity Studio is a web-based editor that lets anyone build and share interactive 3D apps. No coding and no installs. Import your 3D data, add interactivity, and share a link for review.

    Unity 6.4

    6.4 brought faster scene building, smoother workflows, and ECS now built into the Editor: The release integrated Project Auditor, moved ECS packages into the core Editor release cycle, and expanded rendering, input, and platform support.

    Read the launch post

    Real-time collaboration

    Annotations

    Export to Editor

    Q2 2026: From solo tool to team workspace

    Unity Studio: releases for connected collaboration

  • Custom Transformations: More control over 3D imports. Choose optimized or full hierarchy, and keep animations and structure without external tools.
  • Studio to Editor Export: Start fast, scale without rebuilding. Send Studio projects to the Unity Editor with assets, UI, and logic intact. Watch it
  • Annotations: Feedback where it matters. Pin comments and replies to the exact spot in a 3D scene. Watch it
  • Real-time Collaboration: Create together in real time. Co-edit shared 3D scenes live, with presence and comments built in. Watch it

    • Read more about Studio collaboration and Editor export

    Unity Asset Manager: Self-Hosted Deployment

    Deployment in your cloud: Deploy Asset Manager directly to your private cloud. Keep sensitive 3D data in your own environment while you automate heavy prep.

    Read the documentation

    Unity 6.5 and embedded multi-window support

  • Unity 6.5: Faster workflows, stronger foundations. Performance, graphics, 2D, and platform gains across Android, Apple, Web, and Nintendo Switch 2, plus groundwork for CoreCLR. Read the launch post
  • GameWindow multi-window support: Granular, runtime control over every window. Create, arrange, and control multiple Unity windows across one or more displays, built for automotive cockpits and industrial control panels. Read the documentation.
    • Discover Unity IndustryStart 30 day free trial

    Q3 2026: Trust, skills, and new frontiers

    Unite Seoul set the pace for the quarter. Read the recap

    Platform: open and verified

  • Unity Pipeline enters closed beta: Open your Unity production to the whole team. A unified API connects every role and tool, including DCCs, IDEs, the CLI, and supported AI agents. No Editor seat required. Apply for the beta
  • SOC 2 Type 2 certification:Asset Manager, Asset Transformer, Studio, Pipeline, and DevOps are SOC 2 Type 2 certified, audited by Coalfire. Visit the Trust Center

    • Unity Academy Pro

    Scale Unity skills across teams: Structured, role-based training for industrial teams, so they onboard faster and work more efficiently. Explore Academy Pro

    Robotics: Simulation Pro early access

    Simulate robotics workflows in Unity: Prototype, test, and validate robots, sensors, and AI before deployment, with ROS-connected tools. Run on private clouds or local servers, with no hardware lock-in.

    Learn more

    Embedded and HMI: Unity Render Service now in Beta

    One Unity instance, shared across every Android app: Android applications can connect to a shared Unity runtime, reducing startup time and resource duplication compared with running a separate Unity instance for each app.

    Unity 6.6

    Build smoother, deploy further: Fast Enter Play Mode, faster asset loading with Content Directories, a new Hierarchy window, and reach to Android XR devices such as XREAL AURA. Read about Android XR glasses support

    UI Toolkit Connector for Figma (experimental)

    Your Figma file becomes real Unity UI: Push Figma frames into Unity as editable UI Toolkit documents and pick up where design left off in UI Builder. Your design system comes with you: Figma variables carry over as themes, such as Dark and Light, and components become working Unity controls. Supported style and layout edits made in Unity can be pushed back to Figma manually or automatically, so design and build stay in sync. This is an early release and we’d love your feedback as we shape the product. Get the Figma plugin

    Q4 2026 Preview

    Now available: Industry AI Workflows (experimental)

    Weeks of prep work, done in hours: Connect your own AI agent to Asset Manager, Asset Transformer, and Pipeline Automation. Describe the outcome you want, and the agent builds the whole workflow. Point it at a STEP file and it imports, repairs, optimizes, QA-renders, exports, publishes, tags, and versions the result.

  • Use the agent you already have: Works with Claude Code, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot, so models stay under your existing AI policy.
  • Pipelines by description: Author, validate, trigger, and monitor Pipeline Automation jobs without writing JSON by hand.
  • Fast to set up: Install with two commands and one browser login. Run on public Unity Cloud or a self-hosted deployment.
  • No new SKU: Runs on the Asset Manager, Asset Transformer, and Pipeline Automation entitlements you already have.

    • Industry AI Workflows is an experimental release. Try AI Workflows today

    Unity USD Toolkit (experimental)

    Round-trip USD between Unity and Isaac Sim: Bring OpenUSD workflows into Unity. Read, write, and round-trip USD stages used in simulation pipelines, with hierarchy and metadata intact. Live scene sync keeps object positions, rotations, and scales aligned between Unity and NVIDIA Isaac Sim in real time. Prototype robotics workflows, validate digital twins, or iterate on synthetic data scenes without manual re-exports.

    This is an experimental release. Try it and tell us what your simulation team needs next. Explore the USD Toolkit

    Coming later this quarter

    This section describes features and timing still in development. These reflect our current plans, and availability could change.

    Editor agent plugins (beta)

    Official Unity plugins for Claude, Codex and Grok give AI agents Unity-built skills for common development tasks. Agents check your project, use the current API and verify results before handing work back. Skills are developed and maintained by specialist Unity teams, so you can expect better output and fewer coding errors. Kimi and Antigravity plugins coming later this year.

    Asset Manager Folder sharing

    Open the right folder to the right people. Share nested folders with specific people and set a role for each folder, so collaborators go straight to the assets they need.

    Asset Manager Collection sharing

    Protect the project, share the collection. Give external partners and agencies access to one collection of assets while the rest of your repository stays private.

    Unity 6.7 LTS

    Build confidently for the long term. The next Long Term Support release brings a year of Unity 6 performance and workflow gains to teams shipping at scale.

    Which Unity Industry release should you explore first?

    Start with the release that's costing you time:

  • Stuck building interactive 3D HMI? Start with the Unity Industry automotive HMI template or try the Figma plugin (experimental).
  • Testing robots on real hardware? Ask us about Simulation Pro early access.
  • Losing time prepping 3D data by hand? Try Industry AI Workflows (experimental) and let your own AI agent build the pipeline.

    • The thread through all of it: more people can build in real-time 3D, in more places. That means factory floors, car dashboards, and robot test beds.

    Ready to see what you can build with Unity Industry?Try Industry for freeLearn more

    Related resources

    Automotive HMI Template: Take it for a ride

    From simulation to real-world deployment: Unity Simulation Pro early access

    Unite Seoul 2026 Keynote Recap: Announcing Unity 7

    A beginner’s guide to Unity CLI and the Pipeline package

  • 配套还有 Unity Pipeline 内测：统一 API 把 DCC、IDE、CLI 与「受支持的 AI agent」都接进来，且**不需要 Editor 席位**；另外 UI Toolkit 的 Figma 连接器把设计稿变成可编辑 UI

中文摘要：Unity Industry 的年度回顾里，最值得记的是 10 月上线的 Industry AI Workflows（实验性）：开发者可以把自己的 AI agent 接到 Asset Manager、Asset Transformer 与 Pipeline Automation 上，用自然语言描述目标，由 agent 自行搭建整条工作流——官方给的例子是「指向一个 STEP 文件」，随后自动完成导入、修模、优化、QA 渲染、导出、发布与打标签。同期还有两项相关更新：Unity Pipeline 进入内测，用统一 API 把 DCC、IDE、CLI 与受支持的 AI agent 接入，且无需 Editor 席位；UI Toolkit 的 Figma 连接器把 Figma 画板转成可编辑的 Unity UI。整体方向是把「引擎 + 资产管线」变成 agent 可调用的接口集合。

2026 Industry releases and what’s coming in Q4

Oct 30, 2026|7 Min

Avery Vernon-Moore - Unity Technologies

Product Marketing Manager

Asset managementEngineAsset managementEngineAI

2026 has been a big year for Unity Industry, so we're looking back at the major Unity Industry releases and updates, plus a preview on what’s coming in Q4.

In March, Unity Studio made it possible to create interactive 3D experiences directly in a web browser. By September, robotics teams could prototype and validate systems in simulation before deploying them to physical hardware. In between, Unity Industry shipped 15+ releases.

Those releases span every part of the Unity Industry product suite. They serve teams building digital twins, simulations, HMI and embedded systems, robotics, XR training, and product configurators.

TL;DR: Unity Industry's 2026 releases at a glance

Short on time? Here's what Unity Industry shipped this year:

  • AI agents joined the 3D data pipeline:Industry AI Workflows launched in October as an experimental release, so your own AI agent can prep, optimize, and publish CAD data across Asset Manager, Asset Transformer, and Pipeline Automation.
  • Design and simulation tools connected to Unity: The experimental UI Toolkit Connector for Figma turns Figma frames into editable Unity UI, and the Unity USD Toolkit round-trips USD between Unity and NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
  • 3D creation moved into the browser:Unity Studio went GA in March, then added annotations, Editor export, and live co-editing.
  • Collaboration opened up beyond the Editor:Unity Pipeline entered closed beta, giving every role one API into a Unity production.
  • Enterprise security got independent proof: Unity's creator services are now SOC 2 Type 2 certified, and Asset Manager deploys in your own cloud.
  • Robotics and embedded got purpose-built tools: Simulation Pro entered early access. Automotive teams got multi-window control and a shared Android render service.
  • The Editor kept getting faster: Unity 6.4, 6.5, and 6.6 shipped, with Unity 6.7 LTS coming soon.

    • Below, we break down every Unity Industry release from 2026 by quarter and product, then preview what's coming in Q4.

    Unity Studio is generally available

    Bring 3D ideas to life, fast: Unity Studio is a web-based editor that lets anyone build and share interactive 3D apps. No coding and no installs. Import your 3D data, add interactivity, and share a link for review.

    6.4 brought faster scene building, smoother workflows, and ECS now built into the Editor: The release integrated Project Auditor, moved ECS packages into the core Editor release cycle, and expanded rendering, input, and platform support.

  • GameWindow multi-window support: Granular, runtime control over every window. Create, arrange, and control multiple Unity windows across one or more displays, built for automotive cockpits and industrial control panels. Read the documentation.

  • SOC 2 Type 2 certification:Asset Manager, Asset Transformer, Studio, Pipeline, and DevOps are SOC 2 Type 2 certified, audited by Coalfire. Visit the Trust Center

    Scale Unity skills across teams: Structured, role-based training for industrial teams, so they onboard faster and work more efficiently. Explore Academy Pro

    Build smoother, deploy further: Fast Enter Play Mode, faster asset loading with Content Directories, a new Hierarchy window, and reach to Android XR devices such as XREAL AURA. Read about Android XR glasses support

item.title: 发片不该是一串控制点：HairDeck 把每片头发当一个 token，集合式扩散一次去噪，还顺手出弹簧骨链 ｜ HairDeck: Animation-Ready Stylized Hair Cards from a Single Image
item.description:
一句话：单图生成可动画的发片资产：每片卡一个 token，集合扩散并行去噪，导出即可驱动。

要点：

  • 风格化角色的头发在游戏里就是 hair cards——美术摆的带状片，靠 spring bones 驱动；此前唯一的生成器 CHARM 把发型当作「一长串控制点」自回归解码
  • HairDeck 的关键观察是：一头发型其实是**一组无序的、由美术定义的基本体**，于是把每片卡作为单个 token，用集合式扩散 Transformer 对所有卡片一起去噪
  • 从单张图直接生成卡片与驱动它们的 spring-bone 链，得到「可动画」的资产，并可导出到下游工具使用

为什么值得看：「生成资产」和「生成可用的资产」差在结构与绑定：这条把拓扑单位（一片卡）当 token，既符合美术工作流，又天然支持并行生成与后续绑定。做角色资产管线、尤其是风格化项目的团队应当关注这套表示。

中文摘要：游戏与虚拟人里风格化角色的头发通常由 hair cards 构成：美术摆放的带状面片就是可见的头发，再由 spring bones 驱动。已有基于图像的方法要么产出写实头发、要么给一整块融合网格；唯一生成风格化发片的 CHARM 则把发型当成一长串控制点做自回归解码。HairDeck 观察到「一套发片发型其实是一组无序的、由美术定义的基本体」，于是把每片卡编码成单个 token，用集合式扩散 Transformer 一次性对所有卡片去噪；从单张图同时生成卡片与驱动它们的弹簧骨链，得到可直接进入下游工具链的可动画资产。相比自回归的长序列解码，这种表示更贴近美术的实际操作单位。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-30

本期推送：2026-10-31

HairDeck: Animation-Ready Stylized Hair Cards from a Single Image

Abstract

The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is built from hair cards: artist-placed ribbons whose geometry is the visible hair, animated by spring bones. Existing image-based methods produce realistic hair or a single fused mesh, while CHARM, the only generator of stylized hair cards, decodes a hairstyle autoregressively as a long sequence of control points. Observing that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, we propose HairDeck, which generates it as one: each card is a single token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all cards together. From a single image, HairDeck generates the cards and the spring-bone chains that drive them, yielding an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats. On CHARM’s own test set, it lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster, and from single images it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand-based methods.

Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/HairDeck

11footnotetext: Equal contribution.22footnotetext: Corresponding authors.

1 Introduction

3D generators now produce convincing shapes from a single image [83, 72, 71, 77], but not the structure that artists build assets from. The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is a clear example. It is made of hair cards: a few dozen to over a hundred ribbons, each placed by an artist, whose geometry is the visible hair. Unlike the alpha-textured hair cards of realistic hair, flat strips whose texture stands in for many strands [20, 88, 60], these cards have a rhombic or triangular cross-section whose width and thickness vary along the card. Such hair is commonly animated with spring bones: short chains of bones hung from the head whose tips are simulated every frame, so that the hair sways and settles. Similar simulations ship as Dynamic Bone in Unity [18], PhysBones in VRChat [61], Kawaii Physics in Unreal Engine [36] and a node in Godot [10]. Artists place every card and rig every chain by hand.

Existing methods do not produce this asset. Hair generators output realistic strands [49, 13, 42], including recent ones that accept stylized images [28, 31, 44, 65], and card extraction turns such strands into alpha-textured cards for realistic hair [88, 60]. Image-to-3D generators [71, 77] output a single fused mesh with no cards to animate. CHARM [15] is the only generator of stylized hair cards and introduced the benchmark for them. It generates the control points of a hairstyle one at a time, as a sequence of hundreds to thousands of discretized tokens.

We observe that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, and we generate it as one. Like CHARM, we describe each card by its control points (position, width and thickness), and we add its cross-section type and its root normal, the width direction at the root, so each card keeps the cross-section and the orientation the artist gave it. What we change is the unit of generation, with two designs. First, each card becomes one continuous token: a card VAE encodes its variable-length control points into a latent, and the token holds this latent with the card’s root position, root normal and cross-section type, so a hairstyle has one token per card, about 70 on average. Second, all tokens of a hairstyle are generated together: a set diffusion transformer without positional embedding denoises them with flow matching [25, 27], and an existence flag on each token decides how many cards appear. Each design makes generation more accurate and faster. Together they amount to a simple rule for assets made of artist-defined primitives: one token per primitive, and no order among them.

A single image shows the hair relative to the head, so we predict the cards in a head frame anchored to the face, which improves where the hair sits without changing its shape. Images also come in many drawing styles, so we widen the appearance of our training renders in two ways: synthetic style augmentation, which improves accuracy on stylized inputs, and renders restyled by an image-editing model [68], which keep the card structure stable across styles.

Cards alone do not move. We generate the spring-bone chains with the same recipe: each chain becomes one token holding its path, joint count and stiffness, and a second set diffusion transformer generates all chains of a hairstyle together from its card tokens. With a fixed geometric skinning, the cards and chains form an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    A card token for stylized hair: a representation that keeps the cross-section type and the root normal, and a card VAE that encodes the variable-length control points into one continuous latent and decodes the card by arc length.

  • •

    A set formulation of hair-card generation: a set diffusion transformer without positional embedding generates all card tokens of a hairstyle together, and an existence flag on each token decides how many cards appear.

  • •

    Single-image generation with a face-anchored head frame, synthetic style augmentation and restyled renders.

  • •

    Spring-bone chains generated as a second set conditioned on the card tokens, which makes the output animatable.

    • We evaluate on CHARM’s test set with its protocol and also measure the orientation of every card against the original artist meshes. HairDeck lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster. From a single image, it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand generators.

    2 Related Work

    Strand-based hair modeling.

    Hair reconstruction methods can recover strands from multi-view images or videos [35, 41, 48, 69, 57, 32, 80] and from single images [70, 86, 87, 50]. Generative models synthesize strands from latent codes [90, 13], text [49] and images [42]. Recent ones accept stylized or anime images [28, 31, 44, 65], but their output is still strands, the representation of realistic hair. The stylized hair we generate uses cards instead.

    Hair cards.

    Real-time engines render realistic hair with textured strips [20], the alpha-textured hair cards whose texture stands in for many strands. Zheng et al.[88] and Strands2Cards [60] convert strand grooms into such cards, HairLRM [44] applies the former to its generated strands, CGHair [33] reconstructs card-based hair from multi-view images, Lee et al.[22] inpaint strips from the sparse strands of a single portrait with a diffusion model on the scalp UV map, HairCS [30] turns cards back into strands, and production tools ship card generators for grooms [8, 46]. Stylized hair uses a different card, whose geometry is the visible hair. CHARM [15] introduced the generation of such cards with a control-point representation, a dataset of anime hairstyles (the benchmark we use) and an autoregressive transformer that emits the control points of a hairstyle one at a time. We add the cross-section type and the root normal to its description of a card and change the unit of generation.

    Stylized 3D characters.

    Image-based methods for anime characters reconstruct stylized heads [5] or full characters [38, 64], and others separate the body, clothing and hair into components [14, 16, 40]. In all of them the hair is a continuous surface, fused with the character or as a separate component, rather than a set of cards. Earlier work modeled anime and cartoon hair from sketches, skeletons or parametric clumps [34, 43, 76] or as 2.5D layers [79].

    Structured and set generation.

    Native 3D generators encode shapes as latent sets [81, 85, 83, 4] or structured latents [72, 71] and output a single surface. Assets built from discrete elements are mostly generated autoregressively: meshes as sequences of face or vertex tokens [45, 6, 66, 84, 12], ordered along triangle strips and UV charts in Strips as Tokens [73], and shapes as sequences of primitives [78]. Other work generates the elements of an asset together. 3DTopia-XL [7] gives each primitive one token and denoises the tokens with a diffusion transformer without positional encoding. StrokeFusion [89] encodes each sketch stroke with a VAE and diffuses the unordered set of stroke latents with presence flags. DiffuScene [59], SALAD [21], MeshFlow [56], BrepGen [74] and PartCrafter [24] jointly generate the objects of a scene, part latents, the triangles of a mesh, the faces of CAD models and the parts of objects. We build on this set formulation and design it for hair cards: a card VAE turns each card into one token, the set is conditioned on a point cloud or a single image, and a second set of spring-bone chains is conditioned on the cards. On the same tokens, set generation is both more accurate and faster than autoregressive generation.

    Rigging and secondary motion.

    Automatic rigging predicts a skeleton and skinning weights for a given mesh [75, 52, 26, 11, 51, 55]. UniRig [82] also predicts spring bones and their physical attributes on VRoid characters [39], and DRiVE [54] generates skeletons that include hair and skirt bones for anime characters represented as 3D Gaussians. Both rig an existing asset. We generate the spring-bone chains together with the hair they drive, conditioned on the generated cards, and simulate them with the spring-bone update of the VRM specification [62, 63].

    3 Method

    We propose HairDeck, which generates the cards of a hairstyle and the spring-bone chains to animate them (Fig.2). Each card is encoded into one continuous token (Sec.3.1), and a set diffusion transformer (set DiT) generates all card tokens together, conditioned on a single image (Sec.3.3) or on a point cloud (Sec.3.2), the input of CHARM’s benchmark. The card VAE decodes each token back into control points, from which we build the mesh. A second set DiT, the chain DiT, generates the spring-bone chains conditioned on the card tokens, and a fixed geometric skinning attaches the cards to them (Sec.3.4).

    3.1 Hair cards as tokens

    Cards.

    Like CHARM [15], we describe a hair card by a polyline of n control points (pᵢ,wᵢ,hᵢ), each with a position pᵢ∈ℝ³, a width wᵢ and a thickness hᵢ. We add two attributes that this description leaves out: the cross-section type s, rhombic or triangular, instead of one rhombic cross-section for all cards, and the root normal d₁, the width direction of the card at its root, read from the artist mesh instead of being estimated from the first three control points. To build a card mesh, we propagate d₁ along the polyline with a rotation-minimizing (Bishop) frame [1], giving the width direction dᵢ at every control point, and sweep the cross-section along it.

    Card VAE.

    Cards differ in their number of control points, while the generator needs a token of fixed size. A card VAE encodes the control points of a card, relative to its root position p₁, into a latent z∈ℝ³² (Fig.3, top). Its encoder is a transformer over the control points, each tagged with its arc-length fraction uᵢ∈[0,1], together with a learned summary token whose output gives the mean and log-variance of z. The decoder predicts the number of control points n from z with a classification head and evaluates the card at n uniformly spaced arc-length fractions, embedded with low-frequency Fourier features [58], with a transformer modulated by z through adaLN-Zero [37]. The loss is a squared error on positions, widths and thicknesses in world units, plus a cross-entropy on n and a small KL term [19].

    Card tokens.

    Each card becomes a token

    x=(p₁,d₁,z,s,e)∈ℝ⁴⁰

    		(1)

    that holds its root position and root normal, its latent, its cross-section type s (-1 for rhombic, +1 for triangular) and an existence flag e=+1. A hairstyle is a set of N=192 token slots, and an empty slot is all zeros except e=-1. After sampling, we read s and e by their sign.

    3.2 Set diffusion of hair cards

    Set diffusion transformer.

    The set DiT, a diffusion transformer [37], denoises the N token slots of a hairstyle together (Fig.3, bottom). It uses no positional embedding, so it is equivariant to permutations of the slots, and no order of the cards is ever defined. Each block applies self-attention across the slots, cross-attention to the condition tokens C and an MLP, all modulated by the timestep and the pooled condition through adaLN-Zero. For a point cloud, C is the output of a frozen Dora-VAE encoder [4]; for an image, it comes from an image encoder (Sec.3.3).

    Flow matching.

    We train the generator with flow matching [25, 27]. For the token set X₀ of a training hairstyle and Gaussian noise ε, the network v_θ predicts the velocity along the straight path between them:

    Xₜ=(1-t) X₀+t ε,(2)
    L=𝔼_X₀,ε,t ∥v_θ(Xₜ,t,C)-(ε-X₀)∥_w²,(3)

    where ∥·∥_w weights the root position and the existence flag by 4 and the other components by 1. We drop the condition in training to allow classifier-free guidance [17]. At test time we integrate with the Euler method and guidance and decode every slot with e>0. The existence flags let the card count settle during denoising together with the shapes.

    3.3 Generation from a single image

    Image condition.

    The image model is a set DiT of the same architecture, conditioned on the output tokens of a frozen DINOv3 ViT-L/16 [47] applied to a square crop around the hair and the face. For in-the-wild images, SAM 3 [3] provides the hair and face masks.

    Head frame.

    The size and position of a hairstyle follow its head, whereas the dataset frame scales every character to unit height. We therefore predict the cards in a head frame anchored to the face (Fig.5). Each character is mapped by p↦k p+b, where k=W/w scales its face width w to the median face width W of the training set and b moves the top center of its face to a common point O; widths and thicknesses scale with k. On rendered test characters, we map the output back with each character’s own k and b, which places the hair on its real head.

    Training images.

    We render every training character from 8 views in Blender [2], with random body poses, hair motion from spring-bone simulation, and cameras from the front to the back of the head; the target is always the rest-pose card set. We widen the appearance of the renders with synthetic style augmentation, such as halftone, XDoG [67] line drawings, flat colors and painterly filters (AppendixA), and we mix in renders restyled into three drawing styles, gacha (mobile-game) art, thick paint and semi-realistic painting, by an image-editing model [68].

    3.4 Spring-bone chains

    Cards alone are static, but the hair of game and avatar characters must move with them. Artists achieve this with spring-bone chains, sequences of joints hung from the head whose simulated motion the cards follow, and rig them by hand for every hairstyle; we generate the chains so that the output can be animated directly.

    Chain tokens.

    A chain becomes a 27-dimensional token of its path (8 points by arc length), joint count, stiffness and existence flag, and a hairstyle a set of up to 48 chains.

    Chain generation.

    The chain DiT has the same block design as the set DiT and generates the chain tokens of a hairstyle in the head frame with flow matching, cross-attending to its card tokens (Fig.3). It is trained on the ground-truth card tokens and, at test time, reads the generated ones; cards from a point cloud are first mapped into the head frame (AppendixA).

    Skinning and simulation.

    After generation, a fixed geometric skinning binds the cards to the chains. We place the joints uniformly along each generated path. A card follows the chain closest to the lower 60% of its centerline if their mean distance is below 0.4 face widths, and otherwise moves rigidly with the head; each of its points follows the nearest segment of that chain, blended linearly with the neighboring segment within half a segment of each joint, with a weight that rises from 0 at the chain’s root to 1 over 0.05 face widths of arc length. We tune these two thresholds against the artists’ skin weights in the training data. We simulate the chains with the VRM spring-bone update of UniVRM [62, 63], using the predicted stiffness and the drag and gravity of most VRoid chains.

    3.5 Implementation details

    The card VAE has four encoder and four decoder layers of width 256, the set DiT 12 layers of width 768 (181.3M parameters) and the chain DiT 8 layers of width 384 (30.5M). We train the point-cloud model for 80K steps with batch size 64 and the image model for 100K steps with batch size 48, both with AdamW [29] at learning rate 10⁻⁴; the image model starts from the point-cloud model. We sample with 50 Euler steps and a guidance scale of 2; AppendixA lists the remaining settings.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Setup

    Data.

    We use the dataset of CHARM [15], built from VRoid characters [39]: we take 36,440 of its training hairstyles and test on its 100 test hairstyles, with the point clouds CHARM released. For single images, we render the front views of the 76 test characters whose complete models are available, and we collect 40 in-the-wild images, anime illustrations sampled at random and stratified by hairstyle.

    Metrics.

    On point clouds we follow CHARM’s protocol: it compares the generated cards with its ground truth, rebuilt from its card templates, by Chamfer distance (CD), earth mover’s distance (EMD), Hausdorff distance (HD) and voxel IoU. As the templates estimate card orientations, we also evaluate against the original artist meshes. Our orientation metric matches every generated card to the artist card closest in CD and averages the angle between their width directions over 32 positions along the card. Root precision and recall are the shares of generated and ground-truth cards whose root position lies within 2% of the character height of a root position in the other set. For single images, we align every output to the ground truth (AppendixD) and report the aligned CD and IoU on surface samples. The failure rate is the share of results that have fewer than 25% of the ground-truth cards (16 cards for in-the-wild images) or leave the scalp bare (hair covers less than 80% of the top or the back of the head); for the image-to-3D generators, whose output is one fused surface without cards, only the scalp criterion applies. We time every method on one NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU (48 GB) with batch size 1, from the input to the cards, before meshing.

    4.2 Generation from point clouds

    Tables1 and 4 compare HairDeck with CHARM and autoregressive mesh generators on CHARM’s test set. HairDeck lowers CHARM’s CD from 0.0117 to 0.0066 and the orientation error from 40.0° to 16.8°, while taking 1.01 s instead of 33.7 s. Retrieving the training hairstyle with the closest condition reaches a CD of 0.0119, so CHARM is about as accurate as recalling a training hairstyle. The mesh generators output a few large shells (MeshAnything V2, BPT) or triangle fragments (DeepMesh).

    The card-level autoregressive model in Tab.1 generates our card tokens one after another, with about as many parameters as our set DiT. One token per card already lowers CHARM’s CD to 0.0078 and the orientation error to 16.6°. Generating the same tokens as a set lowers CD further to 0.0066 and runs 6.8 times faster than the autoregressive model, which also stops early, with 60.8 cards on average against 68.9 for the set DiT and 67.4 in the ground truth.

    4.3 Generation from single images

    Table2 compares HairDeck with CHARM’s image model, the image-to-3D generators TRELLIS.2 [71] and Hunyuan3D-2.1 [77], and DiffLocks [42], whose strands we convert into cards. On the rendered test characters, HairDeck has the lowest aligned CD (0.0089, against 0.0139 to 0.0186); it fails on 3.5% of them and on 10% of the in-the-wild images, against 13.2% to 34.2% and 17.5% to 77.5% for the other methods, and takes 1.33 s per image, against 15.6 s to 83.0 s. Cascades that pass a point cloud sampled from an image-to-3D output to CHARM or our point-cloud model reach aligned CDs of 0.0138 to 0.0170 and fail on 22.4% to 32.9% of the test characters (Tab.5). Figure6 covers anime illustrations and a photorealistic portrait: the image-to-3D generators produce one fused surface, and the converted DiffLocks strands leave the crown bare and end in blocky clumps on the portrait. Figure7 shows hairstyles generated from in-the-wild images in many drawing styles.

    4.4 Ablations

    Card token.

    The card VAE latent gives a lower CD than raw control points (Tab.3; 0.0066 against 0.0068), and its output is as smooth as the artists’ cards (turn 14.2° against 14.1°), whereas raw control points give jagged cards (21.9°). A VAE that decodes the control points by index, as StrokeFusion [89] decodes the points of a stroke, reaches a CD of 0.0079 with jagged cards (25.3°); our arc-length decoding, adaLN modulation and world-unit loss make the difference (Tab.8). Without the root normal, the orientation error rises from 16.8° to 26.4°. Without the existence flag, a head that predicts the card count first generates too few cards (62.8 against 68.9).

    Data, encoder and size.

    Training on CHARM’s card templates raises the orientation error to 26.7°. With CHARM’s encoder (Michelangelo [85]) or a generator of 54.6M parameters, fewer than CHARM’s 61.2M, CD stays at 0.0068 and 0.0072, far below CHARM’s 0.0117.

    Image model.

    We test the image model on the front views of the 76 test characters and on their restyles into gacha art, thick paint and semi-realistic painting (Fig.20). Without the head frame, the model must infer the head’s size and position: its CD before alignment rises from 0.0136 to 0.0189 and the overlap (IoU) of the reprojected hair with the input’s hair drops from 0.829 to 0.798, while its aligned CD stays at 0.0089. On the restyles, synthetic style augmentation lowers the aligned CD from 0.0100 to 0.0097, and restyled training images raise root precision from 0.781 to 0.849 at a similar root recall: without them, the model adds cards that start where no artist card does.

    4.5 Spring bones

    We evaluate chains on the 58 test hairstyles that have them (Tabs.4 and 8) against the artists’ chains: by position (CD in face widths W, recall and precision at 0.1 W), by the hair motion under a head turn, nod, jump and sway, and by the fit to the cards (AppendixA). On the artists’ cards, the chain DiT recovers the artists’ chains better than retrieval (recall 0.625 against 0.289, precision 0.585 against 0.285) and moves the hair more like the artists’ chains do: the correlation of the per-point motion is 0.702, against 0.622 for retrieval and 0.538 for a procedural rig that places chains by rules (AppendixD). On generated cards, recall is 0.542 from point clouds and 0.390 from single images, and the fit to the cards stays at 0.95.

    4.6 Applications

    Interpolation.

    The Dora encoder computes the condition tokens of a point cloud at query points that farthest point sampling picks from it, so the tokens of two point clouds have no correspondence. To interpolate between two conditions, we match the tokens of the second to those of the first by Hungarian matching on the positions of their query points and blend the matched tokens linearly (Fig.9).

    Rigging existing hairstyles.

    The chain DiT reads only card tokens, so it can also rig card hairstyles that an artist modeled without spring bones; its evaluation on the artists’ cards in Sec.4.5 measures this use.

    5 Limitations and Conclusion

    Limitations.

    HairDeck learns from stylized VRoid hairstyles, so very short hair and the alpha-textured cards of realistic hair lie outside its training data. It generates the geometry and UV coordinates of the cards but no textures. Some VRoid characters model bows and hats with hair cards, so HairDeck generates them as cards when the input shows them; filtering such cards from the training data would avoid this. The chain DiT follows the chain layouts common among VRoid characters and generates fewer chains for unusual ones, such as many chains radiating from the crown. Figure23 shows failure cases.

    Conclusion.

    HairDeck generates the stylized hair cards of a character and the spring-bone chains that animate them from a single image. Treating a hairstyle as an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, with one token per card and all tokens generated together, makes generation more accurate and faster than autoregressive decoding, and the same recipe generates the chains. Assets built from other artist-defined primitives, such as garments sewn from panels or drawings made of strokes, can be generated in the same way.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Implementation details

    Card VAE.

    Cards are padded to 128 control points, with the padding masked in attention. The decoder embeds each arc-length fraction with Fourier features [58] of 6 frequencies. The cross-entropy on the number of control points is weighted by 0.1 and the KL term [19] by 10⁻⁶. We train it for 80K steps with batch size 1,024, drawing each batch from cards of similar length, with AdamW [29] (β=(0.9,0.99), no weight decay) at learning rate 3×10⁻⁴, a linear warmup over 500 steps, a cosine decay to 10% of the peak and gradient clipping at norm 1. It has 8.07M parameters.

    Card tokens.

    Root positions and latents are standardized with their mean and standard deviation over the training set; root normals are unit vectors. Hairstyles with more than 192 cards (0.6% of the training set) are left out of training.

    Set DiT.

    Timesteps are sampled as t=sigmoid(ξ) with ξ∼ℕ(0,1)[9]. Both models use AdamW (β=(0.9,0.99), no weight decay) with gradient clipping at norm 1; the learning rate warms up linearly over 2,000 steps for the point-cloud model and 1,000 for the image model and then stays constant; we sample with an exponential moving average (decay 0.9995). With probability 0.1, learned null tokens replace the condition tokens. Classifier-free guidance [17] combines the two velocities as v_∅+γ (v_C-v_∅) with guidance scale γ=2, and the Euler method takes 50 uniform steps from t=1 to t=0.

    Point-cloud condition.

    We use the released Dora-VAE 1.1 encoder [4] and cache, for every training point cloud, its 512 output tokens of width 768, taken after the final layer norm and before the KL bottleneck.

    Image condition.

    The crop is the square around the union of the hair and face masks, with an 8% margin on each side. During training we jitter it: its scale by a log-normal factor (σ=0.08), its center by ℕ(0,0.04²) times the side length, and with probability 0.15 we cut off its bottom, keeping 45% to 80% of the hair height as in half-body images. DINOv3 [47] runs at 448 pixels and returns one class token, four register tokens and 784 patch tokens; a layer norm, a linear projection to the model width and a learned positional embedding turn them into the condition. For in-the-wild images, SAM 3 [3] segments with the prompts “person”, “anime character”, “hair” and “face”; the union of the four masks, cleaned with a morphological closing and hole filling, is the matte that cuts the character out onto a white background, and the hair and face masks give the crop.

    Head frame.

    Figure5 illustrates the head frame of Sec.3.3. W=0.1276 and O=(0,0.4791,0.0258) are medians over the training set in the dataset frame. The face width w of a character is the width of its face bounding box, and its anchor is the top center of that box (the center in x and z, the top in y). Over the training set, k ranges from 0.70 to 1.24 (5th to 95th percentile).

    Training renders.

    Each training character is rendered from 8 views with Blender 4.2 [2] (EEVEE) at 768 pixels. For each view we draw a body pose (natural 70%, hands near the head 25%, T or A pose 5%, with jittered IK targets, randomly mirrored one-hand poses, random spine, neck and head rotations and finger curls), a hair state from the VRM 0.x spring-bone simulation [62] (at rest in 35% of the views, otherwise swinging or settling after a head turn, nod, body turn, jump or sway; in 30% of the views the hair gravity is set to 0.1 to 0.6), and a camera direction relative to the head (front and three-quarter views 80%, side 10%, back 10%; elevation drawn from ℕ(5\textdegree,(12\textdegree)²) and truncated to [-25\textdegree,40\textdegree]). Lighting is a preset or a random sun, and 80% of the views draw MToon [53] outlines.

    Appearance augmentation.

    The synthetic style augmentation draws from grayscale, halftone, XDoG [67] line drawings, full hue rotation, channel permutation, flat colors, painterly filters, thick ink lines, rim light, low resolution, blur, sharpening, noise and JPEG compression. 40% of the samples keep a light augmentation: brightness, contrast, saturation and hue jitter, blur and JPEG compression with probability 0.3 each, and occasional grayscale.

    Restyled images.

    We restyle training renders with Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 [68] (20 steps) into gacha (mobile-game) art, thick paint and semi-realistic painting, and keep a restyled image only if its hair and character silhouettes (SAM 3) match the original (IoU at least 0.85 for the hair and 0.9 for the character). The pool holds 21,336 images, and a training sample is drawn from it with probability 0.33.

    Spring-bone chains.

    For the point-cloud model, whose cards are in the dataset frame, we map the generated cards into the head frame with the test character’s k and b and re-encode them with the card VAE before running the chain DiT. Chains come from the VRM files of the training characters: 32,979 of the 36,440 training hairstyles have hair chains, and leaving out those with more than 48 chains or more than 192 cards leaves 32,599 hairstyles with 438,672 chains. The chain DiT has 6 attention heads. It is trained for 80K steps with batch size 128, AdamW at learning rate 2×10⁻⁴ after a linear warmup over 1,000 steps, condition dropout 0.1 and an exponential moving average with decay 0.999; all loss weights are 1 except 4 for the existence flag, and the chain slots are randomly permuted for every training sample. We tune the two skinning thresholds of Sec.3.4, the assignment distance and the ramp length, on 200 random training characters with chains. For each character, its own chains with their own physics parameters drive 16 points per card under four head motions (a turn, a nod, a jump and a sideways sway), once with the artists’ skin weights, where each point takes the weights of the nearest vertex of the hair mesh, and once with our skinning. We choose the thresholds that maximize the motion correlation of Tab.4: sweeping the assignment distance over 0.15, 0.25, 0.4 and 0.6 face widths and the ramp length over 0.01 to 0.3 face widths gives 0.4 and 0.05 (correlation 0.84), and the ramp length barely matters. On the 58 test hairstyles with chains, our skinning reaches a motion correlation of 0.77 with the artists’ skin weights. The simulation follows the reference spring-bone update of UniVRM [63]: at every frame, the tip of each bone keeps (1-drag) of its previous displacement, moves toward its rest direction, rotated by the parent, by stiffness times the time step and along gravity by gravity times the time step, and is then pulled back to the bone length. We use no colliders and run at 60 fps. Generated chains use their predicted stiffness, drag 0.4 and no gravity.

    Chain metrics.

    In Tab.4, lengths are in face widths W, and each chain is represented by 8 points along its path. CD is the Chamfer distance between the path points of the generated and the artists’ chains. Recall and precision are the shares of artist and generated chains whose points lie, on average, within 0.1 W of the path of a chain in the other set. For motion, the artists’ cards are skinned to each set of chains as in Sec.3.4, the artists’ chains keep their own physics parameters, and each rig is simulated under four head motions of 2.5 s each: a turn (a yaw of 50° in 0.35 s, then held), a nod (a pitch of 25° down and back in 0.5 s), a jump (0.15 m up and down in 0.6 s) and a sideways sway (6 cm at 1.5 Hz for two cycles). The displacement of each of 16 points per card is taken relative to the moving head, minus its displacement with the head at rest, so that sagging under gravity does not count. Motion is the correlation over card points between the mean displacement of each point and that under the artists’ chains, averaged over the four motions, and Ampl. is the mean displacement. Fit is the share of chain path points within 0.1 W of the card meshes.

    Export.

    Every card mesh carries UV coordinates: the first runs across the width, so the two faces of a card mirror each other and need no seam, and the second is the arc-length fraction, from the root (0) to the tip (1). To export to VRM, we replace the hair of a character model, its hair bones and its hair spring-bone groups with the generated cards, one spring-bone group per generated chain, and use the geometric skinning of Sec.3.4 as skin weights. Results from in-the-wild images are exported the same way, on the body of a test character with the hair color taken from the image.

    Compute.

    Each model trains on one NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU (48 GB): the card VAE in 4 hours, the point-cloud model in about 10 hours, the chain DiT in about 3 hours and the image model, starting from the point-cloud model, in about 27 hours.

    Appendix B Additional comparisons and ablations
item.content:encoded:
一句话：单图生成可动画的发片资产：每片卡一个 token，集合扩散并行去噪，导出即可驱动。

要点：

  • 风格化角色的头发在游戏里就是 hair cards——美术摆的带状片，靠 spring bones 驱动；此前唯一的生成器 CHARM 把发型当作「一长串控制点」自回归解码
  • HairDeck 的关键观察是：一头发型其实是**一组无序的、由美术定义的基本体**，于是把每片卡作为单个 token，用集合式扩散 Transformer 对所有卡片一起去噪
  • 从单张图直接生成卡片与驱动它们的 spring-bone 链，得到「可动画」的资产，并可导出到下游工具使用

为什么值得看：「生成资产」和「生成可用的资产」差在结构与绑定：这条把拓扑单位（一片卡）当 token，既符合美术工作流，又天然支持并行生成与后续绑定。做角色资产管线、尤其是风格化项目的团队应当关注这套表示。

中文摘要：游戏与虚拟人里风格化角色的头发通常由 hair cards 构成：美术摆放的带状面片就是可见的头发，再由 spring bones 驱动。已有基于图像的方法要么产出写实头发、要么给一整块融合网格；唯一生成风格化发片的 CHARM 则把发型当成一长串控制点做自回归解码。HairDeck 观察到「一套发片发型其实是一组无序的、由美术定义的基本体」，于是把每片卡编码成单个 token，用集合式扩散 Transformer 一次性对所有卡片去噪；从单张图同时生成卡片与驱动它们的弹簧骨链，得到可直接进入下游工具链的可动画资产。相比自回归的长序列解码，这种表示更贴近美术的实际操作单位。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-30

本期推送：2026-10-31

HairDeck: Animation-Ready Stylized Hair Cards from a Single Image

Abstract

The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is built from hair cards: artist-placed ribbons whose geometry is the visible hair, animated by spring bones. Existing image-based methods produce realistic hair or a single fused mesh, while CHARM, the only generator of stylized hair cards, decodes a hairstyle autoregressively as a long sequence of control points. Observing that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, we propose HairDeck, which generates it as one: each card is a single token, and a set diffusion transformer denoises all cards together. From a single image, HairDeck generates the cards and the spring-bone chains that drive them, yielding an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats. On CHARM’s own test set, it lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster, and from single images it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand-based methods.

Project page: https://hyzcluster.github.io/HairDeck

11footnotetext: Equal contribution.22footnotetext: Corresponding authors.

1 Introduction

3D generators now produce convincing shapes from a single image [83, 72, 71, 77], but not the structure that artists build assets from. The hair of stylized characters in games and avatars is a clear example. It is made of hair cards: a few dozen to over a hundred ribbons, each placed by an artist, whose geometry is the visible hair. Unlike the alpha-textured hair cards of realistic hair, flat strips whose texture stands in for many strands [20, 88, 60], these cards have a rhombic or triangular cross-section whose width and thickness vary along the card. Such hair is commonly animated with spring bones: short chains of bones hung from the head whose tips are simulated every frame, so that the hair sways and settles. Similar simulations ship as Dynamic Bone in Unity [18], PhysBones in VRChat [61], Kawaii Physics in Unreal Engine [36] and a node in Godot [10]. Artists place every card and rig every chain by hand.

Existing methods do not produce this asset. Hair generators output realistic strands [49, 13, 42], including recent ones that accept stylized images [28, 31, 44, 65], and card extraction turns such strands into alpha-textured cards for realistic hair [88, 60]. Image-to-3D generators [71, 77] output a single fused mesh with no cards to animate. CHARM [15] is the only generator of stylized hair cards and introduced the benchmark for them. It generates the control points of a hairstyle one at a time, as a sequence of hundreds to thousands of discretized tokens.

We observe that a card hairstyle is an unordered set of artist-defined primitives, and we generate it as one. Like CHARM, we describe each card by its control points (position, width and thickness), and we add its cross-section type and its root normal, the width direction at the root, so each card keeps the cross-section and the orientation the artist gave it. What we change is the unit of generation, with two designs. First, each card becomes one continuous token: a card VAE encodes its variable-length control points into a latent, and the token holds this latent with the card’s root position, root normal and cross-section type, so a hairstyle has one token per card, about 70 on average. Second, all tokens of a hairstyle are generated together: a set diffusion transformer without positional embedding denoises them with flow matching [25, 27], and an existence flag on each token decides how many cards appear. Each design makes generation more accurate and faster. Together they amount to a simple rule for assets made of artist-defined primitives: one token per primitive, and no order among them.

A single image shows the hair relative to the head, so we predict the cards in a head frame anchored to the face, which improves where the hair sits without changing its shape. Images also come in many drawing styles, so we widen the appearance of our training renders in two ways: synthetic style augmentation, which improves accuracy on stylized inputs, and renders restyled by an image-editing model [68], which keep the card structure stable across styles.

Cards alone do not move. We generate the spring-bone chains with the same recipe: each chain becomes one token holding its path, joint count and stiffness, and a second set diffusion transformer generates all chains of a hairstyle together from its card tokens. With a fixed geometric skinning, the cards and chains form an animatable asset that exports to ready-to-use downstream formats.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    A card token for stylized hair: a representation that keeps the cross-section type and the root normal, and a card VAE that encodes the variable-length control points into one continuous latent and decodes the card by arc length.

  • •

    A set formulation of hair-card generation: a set diffusion transformer without positional embedding generates all card tokens of a hairstyle together, and an existence flag on each token decides how many cards appear.

  • •

    Single-image generation with a face-anchored head frame, synthetic style augmentation and restyled renders.

  • •

    Spring-bone chains generated as a second set conditioned on the card tokens, which makes the output animatable.

    • We evaluate on CHARM’s test set with its protocol and also measure the orientation of every card against the original artist meshes. HairDeck lowers Chamfer distance by 44% and card-orientation error by more than half while running 33 times faster. From a single image, it outperforms CHARM, image-to-3D pipelines and strand generators.

    2 Related Work

    Strand-based hair modeling.

    Hair reconstruction methods can recover strands from multi-view images or videos [35, 41, 48, 69, 57, 32, 80] and from single images [70, 86, 87, 50]. Generative models synthesize strands from latent codes [90, 13], text [49] and images [42]. Recent ones accept stylized or anime images [28, 31, 44, 65], but their output is still strands, the representation of realistic hair. The stylized hair we generate uses cards instead.

    Hair cards.

    Real-time engines render realistic hair with textured strips [20], the alpha-textured hair cards whose texture stands in for many strands. Zheng et al.[88] and Strands2Cards [60] convert strand grooms into such cards, HairLRM [44] applies the former to its generated strands, CGHair [33] reconstructs card-based hair from multi-view images, Lee et al.[22] inpaint strips from the sparse strands of a single portrait with a diffusion model on the scalp UV map, HairCS [30] turns cards back into strands, and production tools ship card generators for grooms [8, 46]. Stylized hair uses a different card, whose geometry is the visible hair. CHARM [15] introduced the generation of such cards with a control-point representation, a dataset of anime hairstyles (the benchmark we use) and an autoregressive transformer that emits the control points of a hairstyle one at a time. We add the cross-section type and the root normal to its description of a card and change the unit of generation.

    Stylized 3D characters.

    Image-based methods for anime characters reconstruct stylized heads [5] or full characters [38, 64], and others separate the body, clothing and hair into components [14, 16, 40]. In all of them the hair is a continuous surface, fused with the character or as a separate component, rather than a set of cards. Earlier work modeled anime and cartoon hair from sketches, skeletons or parametric clumps [34, 43, 76] or as 2.5D layers [79].

    Structured and set generation.

    Native 3D generators encode shapes as latent sets [81, 85, 83, 4] or structured latents [72, 71] and output a single surface. Assets built from discrete elements are mostly generated autoregressively: meshes as sequences of face or vertex tokens [45, 6, 66, 84, 12], ordered along triangle strips and UV charts in Strips as Tokens [73], and shapes as sequences of primitives [78]. Other work generates the elements of an asset together. 3DTopia-XL [7] gives each primitive one token and denoises the tokens with a diffusion transformer without positional encoding. StrokeFusion [89] encodes each sketch stroke with a VAE and diffuses the unordered set of stroke latents with presence flags. DiffuScene [59], SALAD [21], MeshFlow [56], BrepGen [74] and PartCrafter [24] jointly generate the objects of a scene, part latents, the triangles of a mesh, the faces of CAD models and the parts of objects. We build on this set formulation and design it for hair cards: a card VAE turns each card into one token, the set is conditioned on a point cloud or a single image, and a second set of spring-bone chains is conditioned on the cards. On the same tokens, set generation is both more accurate and faster than autoregressive generation.

    Rigging and secondary motion.

    Automatic rigging predicts a skeleton and skinning weights for a given mesh [75, 52, 26, 11, 51, 55]. UniRig [82] also predicts spring bones and their physical attributes on VRoid characters [39], and DRiVE [54] generates skeletons that include hair and skirt bones for anime characters represented as 3D Gaussians. Both rig an existing asset. We generate the spring-bone chains together with the hair they drive, conditioned on the generated cards, and simulate them with the spring-bone update of the VRM specification [62, 63].

    3 Method

    We propose HairDeck, which generates the cards of a hairstyle and the spring-bone chains to animate them (Fig.2). Each card is encoded into one continuous token (Sec.3.1), and a set diffusion transformer (set DiT) generates all card tokens together, conditioned on a single image (Sec.3.3) or on a point cloud (Sec.3.2), the input of CHARM’s benchmark. The card VAE decodes each token back into control points, from which we build the mesh.
