    For port values v∈ℝᵖ, the boundary trace is u_b=Tv. The interior equilibrium equations Hᵢᵢuᵢ=C^⊤u_b follow from the homogeneous discrete PDE. Since Hᵢᵢ is the interior Dirichlet operator, its inverse G_K=Hᵢᵢ⁻¹ is the discrete Green operator, mapping interior source terms to solutions with zero boundary values. Consequently, defining R=C^⊤T and Φ_K=G_KR gives the screened harmonic extension uᵢ=Φ_Kv of the prescribed port values. Thus the corresponding fine-grid state is u=(u_b,uᵢ)^⊤. Minimizing the energy \min_uᵢu^⊤H_Ku by eliminating uᵢ yields the minimum \tfrac12v^⊤S_Kv where

    (2)

    S_K=T^⊤H_bbT-R^⊤Hᵢᵢ⁻¹R=:D_K-J_K.

    The Schur complement S_K is the corresponding discrete Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator: D_K accounts for boundary contributions, while J_K=R^⊤Φ_K captures transport through the eliminated interior. Thus the coarse system retains the fine-scale response without resolving its interior at every query.

    3.2. Random-Walk Interpretation of Multiscale Operators

    Let L₀ denote the unscreened conductance generator, (L₀f)(x)=∑_y∼xc_xy[f(y)-f(x)]. Its continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) holds at x for t∼Exp(dₓ⁰), where dₓ⁰=∑_y∼xc_xy, before jumping to y with probability c_xy/dₓ⁰. Screening κ(x)≥0 introduces killing at rate κ(x), giving total event rate dₓ^κ=dₓ⁰+κ(x) and killing probability κ(x)/dₓ^κ. Let ∂Kₕ be the fine boundary nodes partitioned into ports Γ_β={b∈∂Kₕ:T_bβ=1} for β∈[p]. For an unscreened walk, with its first boundary-hitting time τ and Y=X_τ∈∂Kₕ, the screened first-exit kernel is F_κ(x,b)=𝔼ₓ⁰[\exp(-∫₀^τκ(Xₜ) dt)1_{Y=b}] with port-exit probabilities φ_β^κ(x)=∑_b∈Γ_βF_κ(x,b). Thus the screened MsFEM basis satisfies (Φ_κ)_xβ=φ_β^κ(x), where Φ_κ denotes the extension under screening κ and Φ_λ_K⁰=Φ_K.

    This interpretation extends naturally to the condensed operators. Since J_κ=R^⊤Φ_κ, its entries (J_κ)_αβ=∑_x∈iR_xαφ_β^κ(x)=ρ_αℙ_X₀∼q_α^κ{Y∈Γ_β} represent unnormalized transport between ports, where ρ_α=∑_x∈iR_xα and q_α(x)=R_xα/ρ_α for ρ_α>0. Accordingly, the Schur complement S_κ=D_κ-J_κ, with D_κ=T^⊤H_bb^κT, induces coarse transitions P_αβ^K,κ=-(S_κ)_αβ/s_α for β≠α and absorption probability P_α†^K,κ=(S_κ1ₚ)_α/s_α where s_α=(S_κ)_αα>0 in the sense of identifying stiffness matrix as transport matrix. While these transitions preserve coarse transport, they discard the precise exit location b, motivating the additional fine-boundary kernel F_κ.

    Doob conditioning.

    The first-exit probabilities also characterize the CTMC conditioned on a prescribed boundary event. With h(x)=φ_β^κ(x), h(b)=1_{b∈Γ_β} and (L₀-κ)h=0 in the interior, conditioning on this event gives the Doob h-transform with jump rates c_xyʰ=c_xyh(y)/h(x) wherever h(x)>0, including jumps to boundary nodes, i.e., a conditioned process can be obtained by merely reweighting. As h(x)=∑_y∼xc_xyh(y)/dₓ^κ, the transition probability P_xyʰ=(c_xy)/(dₓ^κ)h(y)/h(x) has ∑_yP_xyʰ=1 thus having no killing, and also remains its total departure rate since ∑_y∼xc_xyʰ=dₓ^κ.

    Scalar h-transforms.

    For a general positive function h, the scalar h-transform of the unscreened generator is defined by L₀ʰf=h⁻¹L₀(hf)-fh⁻¹L₀h. On the conductance graph, this yields L₀ʰf(x)=∑_y∼xc_xyʰ\allowbreak[f(y)-f(x)]. Writing Vₕ=L₀h/h, the transformed path law relative to the reference CTMC satisfies dℙₓʰ/dℙₓ⁰=h(Y)/h(x)\allowbreak\exp(-∫₀^τVₕ(Xₜ) dt) under the suitable stopped-process regularity conditions. In the continuous setting, the diffusion generator L₀f=∇·(a_K∇f) transforms into L₀ʰf=L₀f+2a_K∇\logh·∇f, inducing the gradient drift bₕ=2a_K∇\logh. By Girsanov’s theorem, the logarithmic likelihood ratio is ∫₀^τ√2a_K∇\logh·dBₜ-a_K|∇\logh|²dt. Applying Ito’s formula to d\logh(Xₜ) converts the stochastic integral into \log[h(Y)/h(x)]-∫₀^τ(L₀h/h-a_K|∇\logh|²)dt, yielding the same endpoint-weighted representation with continuous correction L₀h/h. When h is harmonic with respect to the reference generator, the path-dependent correction vanishes, leaving only the endpoint weight h(Y)/h(x).

    4. Editable and Composable Multiscale Transport Prefabs

    We compile each heterogeneous region K into a reusable stochastic transport prefab

    (3)

    Prefab_K=(K,A_K⁰,T,Φ_K,S_K,𝔼_K,F_K),

    where A_K⁰ specifies the fixed fine-scale diffusion operator, Φ_K and S_K are the multiscale operators defined in Sec. 3.1, and 𝔼_K is a bank of compact event records instead of recording complete trajectories. For each fine-grid interior node x, we generate Nₓ independent unscreened walks indexed by r. Each walk is compressed into an event record (Y_x,r,Π_x,r), where Y_x,r∈∂Kₕ and Π_x,r is the multiset of visited nodes at Poisson candidate events generated along the walk at a fixed rate μ. Reweighting these records under a screening field κ reconstructs the first-exit kernel defined in Sec. 3.2:

    (4)

    F̂_κ(x,b)=1/Nₓ∑ᵣ₌₁^Nₓ1_{Y_x,r=b}∏_z∈Π_x,r(1-κ(z)/μ).

    The same event bank supports incremental updates of the condensed transport operator, while the reconstructed exit kernels provide reusable macro-transitions for hybrid Monte Carlo simulation.

    4.1. Stochastic Prefab Precomputation

    We precompute the multiscale responses and entrance-dependent exit distributions using compact event records. For the baseline screening λ_K⁰, the multiscale basis is estimated by aggregating the weighted terminal exits over each port:

    (5)

    (Φ̂_K)_xβ=∑_b∈Γ_βF̂_λ_K⁰(x,b), Ŝ_K=D_K-R^⊤Φ̂_K.

    Since R is nonzero only at interior nodes adjacent to the boundary, assembling Ŝ_K requires sampling only at these nodes, without evaluating basis gradients or normal derivatives.

    Entrance-dependent transport.

    To enable spatially resolved macro-transitions, we additionally estimate F̂_κ(xₐ,·) at sparse starting anchors xₐ distributed throughout K. Interior anchors use weighted terminal-exit records from 𝔼_K, whereas boundary anchors have deterministic exits and require no sampling. For a starting point x, we select a neighboring anchor xₐ according to nonnegative trilinear weights ωₐ(x) and sample its cached exit distribution. This realizes the interpolated kernel

    (6)

    F̂_κ(x,b)=∑_a∈ℕ(x)ωₐ(x)F̂_κ(xₐ,b), ∑ₐωₐ(x)=1.

    The remaining probability corresponds to absorption. Thus a single macro-transition replaces the fine-scale walk through the prefab interior, while preserving an entrance-dependent fine-boundary exit location. Unlike the coarse stiffness assembly, this construction requires sparse spatial coverage of the interior, neither a distribution at every interior node nor full simulation inward.

    Port-guided sampling.

    Under strong screening, direct sampling can produce many trajectories with negligible surviving exit weight. We also investigated the Doob conditioning introduced in Sec. 3.2 to preferentially sample successful boundary exits. However, the observed improvement was limited. It can be that conditioning on successful exit does not necessarily improve the sampling of localized transport changes, while the guiding function introduces preprocessing overhead and may become less effective after material edits. This motivates shifting the estimation target from the full transport response to its edit-induced difference. Later we use the resolvent identity to express this difference through the edited region and estimate it from the corresponding event records.

    4.2. Incremental Composition via Marked Paths

    Overlapping prefabs require different treatments according to whether they describe the same material or additive physical effects. For the same medium, overlap is only representational: if T₁ and T₂ are consistent first-exit operators, then T₁u(x)=T₂u(x)=u(x) for x∈K₁∩K₂. A weighted split or stochastic choice between these representations therefore preserves the expectation without duplicating the medium, up to discretization and interface-interpolation errors. In contrast, physically superposed screening fields add in the overlap, λ(x)=λ₁(x)+λ₂(x). We focus on such nonnegative edits while keeping the underlying conductances fixed. For brevity, quantities before and after edits are labeled by pre,post or 0,1.

    Edit-local transport difference.

    For one prefab, write κ₀=λ_K⁰+v₀ and κ₁=κ₀+v, with v₀,v≥0. On the interior nodes, let A₀=Hᵢᵢ+diag(v₀) and A₁=A₀+V, where V=diag(v|ᵢ). We seek to update the condensed operator S_K. Since the boundary contribution changes explicitly as D_Kᵖᵒˢᵗ=D_Kᵖʳᵉ+T^⊤V_bT, it suffices to estimate the change in J_K. Using Φₜ=Aₜ⁻¹R and Jₜ=R^⊤Φₜ, the resolvent identity yields

    (7)

    ΔJ:=J₀-J₁=Φ₀^⊤VΦ₁,(ΔJ)_αβ=∑_x∈Sv(x)φ_αᵖʳᵉ(x)φ_βᵖᵒˢᵗ(x),

    where S={x∈i:v(x)>0}. Unlike recomputing the modified J₁ from the ground up, this expression requires first-exit probabilities only at the edited interior nodes.

    Unbiased replay from event records.

    The bank 𝔼_K stores the unscreened terminal-exit and Poisson-mark records defined at the beginning of this section. For local screening-edit updates, records are recompiled by reweighting to fetch new path weight W_x,rᵖᵒˢᵗ rather than rerunning simulations. Assuming κ₁≤μ, we compute

    (8)

    W_x,rᵗ=∏_z∈Π_x,r(1-κₜ(z)/μ),a_rα=W_x,rᵖʳᵉ1_{Y_x,r∈Γ_α},b_rβ=W_x,rᵖᵒˢᵗ1_{Y_x,r∈Γ_β}.

    The corresponding expectations are φ_αᵖʳᵉ(x) and φ_βᵖᵒˢᵗ(x). Since weights from one record are correlated, their sample means cannot simply be multiplied without bias. Instead, define A_α(x)=∑ᵣa_rα, B_β(x)=∑ᵣb_rβ, and C_α(x)=∑ᵣa_rαb_rα. To obtain an unbiased estimator of the product φ_αᵖʳᵉ(x)φ_βᵖᵒˢᵗ(x), we adopt a second-order U-statistic that pairs distinct independent samples, thereby eliminating the diagonal bias arising from products of sample means:

    (9)

    ΔĴ_αβ=∑_x∈Sv(x)/N(N-1)[A_α(x)B_β(x)-1_{α=β}C_α(x)].

    The correction removes same-record products; those products vanish for α≠β because each record has a single terminal port. We symmetrize ΔĴ and update the condensed operator by

    (10)

    Ŝₚₒₛₜ=Ŝₚᵣₑ+ΔĴ+T^⊤V_bT.

    No new spatial walks are needed. For the fine-boundary kernels used by the hybrid solver, the same post-edit weights are applied to records at the sparse interior interpolation anchors to obtain F̂_κₚₒₛₜ through the estimator already defined above while boundary anchors remain deterministic. Thus the coarse response is updated from the edited-node records, whereas macro-transition distributions are refreshed only at their interpolation anchors.

    Theorem 4.1 (Unbiased edit-local replay).

    Assume that the unscreened records are independent within and across starting nodes, and 0≤κₚᵣₑ≤κₚₒₛₜ≤μ. With N≥2 records per edited node, Eq. (9), before or after symmetrization, satisfies

    (11)

    𝔼[ΔĴ_αβ]=ΔJ_αβ, Var(ΔĴ_αβ)≤1/N∑_x∈Sv(x)².

    Proof.

    Poisson marking gives 𝔼[a_rα]=φ_αᵖʳᵉ(x) and 𝔼[b_rβ]=φ_βᵖᵒˢᵗ(x). The bracket in Eq. (9) equals ∑_r≠sa_rαb_sβ, whose expectation is N(N-1)φ_αᵖʳᵉ(x)φ_βᵖᵒˢᵗ(x). This proves unbiasedness by Eq. (7). For each x, the distinct-record average is an order-two U-statistic with symmetric kernel (a_rαb_sβ+a_sαb_rβ)/2∈[0,1], and hence variance at most 1/N. Independence across starting nodes gives the bound and symmetrization preserves it by Cauchy–Schwarz. ∎

    Remark 1(Computational Cost of Edit-Local Replay).

    For p ports, N records per edited node, and at most M marks per record, updating the coarse operator costs O(|S|[N(1+M)+p²]) and requires no new spatial trajectories.

    Remark 2(Scalar rescaling of diffusion).

    Uniform rescaling of a prefab’s diffusion tensor requires no new spatial trajectories. For any c>0, replacing A_K with cA_K while keeping the screening field κ unchanged yields F_cA_K,κ=F_A_K,κ/c,S_cA_K,κ=cS_A_K,κ/c. Thus, diffusion rescaling is handled by reweighting the existing Poisson-marked records with effective screening κ/c, provided κ/c≤μ. In the absence of screening, exit distributions remain unchanged and the condensed operator is simply scaled by c. Different coarse cells may be rescaled independently, with their updated operators reassembled into the transport skeleton.

    4.3. Low-Dimensional Steering and Temporal Edits

    Gradient-field steering.

    The scalar h-transform introduced in Sec. 3.2 provides a way to modify transport direction while preserving the underlying diffusivity and physical screening. In particular, a positive field h induces the drift bₕ=2a_K∇\logh, with the path-dependent correction Vₕ=L₀h/h. Rather than prescribing a full-resolution vector field, we parameterize steering by positive port weights w∈ℝ_>0ᵖ and construct their unscreened harmonic extension:

    (12)

    h_w|_b=Tw, h_w|ᵢ=(Hᵢᵢ-Λᵢ)⁻¹Rw, Λᵢ=diag(λ_K⁰|ᵢ).

    Since L₀h_w=0 in the interior, its scalar correction vanishes. The steered first-exit kernel therefore reduces to endpoint reweighting:

    (13)

    F_κʷ(x,b)=(w_β(b))/(h_w(x))F_κ(x,b),

    where β(b) identifies the port containing b. This transformation preserves the physical screening field κ and requires only p-1 independent port-weight ratios. For directional control, the weights may be chosen as w_β=\exp(θd·(p_β-p_K)), where d specifies the preferred direction, θ controls its strength, and p_β,p_K denote the port and prefab centers.

    More generally, nonharmonic steering can also be evaluated using the existing event records. For a record starting at x and terminating at Y, the combined steering and screening weight is

    (14)

    W_x,r^h,κ=(h(Y_x,r))/(h(x))∏_z∈Π_x,r(1-κ(z)+Vₕ(z)/μ).

    Poisson averaging reproduces the path likelihood ratio and screening survival factor, provided κ+Vₕ≤μ. Unlike the harmonic construction, a nonzero Vₕ introduces additional weight variance, particularly when it takes negative values. We therefore favor harmonic steering, for which the cached exit statistics require only endpoint reweighting.

    Temporal Heat Capacity Edits.

    We also support spatially varying heat capacity m_K(x)>0 in the transient screened diffusion equation

    (15)

    m_K∂ₜu-∇·(a_K∇u)+(λ_K⁰+v)u=0.

    For zero initial data, the Laplace transform with parameter σ≥0 reduces this equation to the same elliptic problem with effective screening κ_σ=λ_K⁰+v+σm_K. Its interior operator is

    (16)

    A_σ=Hᵢᵢ+diag((v+σm_K)|ᵢ).

    Consequently, temporal effects require no new spatial transport process. The existing Poisson marks yield the Laplace-domain weight

    (17)

    W_x,r^σ=∏_z∈Π_x,r(1-(κ_σ(z))/(μ)), 0≤κ_σ≤μ.

    Its conditional expectation introduces the Laplace factor e^-σ∫₀^τm_K(Xₜ) dt. Hence screening, non-harmonic steering part and heat capacity enter through the same effective potential κ_σ+Vₕ, while drift steering contributes only an endpoint factor. These modifications can therefore be composed by reweighting the existing event records. At a fixed σ, the edit-local U-statistic in Sec. 4.2 applies directly with v replaced by δv+σδm_K, without introducing another estimator.

    Remark 3(Extension to direct time-domain walks).

    General transient problems, including nonzero initial conditions, can be addressed using time-budgeted walks such as Walk-on-Heat-Balls (WoHB) [(Deaconu and Herrmann, 2018)], which jointly sample spatial displacements and elapsed times. Let s denote the operational time of the reference diffusion Xₛ, and define the physical clock Θₘ(s)=∫₀ˢm_K(X_q) dq for a time-independent capacity field. A walk queried at time t terminates either upon reaching the spatial boundary or when Θₘ(s)=t, contributing boundary data at the remaining time or the initial condition at the stopping position, respectively.

    To make such walks reusable, an extended event bank would retain ordered spatial transitions and operational-time increments, time-stamped Poisson events, and terminal states. For a screening field λ(x,t), the marks before the stopping time s_*=\min{τ,Θₘ⁻¹(t)} give the weight

    (18)

    W_λ,t=∏_\beginsubarrayc(z,s)∈Π s

    where μ bounds the screening rate. Changing m_K modifies the physical clock and the stopping event, while changing λ only requires reevaluating these weights. If the time budget expires within a heat-ball step, its intermediate position must be sampled from the corresponding conditional heat kernel. Exact replay for spatially heterogeneous capacity or screening also requires within-step occupation information, or sufficiently localized steps with constant coefficients. Thus screening edits admit direct event reweighting, whereas capacity edits additionally require reevaluating the physical clock and potentially the stopping location. Such time-domain reuse extends the present framework but requires richer space–time records than the elliptic implementation.

    4.4. Hybrid Continuous–Discrete Monte Carlo Walks

    We couple continuous WoS with multiscale transport within each prefab. A prefab K consists of coarse cells {Kⱼ}, whose condensed operators S_Kⱼ define an internal transport skeleton. The fine-boundary kernels F_κ,j connect continuous positions to this skeleton, while the coarse operators propagate the walk across cells. Upon reaching the outer boundary of the prefab, the exit location is recovered at fine resolution before returning to continuous WoS as described in Algorithm 1.

    Continuous–coarse coupling.

    Let M_K⊂E_in,K\SubsetK denote the heterogeneous support, inner trigger region, and outer exit envelope, respectively, with a homogeneous buffer between M_K and ∂K. Outside the trigger regions, WoS proceeds on spheres contained in the homogeneous exterior. Once a walk reaches x∈E_in,K, we locate its containing coarse cell Kⱼ and sample F̂_κ,j(x,·) using the spatial interpolation described in Sec. 4.1. The sampled location lies on the boundary ∂Kⱼ of the coarse cell (not necessarily on the outer prefab boundary ∂K). Its corresponding port initializes the coarse walk while missing probability mass represents absorption.

    Coarse transport and fine-boundary exit.

    The local operators are assembled into an internal skeleton by identifying shared coarse-cell ports, giving Sₛₖₑₗ=∑ⱼEⱼ^⊤S_KⱼEⱼ, where Eⱼ maps local ports to skeleton degrees of freedom. Its conductances and killing rates induce the Markov transitions established in Sec. 3.2. Consequently, the walk traverses the prefab through coarse port transitions without resolving fine-grid diffusion inside each cell.

    When the coarse walk leaves the skeleton through an exterior-facing port β, we restore its fine-boundary exit location using the first-exit statistics of the final coarse cell Kⱼ. Conditioned on its final transition α→β, the exit distribution is

    (19)

    Q_αβ^Kⱼ(b)=-(∑_a∈Γ_j,αc_ab+∑_x∈iⱼR^Kⱼ_xαF_κ,j(x,b))/(S_Kⱼ)_αβ

    Here Γ_j,α and Γ_j,β are ports of Kⱼ, and iⱼ denotes its interior nodes. The numerator resolves the effective transport reaching the particular boundary node b, while summing over Γ_j,β recovers the coarse inter-port conductance. The sampled exit is transformed into world coordinates, and exterior WoS resumes.

    Interface consistency.

    The three stages operate at distinct spatial resolutions: the local first-exit kernel connects a continuous position to the coarse-cell boundary, the condensed operators transport the walk across the internal skeleton, and the conditional exit distribution restores the location on the prefab boundary. This avoids repeated fine-scale simulation while retaining the boundary resolution needed for continuous coupling. The inner-trigger/outer-exit separation prevents immediate repeated switching at artificial interfaces. Screening, steering, and temporal edits update the compiled kernels and condensed operators through the event-reweighting mechanisms developed above, without modifying the exterior WoS sampler.

    4.5. Adaptive Multiscale Transport

    For each query q, we adaptively select the resolution of each prefab K based on its spatial proximity to the query. Specifically, K uses the fine level if d(q,K)≤r and the coarse level otherwise, where d(q,K) denotes the Euclidean distance to the prefab and r controls the refinement radius. This assignment is determined once per query and remains fixed across all subsequent random walks, allowing nearby regions to retain detailed transport while distant regions use cheaper approximations. Both levels follow the same prefab interface, so switching resolution requires no modification to the global solver.

    5. Experiments

    We evaluate how accurately reusable transport prefabs preserve heterogeneous diffusion, how their responses change under physical edits, and how much work they eliminate during repeated Monte Carlo queries. Our main benchmark uses a heterogeneous medium divided into 27 coarse cells, with stochastic first-exit kernels coupled by an internal Schur-complement skeleton. The complete Hybrid alternates between continuous WoS outside the medium, cached first exits inside coarse cells, skeleton transitions, and fine-resolution exit reconstruction. We use independent finite-volume references for solution accuracy and single-threaded CPU timings. Additional local and multi-instance experiments examine individual components and spatial reuse.

    5.1. Stochastic Compilation and Multiscale Accuracy

    Stochastic basis and coarse transfer.

    We first ask whether estimating local first exits introduces noticeable errors into the condensed operator that drives the coarse walk. On a strongly heterogeneous conductivity field, individual multiscale basis values exhibit visible Monte Carlo fluctuations, whereas their port-aggregated transfer response is substantially more stable. Table 1 shows that increasing the compilation budget reduces both errors, but the transport response converges to a small error long before every basis value becomes accurate. Aggregation over the fine-scale boundary interactions therefore filters much of the sampling noise relevant to the coarse walk. This is the reason to compile and reuse port-level transport rather than reconstruct a uniformly precise interior basis for each query.

    Port resolution and entrance interpolation.

    The Hybrid introduces spatial compression at two stages: the Schur skeleton retains a finite set of boundary ports, while the entrance-dependent exit kernel is interpolated from cached anchors. We vary these resolutions independently and measure the resulting full-solution error (Fig. 2). With only eight ports, the skeleton is too coarse to preserve the exit dependence of smooth boundary data; increasing the port count sharply improves the solution, with gains tapering toward the finest configuration. The oscillatory case is less sensitive to port count in this particular field. Entrance-kernel spacing exhibits a different pattern: sparse anchors mainly degrade the smooth-field result, while denser anchors recover the spatial variation in where a walk exits a coarse cell. These observations separate the roles of coarse inter-port transport and spatially resolved entrance-to-exit interpolation.

    Offline event-bank size.

    A larger event bank improves the estimates used to build the prefab but also increases its one-time compilation and storage costs. We therefore repeat the complete hybrid evaluation with independently compiled banks of increasing size while keeping the online sampling budget fixed (Fig. 3). The solution errors change only moderately and do not decrease monotonically across these finite-bank runs. This behavior indicates that, once the coarse transitions are reasonably resolved, online sampling and spatial approximation can dominate differences between event-bank sizes. The default bank balances reusable transport quality with compilation cost.

    5.2. End-to-End Solver Performance

    We next compare the complete F → S → fine-exit Hybrid with the official variable-coefficient WoS implementation of [(Sawhney et al., 2022)]. Both solvers evaluate the same heterogeneous configuration before and after a screening edit, under smooth and oscillatory boundary conditions. The comparison covers the full query path rather than a standalone local exit sampler. We use the same number of online draws and assess both solutions against a common refined finite-volume reference.

    The main difference is the work repeated during each query. Conventional WoS must revisit the heterogeneous coefficients as its paths evolve; the Hybrid replaces most of those interior steps with cached exits and coarse transitions. Consequently, the Hybrid achieves substantially lower online costs across all four configurations (Table 2), with speedup ratios of approximately 22–28× relative to the archived official WoS measurements. Its solution accuracy remains comparable to the direct solver: the Hybrid achieves lower RMSE in three of the four configurations, while direct WoS performs slightly better in the unedited smooth case. The online-budget comparison in Fig. 4 further illustrates the separation in computational cost as the number of sampled trajectories increases.

    5.3. Incremental Editing Accuracy

    Edit-local transport increments.

    The resolvent estimator in Sec. 4.2 updates the condensed transport operator from trajectories originating in the edited region. Its main challenge is not estimating a large operator response, but recovering the comparatively small change caused by an edit. We test screening and Laplace-domain capacity changes over 40 translated, rotated, and rescaled absorber poses, using independent discrete resolvent increments as references. Each pose is evaluated with four separately compiled event banks. Figure 5 shows representative absorber poses used in the replay and full-Hybrid edit experiments.

    Figure 6 summarizes the three edit controls evaluated in this section and makes explicit what is changed before the transport increments are estimated. The incremental estimates remain consistent across poses (Fig. 7), with sub-percent average relative error for ordinary edit supports. When an edit occupies a much smaller region, the relative error rises: fewer starting nodes contribute, and the change being estimated is smaller. Screening and capacity edits follow almost the same pattern because both enter the local operator as nonnegative diagonal perturbations. Increasing the number of cached paths reduces the pose-level error (Fig. 8), showing that the replay quality can be improved offline without regenerating trajectories for each edit.

    Strong screening edits in the complete Hybrid.

    Accurate local operator increments must also produce meaningful changes in the assembled solution. We therefore apply 24 relatively strong screening edits of different shapes, positions, and orientations to the complete Hybrid, reusing a fixed event bank. These edits visibly alter the physical response rather than merely perturbing it near the Monte Carlo noise level. The estimated solutions track the overall changes in both boundary-condition families, although their incremental errors are more pronounced than in the isolated local-operator test (Table 3). Figure 9 makes the distinction clear: a reliable local transfer update still passes through port compression, entrance interpolation, and random sampling when used in the full solver. The experiment therefore measures how those approximations accumulate during substantial material edits.

    Response to smaller edits.

    We also evaluate 48 more localized screening edits with two online sampling budgets (Fig. 10). Here the final fields stay close to their references, but the physical edit signal is weaker and is harder to resolve separately from sampling noise. Increasing the online draws improves both final-solution and increment errors, particularly for the oscillatory boundary condition. Together with the strong-edit sweep, these results show why edit fidelity should be inspected through both the complete post-edit field and its change from the unedited solution: the two can behave differently for localized perturbations.

    5.4. Edit-Local Schur Updates

    Repeated screening edits require updating the condensed transport operator. We compare our edit-local U-statistic with full Schur refactorization, with both methods reusing the same geometry, conductances, port mappings, and pre-edit operator. The local method reconstructs only the contributions of edited interior nodes from cached event records; the baseline refactorizes the interior matrices and recomputes the Schur complements of all 27 coarse cells. We measure their operator-update costs for progressively larger edited regions, using 256 cached records per interior node (Table 4 and Fig. 11).

    The local update is particularly inexpensive for small, spatially confined edits. Its cost grows as more edited nodes contribute to the resolvent correction, while full Schur reconstruction remains relatively stable because it refactorizes the same coarse-cell system regardless of edit support. Consequently, the greatest speedups occur for local edits, reaching 25.9–42.9× below 5% edited nodes. The advantage decreases gradually with support size but remains 1.8× even when the entire interior is edited. This behavior illustrates the main benefit of caching transport: editing a small region requires updating its influence rather than reconstructing the complete operator.

    Accuracy–cost trade-off.

    The local correction is estimated from finite cached paths, so we also measure how its approximation affects the coarse response. We evaluate each updated operator with the same exact post-edit interface coupling and compare its coarse solution with the exact edited Schur response. Increasing the event-record budget from 64 to 256 generally moves the local-update results toward lower response error (Fig. 12). Across edit sizes, the approximate updates retain small coarse-response errors while requiring substantially less work than full refactorization. The curve exposes a controllable exchange between the number of reused samples and the fidelity of the edited transport operator.

    5.5. Transport Steering and Temporal Responses

    Harmonic steering.

    To test whether the cached transport can be directed without changing the diffusion field, we assign positive preferences to the prefab ports and apply the harmonic endpoint reweighting of Sec. 4.3. The edited solution increasingly favors the selected exit directions while retaining the structure imposed by the heterogeneous medium. Against directly solved discrete reference problems, the estimate follows this change as steering becomes stronger (Fig. 13a). The discrepancy grows with steering strength because the same finite set of cached exits represents a more unevenly weighted distribution. No new spatial trajectories are needed to explore these steering choices.

    Heat-capacity editing in the Laplace domain.

    A capacity change modifies the time scale of diffusion rather than the direction of its stationary transport. After Laplace transformation, the capacity field appears as an additional effective screening term, so the existing marked paths can be reweighted for different transform parameters. Figure 13b shows that the estimates remain close to the independently solved discrete responses throughout the tested range. Unlike steering, the relative error changes only slightly as the effective capacity contribution increases. This demonstrates reuse of the same local transport samples for a second, physically distinct edit control.

    Direct-time heat-ball transport.

    We additionally evaluate a direct time-domain implementation using WoHB. With a nonzero sinusoidal initial condition, the unit-cube heat equation has an analytic solution, allowing the effects of capacity and screening to be checked separately. The heat-ball estimates follow the expected decay across the tested capacities; increasing the capacity slows the evolution at a fixed physical time. Reweighting the same walks for different screening values produces estimates close to fresh direct-time sampling (Table 5, Fig. 14). Thus Poisson events also provide reusable screening information along time-dependent walks.

    Spatially varying capacity and cached clocks.

    We next consider a discrete conductance graph whose thermal capacity increases in a localized region. In this test, the cache also stores the visited states and holding times needed to reconstruct elapsed physical time. Replaying these histories under several capacity fields reproduces the corresponding matrix-exponential reference responses with similar accuracy (Fig. 15). The estimates capture the delayed propagation caused by increased local storage, demonstrating that spatial transport trajectories can be reused even when their physical clocks change.

    5.6. Spatial Reuse and Query-Centric Resolution

    To evaluate query-centric resolution selection at scene scale, we randomly distribute 12 spatially separated instances of the same heterogeneous medium in a homogeneous exterior (Fig. 16). Each instance reuses two precompiled transport representations, comprising 6³ and 24³ coarse cells, respectively. Both resolutions follow the same continuous–discrete hybrid walk, coupling local first-exit kernels, Schur-complement skeleton transport, and fine-boundary exit reconstruction. For each query q, an instance K uses the fine representation if d(q,K)≤r and the coarse representation otherwise, with the assignment fixed throughout all subsequent walks. We vary r across successive query-to-prefab distance thresholds, progressively increasing the number of fine-resolution instances, and compare the resulting responses with an all-fine reference (Fig. 17).

    As the refinement radius increases, the paired discrepancy between the adaptive LoD response and the all-fine response decreases rapidly as nearby prefabs switch to finer representations. Further refinement yields diminishing improvements, while the measured online CPU time generally increases, with minor timing fluctuations (Fig. 17). Both smooth and oscillatory boundary conditions exhibit this behavior. The paired discrepancy isolates the effect of resolution selection under matched random sampling; it should not be interpreted as the absolute error relative to the continuum PDE solution. These results demonstrate a controllable trade-off between online computational cost and transport representation fidelity while reusing the same heterogeneous medium across instances.

    6. Conclusion

    We demonstrated that fine-scale heterogeneous transport can be compiled into reusable stochastic prefabs, enabling efficient multiscale Monte Carlo simulation and interactive material editing. By combining probabilistic operator condensation with cached-path replay, our framework substantially accelerates repeated queries and localized updates while supporting spatial composition, transport steering, and transient diffusion. The main limitation is that the compiled representation assumes fixed underlying diffusivity up to scaling and requires upfront preprocessing, making it most beneficial for repeatedly queried or edited scenes. Extending this framework to dynamically changing diffusion structures remains an important direction for future work.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 几何预测不准就别全信它：RGMV 先用自一致性门控判断几何可靠性，再决定注入多少 ｜ Self-Consistency Geometry Injection for Multi-view Consistent Image Generation
item.description:
一句话：把预测几何当「固定条件」是脆弱点；加一个无参门控 + 可靠性加权的几何注入模块。

要点：

  • 现状问题：单图生成多视图的方法通常显式或隐式地把几何推断与纹理合成分辨不开，几何一错，生成就崩；一些几何引导方法虽做了解耦，但把预测几何当固定条件，不建模「它可不可靠」
  • RGMV 由两个部件组成：无参数的**自一致性几何门控（SCG）** 与 **可靠性感知的几何注入（RGI）**
  • 几何提案生成器产出候选几何后，门控按自一致性判断其可信度，注入模块再按可靠性决定几何条件的影响权重

为什么值得看：多视图生成是「AI 贴图/资产重建」链路的前置环节，而它的失败几乎都来自几何被当成硬条件。用一个零参数的自一致性门控替代「无条件信任」，是低成本、可直接移植到现有管线的改法。

中文摘要：扩散模型在单图生成多视图上进展很快，但现有方法通常显式或隐式地把几何推断与纹理合成绑在一起，一旦几何预测不准，生成就跟着出错。部分几何引导方法虽然做了解耦，却把预测的几何当成固定条件，没有显式建模「这份几何是否可靠」。作者提出 Reliability-Guided Multi-View Generation（RGMV），包含两个部件：参数无关的自一致性几何门控（SCG）与可靠性感知的几何注入（RGI）。几何提案生成器先给出候选几何，SCG 依据自一致性判断其可信程度，RGI 再按可靠性调节几何条件对生成的影响。这样几何从「硬条件」变成「带权提示」，在几何不可靠时不会把错误放大。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-30

本期推送：2026-10-31

Self-Consistency Geometry Injection for Multi-view Consistent Image Generation

Abstract

Recent diffusion models have achieved impressive progress in single image to multi-view generation by synthesizing consistent novel views efficiently. Existing methods usually explicitly or implicitly couple geometry inference and texture synthesis, making generation vulnerable to inaccurate geometry prediction. Although several geometry-guided methods have explored decoupling, they usually treat predicted geometry as a fixed condition and do not explicitly model whether the geometry is reliable. We therefore propose Reliability-Guided Multi-View Generation (RGMV), which comprises a parameter-free Self-Consistency Geometry Gate (SCG) and a Reliability-aware Geometry Injection (RGI) module. Specifically, a geometry proposal generator produces multiple geometry predictions for the same reference image and target viewpoints under different stochastic sampling configurations. SCG measures their spatial agreement to derive a reliability map, which RGI uses to modulate the injection strength of geometry-conditioned residuals in the RGB synthesis model. Moreover, RGMV can adapt to different geometry proposal generators. As a result, RGMV preserves stronger geometric guidance in stable regions while attenuating unreliable geometry cues before they propagate into multi-view RGB generation. Extensive experiments show that reliability-aware geometry injection improves the geometric quality of multi-view generation. Code: https://github.com/WISLab-GDUT/RGMV.

Keywords:

Multi-view image generation Geometry-conditioned diffusion Self-consistency reliability estimation

1 Introduction

Multi-view Consistent Image Generation aims to synthesize visually coherent images of an object from novel viewpoints given only one reference image. Recent diffusion-based approaches have substantially improved the realism and efficiency of multi-view synthesis [39, 33, 31, 8, 29, 27, 43, 25, 4, 7] by leveraging large-scale image priors and joint view generation [37, 28, 21, 38, 16, 44]. Nevertheless, a single reference image provides only partial observations of the underlying object. The geometry of occluded and unseen regions therefore remains underconstrained, making it difficult to preserve plausible object structure and multi-view consistent local appearance.

To reduce this ambiguity, geometry-guided methods [19, 20, 26, 15, 6, 13, 42] introduce normal maps, depth maps, or other structural representations as explicit conditions for multi-view RGB synthesis. When the geometry condition is accurate, it provides view-aware structural cues that help constrain object shape and appearance in unseen regions. Figure 1(a,b) highlights two alternative formulations for multi-view generation. Direct methods do not expose geometry as an independently controllable signal, whereas geometry-guided pipelines expose it without accounting for its non-uniform reliability. However, geometry predicted from a single reference image is not uniformly reliable. Ambiguity in occluded regions, thin structures, and local boundaries can lead to spatially and view-wise varying errors in the predicted geometry. Existing geometry-conditioned pipelines [45, 25, 19, 20, 26] typically inject predicted geometry with a globally fixed strength, implicitly treating all geometric cues as equally trustworthy. This design creates an unavoidable trade-off that weak conditioning underuses reliable geometry, whereas strong conditioning propagates local geometric errors into RGB synthesis. Because the reliability of predicted geometry varies across spatial locations and target views, no single global injection scale can simultaneously preserve trustworthy structural cues and suppress unreliable ones. This limitation motivates a selective geometry-conditioning mechanism that preserves stable geometric cues while suppressing unreliable ones.

Therefore, we propose RGMV, a reliability-guided framework for geometry-guided multi-view generation. Figure 1(c) summarizes the resulting alternative. RGMV retains the decoupled pipeline but selectively controls the influence of predicted geometry rather than modifying the geometry itself. RGMV obtains multiple normal predictions for the same reference image and target poses from a geometry proposal generator under different stochastic seeds. SCG converts their agreement into spatial reliability maps, and RGI uses these maps to modulate the geometry residuals injected into the multi-view RGB synthesis model. This design preserves stronger geometry guidance in stable regions while limiting the influence of inconsistent predictions. Experiments show that SCG-guided RGI improves over spatially uniform injection with a frozen RGB synthesis model, and parameter-efficient adaptation further improves the full RGMV framework.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

  • •

    We propose RGMV, which couples a parameter-free Self-Consistency Geometry Gate (SCG) for estimating spatial reliability from stochastic geometry agreement with a Reliability-aware Geometry Injection (RGI) module for modulating normal-conditioned residuals.

  • •

    We introduce a parameter-efficient adaptation scheme for the RGI-equipped RGB synthesis model, which uses ground-truth normals during training and SCG-derived spatial variation only at inference, without dependence on a particular geometry proposal generator.

  • •

    Extensive experiments on Objaverse and GSO demonstrate that RGMV consistently improves multiple geometry proposal generators in both multi-view RGB synthesis and downstream 3D reconstruction. Qualitative results show more stable structures on rendered objects and real captured images.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Multi-view Consistent Image Generation

    Diffusion-based models [17, 32, 18, 33, 36, 35] have become a major approach for synthesizing novel views from a single reference image. Zero-1-to-3 [17] introduces camera-conditioned diffusion, enabling novel-view generation under specified relative camera transformations. SyncDreamer [18] further models the joint distribution of multiple target views and synchronizes their denoising process through cross-view feature interaction to improve multi-view consistency. SV3D [36] adapts latent video diffusion to orbital multi-view synthesis and incorporates explicit camera control for image-conditioned view generation. Era3D [14] improves high-resolution multi-view generation through camera prediction and efficient row-wise attention that exploits epipolar correspondence across views. More recently, MV-Adapter [10] introduces a lightweight adapter-based design that equips pretrained text-to-image diffusion models with multi-view generation capability while preserving the original backbone. These methods[35, 34, 47, 7, 1] improve the realism, camera controllability, and cross-view coherence of image-based multi-view synthesis. Their primary focus is on constructing stronger multi-view generation priors or more effective cross-view interactions. In this work, we study how external geometry predicted from a single reference image should be used within an existing multi-view diffusion pipeline when the reliability varies across spatial regions and target views.

    2.2 Geometry-conditioned Diffusion Models

    Geometry conditions have been widely used to provide explicit spatial control for diffusion models[45, 25, 43, 9, 22, 40, 24, 2]. ControlNet [45] introduces an additional trainable branch that injects spatial conditions, such as edges, depth maps, and normal maps, into a pretrained diffusion backbone. T2I-Adapter [25] instead learns lightweight adapters for external structural signals while keeping the original text-to-image model frozen. These methods establish effective mechanisms for incorporating geometry into image diffusion. Several works further incorporate geometry into multi-view or 3D generation[19, 20, 6, 13, 15]. Wonder3D [19] jointly generates multi-view RGB images and normal maps through cross-domain diffusion and multi-view cross-domain attention. Direct2.5 [20] models multi-view normal maps as a 2.5D representation and uses normal-conditioned multi-view image generation for appearance synthesis. PointmapDiff [26] uses predicted pointmaps as geometric conditions for single-image novel-view synthesis through reference attention and ControlNet-based conditioning. In a related texture-generation setting, CaliTex [15] calibrates attention with known 3D structure to improve view-coherent texture synthesis. These methods demonstrate that explicit geometry can substantially improve view synthesis and appearance generation. However, they generally use the available geometric representation directly or condition generation with a globally fixed mechanism[45, 19, 20, 26]. Regarding this issue, RGMV uses multi-sample agreement to adapt the strength of geometry-conditioned residual injection at inference time.

    2.3 Consistency-based Reliability Estimation

    Multi-sample consistency has been explored as an inference-time signal for assessing the reliability of generative outputs[23, 12, 11]. Generative Uncertainty in Diffusion Models [12] estimates the uncertainty of diffusion samples to identify potentially low-quality generations. Self-Refining Video Sampling [11] uses self-consistency to identify regions that benefit from selective refinement during video generation. These studies show that repeated stochastic generations can provide useful evidence about output stability without requiring an additional manually annotated reliability label. RGMV evaluates the stability of the geometry condition before it is injected into downstream multi-view RGB synthesis. Specifically, SCG measures agreement among normal predictions generated under different stochastic seeds and converts it into a spatial reliability map. This parameter-free signal directly modulates normal-conditioned residuals at inference time, allowing the multi-view diffusion model to retain stable geometric cues while attenuating geometry conditions that are locally inconsistent.

    3 Method

    3.1 Overview

    Given a reference image I_ref and a set of target camera poses ℙ={Pᵥ}ᵥ₌₁^V, our goal is to synthesize a set of multi-view RGB images Î={Îᵥ}ᵥ₌₁^V that are consistent with the reference appearance and the target viewpoints. As illustrated in Fig. 2, RGMV couples a geometry proposal generator with a multi-view RGB synthesis model equipped with the proposed SCG and RGI modules. In this work, we instantiate the geometry representation with multi-view normal maps.

    The geometry proposal generator produces K sets of normal predictions under different random seeds:

    ℕ̂⁽ᵏ⁾={N̂ᵥ⁽ᵏ⁾}ᵥ₌₁^V=G(I_ref,ℙ;sₖ), k=1,…,K,

    		(1)

    where G denotes the geometry proposal generator and sₖ is the k-th random seed. We designate one prediction, ℕ̂⁽¹⁾, as the anchor geometry condition for the RGB synthesis model, while the full prediction set is used to estimate its spatial reliability. Instead of treating the anchor normal maps as uniformly reliable, the proposed Self-Consistency Geometry Gate (SCG) measures agreement among the K predictions and derives a set of spatial reliability maps ℝ={Rᵥ}ᵥ₌₁^V.

    The proposed Reliability-aware Geometry Injection (RGI) module does not modify the normal maps themselves. Rather, it uses these reliability maps to control the strength with which normal-conditioned residuals are injected into the denoising network of the RGB synthesis model. The overall reliability-aware synthesis process can thus be written as:

    Î=T(I_ref,ℙ,ℕ̂⁽¹⁾,ℝ),

    		(2)

    where T denotes the reliability-aware multi-view RGB synthesis process. Through RGI, RGMV preserves stronger geometry guidance in high-agreement regions and attenuates the corresponding geometry residuals in low-agreement regions. SCG is parameter-free and can be directly paired with a frozen RGB synthesis model through RGI, while the full RGMV further adapts the RGB synthesis model with ground-truth normal conditions through the same RGI pathway. The following sections describe the construction of the self-consistency reliability map and its use in reliability-aware geometry injection.

    3.2 Self-Consistency Geometry Gate

    Predicted normal maps can be reliable in some regions while remaining unstable in others. To estimate this variation without reliability supervision, SCG (Fig. 2(a)) measures agreement among multiple normal predictions generated from the same reference image and target poses. At inference time, we sample the geometry proposal generator K times with different random seeds.

    For the v-th target view and pixel location p, let n̂ᵥ⁽ᵏ⁾(p)∈ℝ³ denote the normal vector from the k-th prediction. We ℓ₂-normalize each normal vector before aggregation and compute the mean normal direction as

    n̄ᵥ(p)=(∑ₖ₌₁^Kn̂ᵥ⁽ᵏ⁾(p))/(\lVert∑ₖ₌₁^Kn̂ᵥ⁽ᵏ⁾(p)\rVert₂+ε),

    		(3)

    where ε is a small constant for numerical stability. We then measure disagreement by the mean angular deviation from the mean direction:

    dᵥ(p)=1/K∑ₖ₌₁^K\arccos(clip(⟨n̂ᵥ⁽ᵏ⁾(p),n̄ᵥ(p)⟩,-1,1)),

    		(4)

    where clip(·,-1,1) restricts the inner product to the valid range of \arccos(·). We convert the disagreement map into a raw agreement-based reliability response:

    Rᵥ(p)=\exp(-γdᵥ(p)),

    		(5)

    where γ>0 controls the sensitivity of the response to prediction disagreement.

    The resulting reliability map is an agreement-based proxy for the stability of predicted geometry. It is not supervised by ground-truth normal errors and does not assume that prediction agreement exactly measures geometric accuracy. Instead, it provides a spatial signal for selectively controlling the influence of predicted geometry during RGB synthesis. SCG produces spatially varying reliability maps only at inference time from multiple predicted normal maps.

    3.3 Reliability-aware Geometry Injection

    The proposed RGI module (Fig. 2(b)) injects geometry into the denoising network of the RGB synthesis model through residuals produced by a normal-conditioned ControlNet [45]. For notational clarity, let H_v,l denote the feature map for target view v at the l-th denoising block, and let ΔH_v,l denote the corresponding geometry residual. Conventional geometry-guided synthesis applies a spatially uniform injection strength:

    Hᵘⁿⁱ_v,l=H_v,l+αᵤₙᵢΔH_v,l,

    		(6)

    where αᵤₙᵢ is a fixed geometry injection scale. This formulation treats all spatial locations of the predicted geometry as equally reliable.

    In contrast, RGI modulates geometry residuals using the reliability map derived by SCG in Sec. 3.2. For each denoising block, we resize the reliability map to match the spatial resolution of H_v,l and apply an affine calibration:

    R̃_v,l=r_\min+(r_\max-r_\min)Uₗ(Rᵥ),

    		(7)

    where Uₗ(·) denotes spatial resizing to the resolution of H_v,l. The parameters r_\min and r_\max specify an affine calibration of the raw reliability response. They are not clipping bounds, and Eq. 7 does not normalize the gate to a prescribed value range. The single-channel map R̃_v,l is broadcast along the feature-channel dimension before multiplication. The reliability-aware feature update is

    Hˢᶜᵍ_v,l=H_v,l+α_scgR̃_v,l⊙ΔH_v,l,

    		(8)

    where ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication and α_scg is the base injection scale. Thus, RGI uses the SCG-derived reliability map to preserve stronger geometry residuals in high-agreement regions and attenuate residuals in regions with low geometric agreement. Uniform geometry injection in Eq. 6 is a special case of Eq. 8 with R̃_v,l=1.

    We consider uniform and RGMV adaptation settings. Both use ground-truth normal maps: the former applies the constant scale αᵤₙᵢ, whereas the latter follows the RGI update in Eq. 8 with base scale α_scg. For RGMV, K identical normal copies yield a raw reliability map of one and thus a constant calibrated gate of r_\max. Training therefore retains the RGI pathway without spatial variation and remains independent of the geometry proposal generator. At inference, ground-truth normals are replaced by the anchor predicted normals, and SCG derives spatially varying reliability maps from the K predicted sets.

    During RGB synthesis model adaptation, we keep the normal-conditioned ControlNet [45] frozen and optimize the MV-Adapter parameters with the standard diffusion denoising objective:

    L_denoise=𝔼_z₀,t,ε[\lVertε-ε_θ(zₜ,t,I_ref,ℙ;ℕ_cond,ℝ_cond)\rVert₂²],

    		(9)

    where zₜ is the noisy latent of the clean target latent z₀ at timestep t, ε is the sampled Gaussian noise, and ε_θ denotes the denoising network of the RGB synthesis model. During RGMV fine-tuning, ℕ_cond is the ground-truth normal condition and ℝ_cond is the spatially constant reliability condition induced by its identical copies. During inference, they are replaced by ℕ̂⁽¹⁾ and the SCG reliability maps computed from multiple geometry predictions, respectively, which are supplied to RGI for residual modulation. The uniform baseline follows the same objective but applies the update in Eq. 6 without a reliability condition.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Dataset and Metric

    We train RGMV on a curated Objaverse [3] subset of approximately 100K objects, with more than 60K for training and the remainder for validation. Ablations use a fixed 100-object validation subset, and the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) [5] provides a fixed 100-object test set. Both of them are selected with seed 42. For 2D synthesis, we report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [46], which measure pixel fidelity, structural similarity, and perceptual similarity respectively. For 3D reconstruction, lower Chamfer Distance (CD) and higher Volume IoU indicate better geometric quality.

    4.2 Implementation Details

    Our multi-view RGB synthesis model is built on Stable Diffusion v2.1-base [30]. We use MV-Adapter [10] as the multi-view consistency module and a normal-conditioned ControlNet [45] for geometry residual injection. We use K=3, γ=0.20, α_scg=0.08, and [r_\min,r_\max]=[0,1], selected in Sec. 4.4. During training, we optimize only the parameters of MV-Adapter for 120,000 steps with batch size 3 and learning rate 1×10⁻⁵, while freezing the diffusion backbone and ControlNet, and the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) scale is 3.0. For each reference image, the proposal generator produces K stochastic sets of six-view normal maps, and RGMV synthesizes the corresponding RGB views at 0^∘ (front), 45^∘ (front-right), 90^∘ (right), 180^∘ (back), 270^∘ (left), and 315^∘ (front-left). SCG assumes no specific camera angles, but arbitrary or continuous pose evaluation is beyond the scope of this work. Peak GPU memory is approximately 45 GB for training. Unless specified otherwise, the default geometry proposal generator of RGMV is a separately trained MV-Adapter for multi-view normal generation, trained with the same optimization settings and parameter-efficient adaptation strategy as the RGB synthesis model.

    4.3 Performance Comparison

    Compared Methods. We compare RGMV with two representative multi-view image generation baselines, Zero-1-to-3 [17] and SyncDreamer [18], as well as three recent systems with distinct multi-view generation designs, including Wonder3D++ [41], MV-Adapter [10], and Era3D [14]. Zero-1-to-3 performs camera-conditioned novel-view synthesis from a single reference image, whereas SyncDreamer [18] explicitly models the joint distribution of multiple target views. Wonder3D++ [41], MV-Adapter, and Era3D [14] represent complementary approaches based on joint RGB–geometry generation, lightweight multi-view adaptation, and epipolar-aware multi-view generation, respectively. The latter three methods can additionally provide multi-view geometry proposals for RGMV. We therefore evaluate each of them both as a standalone multi-view generation method and as a geometry proposal generator integrated with RGMV.

    Quantitative Comparison. Table 1 compares multi-view image generation and downstream 3D reconstruction on GSO [5]. Among the standalone methods, Era3D achieves the highest PSNR and lowest LPIPS, whereas MV-Adapter provides the highest SSIM. RGMV improves PSNR by 1.16, 1.25, and 1.17 dB when using geometry proposals from Wonder3D++ [41], MV-Adapter [10], and Era3D [14], respectively, with corresponding improvements in SSIM and LPIPS. All RGMV variants share the same adapted RGB synthesis model, supporting compatibility with different geometry sources. Downstream reconstruction using Trellis [38] yields lower Chamfer Distance and higher Volume IoU than the corresponding standalone method for all three geometry sources. RGMV using Era3D proposals achieves the best multi-view image generation results, while RGMV using MV-Adapter proposals achieves the lowest Chamfer Distance of 0.026 and the highest Volume IoU of 0.62. The specific contribution of SCG-guided RGI is examined through controlled ablations in Sec. 4.4.

    Qualitative Comparison. Figure 3 compares generated views of held-out rendered objects with ground-truth targets. For “Dug Well” and “Propeller Aircraft”, RGMV produces more faithful object structures and local details across viewpoints, bringing the generated views closer to ground truth. Figure 4 compares results on real captured images without ground-truth target views. RGMV alleviates structural collapse, distortions, hollow regions, duplicated components, and other geometry artifacts. The red circles mark the affected baseline regions. In an audit of a fixed random sample of 50 real images, the baseline (MV-Adapter [10]) exhibits geometry-related failures in 18/50 cases (36.0%). RGMV fixes or alleviates 14 of these 18 failures (77.8%), while 4 remain unresolved. It also introduces a new geometry artifact in 1/50 cases (2.0%). Together, the rendered and real-image examples indicate that RGMV improves the use of predicted geometry in both controlled evaluation settings and unconstrained real-world inputs.

    4.4 Ablation Study

    We conduct controlled ablations on the fixed 100-object Objaverse [3] validation subset to isolate the effects of predicted-normal conditioning, SCG-guided reliability-aware geometry injection, and RGB synthesis model adaptation. All geometry-conditioned variants use multi-view normal proposals from our separately trained MV-Adapter. The “Pure i2mv” row in Table 3 corresponds to the image-only MV-Adapter RGB synthesis model and is evaluated without normal-conditioned residual injection. All geometry-conditioned variants retain the same MV-Adapter RGB backbone and are evaluated under the same reference images, target viewpoints, and generation protocol. Because RGI operationalizes the spatial reliability maps estimated by SCG, we evaluate their joint contribution by replacing the SCG-derived spatial gate with uniform injection rather than treating RGI as a separately removable component. The adapted variants follow the same training configuration described in Sec. 4.2.

    Validity of the Reliability Signal. To assess whether the SCG reliability map is a useful proxy for geometry reliability, we examine the association between angular disagreement d across predicted normals and anchor-to-GT angular error e. With K=3, we evaluate over 30 million pixel locations using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient ρ for correlation and AUROC for high-error discrimination. Table 2 shows that d correlates positively with e, and SCG helps distinguish high-error pixels from lower-error ones.

    Effect of SCG-guided RGI. With the RGB synthesis model frozen, adding spatially uniform normal-conditioned residuals to the image-only MV-Adapter baseline improves PSNR and SSIM, confirming that predicted geometry provides useful structural cues for multi-view generation. However, its LPIPS score does not improve, indicating that a fixed global injection strength cannot consistently translate predicted geometry into better perceptual synthesis. Replacing the uniform scalar with the SCG-derived reliability map in RGI improves all three metrics, yielding a further 0.20 dB gain in PSNR, a 0.0047 improvement in SSIM, and a 0.0138 reduction in LPIPS. Since these variants share the same predicted normal maps, frozen MV-Adapter RGB synthesis model, and normal-conditioned residual pathway, the gain isolates the benefit of SCG-guided RGI over spatially uniform geometry injection. Figure 5 shows that αᵤₙᵢ=0.1 achieves the highest PSNR and SSIM among the tested uniform scales and is therefore used in Table 3. At a matched mean gate of 0.9138, SCG outperforms the constant and best Sobel-edge controls on all three metrics, with PSNR of 24.63 versus 24.52 and 24.54, respectively. Uniform injection remains a global compromise across regions with different geometry reliability, whereas SCG-guided RGI performs spatially varying modulation at the pixel level.

    Effect of RGB Synthesis Model Adaptation. Table 3 further evaluates the contribution of adapting the multi-view RGB synthesis model. Compared with the frozen uniform-injection variant, model adaptation improves PSNR from 24.43 to 25.14, SSIM from 0.8498 to 0.8569, and LPIPS from 0.2073 to 0.1948. This result shows that adaptation improves the compatibility between the RGB synthesis model and normal-conditioned residuals. More importantly, RGMV remains superior under the same adapted synthesis model. Replacing uniform injection with SCG-guided RGI improves PSNR by 0.17 dB, SSIM by 0.0052, and LPIPS by 0.0125. Therefore, the gain of RGMV cannot be attributed only to model adaptation. Adaptation improves the model’s ability to exploit geometry conditions, whereas SCG supplies spatial reliability maps and RGI uses them to determine how strongly the predicted geometry should influence generation at each spatial location. Their combination yields the best result.

    Sensitivity to SCG and RGI Hyperparameters. Table 4 evaluates the sensitivity to γ, α_scg, K, and [r_\min,r_\max]. The default setting, γ=0.20, α_scg=0.08, K=3, and [r_\min,r_\max]=[0,1], provides the strongest overall trade-off across PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS. The selected configuration avoids both overly aggressive suppression of geometry cues and insufficient discrimination between stable and unstable prediction regions. The results remain stable over a moderate range of γ, with γ=0.20 achieving the best structural metrics and nearby values producing comparable perceptual quality. This indicates that SCG does not require an excessively sharp reliability response. Large γ instead suppresses useful geometry cues in moderately consistent regions. The base injection scale exhibits a clearer optimum at α_scg=0.08. Smaller values underuse reliable normal cues, whereas larger values amplify geometry-conditioned residuals beyond what reliability modulation can compensate for. Using K=3 geometry predictions improves PSNR and SSIM over K=2, although K=2 achieves slightly lower LPIPS. Increasing to K=4 yields only negligible quality changes, which are obscured by rounding in Table 4, while increasing total runtime by approximately 23% (Table 5). We therefore select K=3 as a trade-off between synthesis quality and inference cost. Finally, the affine calibration interval [0,1] performs best overall, since a lower upper bound weakens reliable geometry guidance across high-agreement regions during RGB synthesis, whereas a larger one over-amplifies residual injection.

    Inference Cost. Table 5 reports the runtimes of geometry proposal generation, SCG computation, and RGB synthesis on an RTX 4090 GPU. At K=3, runtime is 16.65 seconds, approximately 1.88× that at K=1. SCG accounts for approximately 0.7% of runtime. Repeated geometry proposals dominate the overhead. Increasing K from 3 to 4 raises runtime by approximately 23%.

    5 Conclusion

    In this paper, we presented RGMV, a reliability-guided framework for multi-view image generation. RGMV considers geometry predicted from a single reference image useful but not uniformly reliable across spatial regions and target views. The proposed SCG is parameter-free and operates at inference time to construct a reliability map from the agreement among multiple stochastic geometry predictions, while RGI uses this map to selectively modulate geometry residuals during RGB synthesis. Experiments demonstrate that RGMV improves multiple geometry proposal generators on both multi-view image synthesis and downstream 3D reconstruction. Qualitative results further show that reliability-guided conditioning reduces geometry-related artifacts and produces more stable object structures across viewpoints.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：把预测几何当「固定条件」是脆弱点；加一个无参门控 + 可靠性加权的几何注入模块。

要点：

  • 现状问题：单图生成多视图的方法通常显式或隐式地把几何推断与纹理合成分辨不开，几何一错，生成就崩；一些几何引导方法虽做了解耦，但把预测几何当固定条件，不建模「它可不可靠」
  • RGMV 由两个部件组成：无参数的**自一致性几何门控（SCG）** 与 **可靠性感知的几何注入（RGI）**
  • 几何提案生成器产出候选几何后，门控按自一致性判断其可信度，注入模块再按可靠性决定几何条件的影响权重

为什么值得看：多视图生成是「AI 贴图/资产重建」链路的前置环节，而它的失败几乎都来自几何被当成硬条件。用一个零参数的自一致性门控替代「无条件信任」，是低成本、可直接移植到现有管线的改法。

中文摘要：扩散模型在单图生成多视图上进展很快，但现有方法通常显式或隐式地把几何推断与纹理合成绑在一起，一旦几何预测不准，生成就跟着出错。部分几何引导方法虽然做了解耦，却把预测的几何当成固定条件，没有显式建模「这份几何是否可靠」。作者提出 Reliability-Guided Multi-View Generation（RGMV），包含两个部件：参数无关的自一致性几何门控（SCG）与可靠性感知的几何注入（RGI）。几何提案生成器先给出候选几何，SCG 依据自一致性判断其可信程度，RGI 再按可靠性调节几何条件对生成的影响。这样几何从「硬条件」变成「带权提示」，在几何不可靠时不会把错误放大。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-30

本期推送：2026-10-31

Self-Consistency Geometry Injection for Multi-view Consistent Image Generation

Abstract

Recent diffusion models have achieved impressive progress in single image to multi-view generation by synthesizing consistent novel views efficiently. Existing methods usually explicitly or implicitly couple geometry inference and texture synthesis, making generation vulnerable to inaccurate geometry prediction. Although several geometry-guided methods have explored decoupling, they usually treat predicted geometry as a fixed condition and do not explicitly model whether the geometry is reliable. We therefore propose Reliability-Guided Multi-View Generation (RGMV), which comprises a parameter-free Self-Consistency Geometry Gate (SCG) and a Reliability-aware Geometry Injection (RGI) module. Specifically, a geometry proposal generator produces multiple geometry predictions for the same reference image and target viewpoints under different stochastic sampling configurations. SCG measures their spatial agreement to derive a reliability map, which RGI uses to modulate the injection strength of geometry-conditioned residuals in the RGB synthesis model. Moreover, RGMV can adapt to different geometry proposal generators. As a result, RGMV preserves stronger geometric guidance in stable regions while attenuating unreliable geometry cues before they propagate into multi-view RGB generation. Extensive experiments show that reliability-aware geometry injection improves the geometric quality of multi-view generation. Code: https://github.com/WISLab-GDUT/RGMV.

Keywords:

Multi-view image generation Geometry-conditioned diffusion Self-consistency reliability estimation

1 Introduction
