一句话：HDR 数据稀缺不是死结：线性 RGB 与 sRGB 的强度/色彩统计差异才是拦路虎。

要点：

  • 现状：HDR 格式与显示越来越普及，但主流图像生成器（SD、FLUX）仍只输出 LDR，根因是缺少大规模 HDR 训练数据
  • 作者的判断是可以不改架构、不从头重训：预训练扩散模型能「很容易地被适配」到 HDR 生成
  • 关键难点被点明：HDR 原生用线性 RGB 表示，其强度与色彩统计和 sRGB 编码的 LDR 图像差异很大——这一差距是适配的核心障碍，也是这篇文章主要处理的对象

为什么值得看：游戏里 HDR 管线（色调映射、曝光、泛光）一直缺「HDR 素材」这一环；如果能用现成扩散模型产出 HDR 而不是先出 LDR 再暴力拉，资产与光照参考的做法会变。对做 HDR 显示、天光/环境贴图、影视级后处理的团队值得跟进。

中文摘要：HDR 格式与显示设备越来越普及，但当前最好的图像生成器（如 Stable Diffusion、FLUX）基本仍局限在 LDR 输出，原因是缺少大规模 HDR 训练数据。作者指出，预训练扩散模型其实可以被轻松适配到 HDR 生成，不必从头重训；真正的障碍在于表示差异——HDR 原生是线性 RGB，其强度与色彩统计与 sRGB 编码的 LDR 图像差别很大，直接把 LDR 模型套上去会失真。文章围绕这个差距设计适配方案（在感知均匀空间里处理 HDR），目标是让现成模型直接产出可用的 HDR 结果，从而绕开「HDR 数据集稀缺」这个死结。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-30

本期推送：2026-10-31

X2HDR: HDR Image Generation in a Perceptually Uniform Space

Abstract

High-dynamic-range (HDR) formats and displays are becoming increasingly prevalent, yet state-of-the-art image generators (e.g., Stable Diffusion and FLUX) typically remain limited to low-dynamic-range (LDR) output due to the lack of large-scale HDR training data. In this work, we show that existing pretrained diffusion models can be easily adapted to HDR generation without retraining from scratch. A key challenge is that HDR images are natively represented in linear RGB, whose intensity and color statistics differ substantially from those of sRGB-encoded LDR images. This gap, however, can be effectively bridged by converting HDR inputs into perceptually uniform encodings (e.g., using PU21 or PQ). Empirically, we find that LDR-pretrained variational autoencoders (VAEs) reconstruct PU21-encoded HDR inputs with fidelity comparable to LDR data, whereas linear RGB inputs cause severe degradations. Motivated by this finding, we describe an efficient adaptation strategy that freezes the VAE and finetunes only the denoiser via low-rank adaptation in a perceptually uniform space. This results in a unified computational method that supports both text-to-HDR synthesis and single-image RAW-to-HDR reconstruction. Experiments demonstrate that our perceptually encoded adaptation consistently improves perceptual fidelity, text-image alignment, and effective dynamic range, relative to previous techniques. Complete HDR results and code are available at https://X2HDR.github.io/.

1 Introduction

High-dynamic-range (HDR) imagery provides a more faithful representation of natural scene luminance and color than conventional low-dynamic-range (LDR) formats, offering a more realistic and appealing visual appearance. Yet, creating HDR content in practice is still inconvenient. The standard solution—multi-exposure bracketing—often suffers from motion-induced misalignment and ghosting, and it increases both capture and processing cost. Specialized HDR sensors can mitigate these issues, but remain expensive and are not widely available.

In parallel, recent advances in text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models have made visual content creation accessible from simple inputs such as text prompts and coarse visual guidance (e.g., scribbles, drafts, or low-resolution images). Extending this convenience to the HDR domain is highly desirable: users should be able to create HDR content directly from text or from a low-quality camera input, without relying on bracketing software or specialized hardware.

Several recent methods attempt to adapt pretrained T2I models to support HDR by emulating the classic HDR pipeline: generate multi-exposure “brackets” and then merge them into an HDR output [Debevec and Malik (1997)]. While effective in principle, this strategy introduces substantial architectural and algorithmic complexity. For example, LEDiff [Wang et al. (2025)] trains separate denoisers for highlight hallucination and shadow recovery, and additionally finetunes the variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder [Kingma and Welling (2013)] to output linear HDR values. Bracket Diffusion [Bemana et al. (2025)] jointly denoises multi-exposure latents, incurring inference time and memory costs that scale with the number of brackets. These design choices complicate deployment and hinder adoption of newer, more memory-intensive backbone architectures.

We argue that much of this complexity stems from a simpler root cause: a representational mismatch between LDR and HDR imagery. Most contemporary diffusion models are trained on billions of display-encoded, nonlinearly compressed LDR images, whereas HDR and RAW data are natively expressed in a linear-light space prior to the image signal processor (ISP), resulting in dramatically different pixel-intensity statistics. In particular, human visual sensitivity to luminance changes is much higher in shadows than in highlights [Mantiuk et al. (2004)], making the linear HDR distribution poorly aligned with the perceptually shaped LDR data.

Building on this insight, we present X2HDR, a unified computational method for HDR image synthesis and reconstruction with minimal changes to existing T2I models. The key to X2HDR is to operate in a perceptually uniform space (e.g., induced by PU21 [Mantiuk and Azimi (2021)] or PQ [Miller et al. (2013)]). Specifically, we first map HDR data into this perceptual space, which compresses extreme highlights and reallocates precision toward shadows, in a way that reshapes HDR luminance statistics to better match LDR pretraining data. Empirically, this simple form of preprocessing empowers LDR-pretrained VAEs to recover PU21-encoded HDR inputs with fidelity comparable to LDR reconstructions, whereas linear HDR leads to distorted latents and severe artifacts. Leveraging this, X2HDR freezes the VAE and acquires HDR capability by finetuning only the denoiser through parameter-efficient low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [Hu et al. (2021)].

We instantiate X2HDR on two representative tasks: 1) text-to-HDR generation, synthesizing HDR images directly from text, and 2) single-image RAW-to-HDR reconstruction, in which the strong generative prior of the pretrained T2I model facilitates plausible hallucination of missing content in overexposed regions while suppressing noise in underexposed areas. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations, together with a formal perceptual study (see Supplemental Section F.8) on a calibrated HDR display, show that the proposed X2HDR consistently improves perceptual fidelity, text-image alignment, and effective dynamic range over prior approaches (see Figure 1).

In summary, our main contributions are

  • •

    A simple yet effective practice for HDR adaptation—encoding HDR/RAW inputs in a perceptually uniform space—which avoids complex bracket-and-merge pipelines and enables pretrained T2I models to support HDR with minimal modification;

  • •

    A unified computational method for text-to-HDR generation and RAW-to-HDR reconstruction with substantial perceptual improvements over previous methods.

    • 2 Perceptually Uniform HDR Representation

    In this section, we present X2HDR’s PU21-based HDR representation [Mantiuk and Azimi (2021)], supporting faithful reconstruction with an LDR-pretrained VAE.

    2.1 HDR Image Representation

    HDR (and RAW) images are typically stored in a linear color space, where pixel values are proportional to the underlying scene/sensor light signal up to a scale factor. However, linear representation is not perceptually uniform: an equal luminance increment is far more noticeable at low levels than at high levels. Perceptually uniform encodings address this mismatch by redistributing encoded values according to human visual sensitivity, including SMPTE PQ [Miller et al. (2013)] and PU21 [Mantiuk and Azimi (2021)]. For example, under PQ, an increase of 1 cd/m2 near darkness (0.005 cd/m2) is over 150× more salient than the same increase at 100 cd/m2. Beyond perceptual motivation, prior work [Ke et al. (2023)] also shows that networks train more effectively on PQ/PU21-encoded HDR/RAW data, rather than represented in linear space. These observations suggest adopting a perceptually uniform representation for HDR synthesis.

    In X2HDR, we encode linear HDR values using PU21, approximated by a log-quadratic function [Ke et al. (2023)]:

    V=f_PU21(L) = a (\log₂(L)-L_\min)² + b (\log₂(L)-L_\min),

    		(1)

    where L denotes an absolute linear RGB value within [0.005,10,000]. The fitted parameters are a=0.001908 and b=0.0078, and L_\min is set to \log₂(0.005). PU21 compresses extreme highlights while allocating more representational resolution to low-luminance values (see Supplemental Section E). The inverse transform is

    L=f_PU21⁻¹(V) = 2^(2aL_\min-b+√ b²+4aV)/(2a).

    		(2)

    For all HDR images, we globally rescale linear RGB values so that the maximum luminance corresponds to Lₚₑₐₖ=4,000 cd/m2 (matching the peak luminance of commercially available HDR displays). We then apply f_PU21(·) channel-wise to map the rescaled values to [0,1]. For generated outputs, we apply f_PU21⁻¹(·) to recover linear RGB values.

    2.2 Pretrained VAEs for HDR Reconstruction

    Modern diffusion models typically employ a VAE to map LDR images into a compact latent space, while reconstructing them with high fidelity. This raises a practical question central to X2HDR: must the VAE be finetuned for HDR reconstruction, or can an LDR-pretrained one already reconstruct HDR content accurately, provided an appropriate encoding is used?

    Setups

    We curate a Blu-ray movie (namely, “BBC Blue Planet II Episode 2 - The Deep”) that provides both LDR and HDR versions of the same content. Frames are time-synchronized by selecting the temporal offset that maximizes cross-correlation between corresponding pixel values. After temporal alignment and resolution matching, we randomly crop and resize paired frames to 768×768, producing a set of 512 (LDR, HDR) pairs with identical scene content. LDR frames are rescaled to [0,1], while HDR frames are processed in two ways: 1) converted into a perceptually uniform space using Equation (1), or 2) kept in linear space but normalized to [0,1]. We then encode and decode all images using the pretrained FLUX.1-dev VAE. Reconstruction fidelity is evaluated by ColorVideoVDP [Mantiuk et al. (2024)], which reports perceptual just-objectionable-difference (JOD) scores (one JOD corresponds to roughly a 75% observer preference), together with standard LDR metrics [Zhang et al. (2018); Wang et al. (2004)] applied via exposure-optimized inverse display models [Cao et al. (2024)].

    Results

    As summarized in Table 1, PU21-encoded HDR inputs are reconstructed nearly as well as LDR inputs: the JOD score drops only slightly (9.86→9.44), and the other metrics show similarly small gaps. In contrast, linear HDR inputs exhibit substantial degradation across all metrics. These quantitative trends are consistent with Figure 2: LDR and PU21 reconstructions preserve scene structure and texture with only minor (and imperceptible) artifacts, whereas linear HDR reconstructions present widespread distortions.

    Analysis

    PU21 improves VAE reconstruction by mapping HDR values to a perceptually meaningful representation that more closely matches the statistics of the LDR pretraining data. To illustrate this effect, we construct the inset histograms from 512 aligned LDR-HDR image pairs. We average the three RGB channels at each pixel, pool the resulting values across all images, and plot their probability densities on a logarithmic y-axis. Under linear HDR encoding, values are concentrated near zero, leaving much of the normalized input range underutilized. This highly skewed distribution differs substantially from that of the LDR training data.

    The mismatch also extends to the VAE latent space: linear HDR inputs produce a latent distribution that deviates from the LDR latent prior, with a Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence of 0.231 across the 512 pairs. By compressing extreme highlights and allocating greater representational resolution to shadows and midtones, PU21 distributes HDR values more broadly across the normalized range and reduces their concentration near zero. This transformation brings the inputs into closer alignment with the statistics expected by the LDR-pretrained VAE, reducing the latent-space KL divergence to 0.033. Additional analysis and a t-SNE visualization of the VAE latent space are provided in Supplemental Sections D and F.4.

    3 Text-to-HDR Image Generation

    As demonstrated in Section 2, the pretrained VAE can faithfully encode and decode HDR images after PU21 mapping, achieving reconstruction fidelity close to that obtained on standard LDR images. This observation simplifies text-to-HDR image generation: we keep the text encoder and VAE fixed, and finetune only the denoiser (through LoRA) while operating entirely in a perceptually uniform space. Our system diagram is shown in Figure 3.

    Training Data Preprocessing

    For each training HDR image I_HDR, we first apply a global rescaling so that its maximum luminance corresponds to Lₚₑₐₖ=4,000 cd/m2, and then map the rescaled values into the PU21 space. This conversion is the only departure from standard LDR finetuning; all subsequent steps follow the standard latent generative training procedure.

    Latent Formulation and Objective

    We map the PU21-encoded HDR image into VAE latents x₀ and tokenize the paired text prompt into cₚ. We then adopt the FLUX.1-dev T2I backbone and finetune it with flow matching. Specifically, for a timestep t∈[0,1], we sample ε∼ℕ(0,I) and construct an interpolated noisy latent z=(1-t)x₀+tε. We then finetune the model by optimizing the flow-matching objective [Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden (2022); Lipman et al. (2022); Esser et al. (2024)]:

    ℓ_flow(Θ;cₚ,x₀)=𝔼_t,ε ∥v_Θ(z,t,cₚ)-(ε-x₀)∥₂²,

    		(3)

    where v_Θ(·) denotes the learned velocity field with trainable parameters Θ, implemented via LoRA injection into the backbone.

    LoRA Finetuning

    We employ LoRA [Hu et al. (2021)], a parameter-efficient finetuning method to adapt the pretrained denoiser to the PU21-encoded HDR representation. LoRA represents the weight update of a linear layer as a low-rank decomposition: for a pretrained weight matrix W∈ℝ^dₒᵤₜ×dᵢₙ, instead of directly optimizing W, we freeze it and learn an additive update ΔW=BA with rank r, where A∈ℝ^r×dᵢₙ and B∈ℝ^dₒᵤₜ×r. The adapted layer becomes

    W^′=W+α/rBA,

    		(4)

    where α is a scaling factor. We insert LoRA modules into linear layers of attention blocks (e.g., query, key, value, and output projections) and optimize only the LoRA parameters while keeping the text encoder and VAE frozen. This yields an HDR-capable model with minimal trainable parameters and unchanged inference architecture.

    Inference

    At test time, given a text prompt, we sample an initial noise latent and integrate the learned flow (with merged low-rank updates) to generate a PU21-encoded HDR latent. The final HDR image in linear space is produced by the frozen VAE decoding and the inverse PU21 transform.

    4 RAW-to-HDR Image Reconstruction

    We next show that the same paradigm extends naturally to HDR reconstruction from a single RAW capture. Unlike sRGB-encoded LDR images, RAW offers a physically meaningful (albeit noisy) linear measurement that is approximately proportional to the incident light at the sensor before the ISP’s nonlinear stages of processing.

    We cast RAW-to-HDR as a direct mapping from a single RAW image to an HDR output, simultaneously denoising the sensor measurement and plausibly inpainting saturated or clipped regions. Although our method could be applied to enhance sRGB-encoded LDR images (see Supplemental Section F.7 for experiments in this setting), we focus on RAW inputs because 1) they typically retain more information in both underexposed and overexposed areas, and 2) they preserve approximately linear sensor values, avoiding the ill-posed problem of inverting in-camera processing. Accordingly, our goal is integration with the camera ISP rather than post-processing legacy LDR content.

    Given a RAW input, we first demosaic it following Ramanath et al.[Ramanath et al. (2002)]. We then rescale the peak luminance of both the RAW input and the ground-truth (GT) HDR target to Lₚₑₐₖ=4,000 cd/m2, and convert both to the PU21 space. We next encode the text prompt, RAW input, and target HDR to cₚ, c_RAW, and x₀, respectively. Training is guided by the same flow-matching objective ℓ_flow with LoRA finetuning as in the text-to-HDR setting, except that the learned velocity field additionally conditions on the RAW input:

    ℓ_flow(Θ;cₚ,c_RAW,x₀)=𝔼_t,ε ∥v_Θ(z,t,cₚ,c_RAW)-(ε-x₀)∥₂².

    		(5)

    Because our FLUX.1-dev backbone is DiT-based [Peebles and Xie (2023)], supporting variable-length token sequences, we inject RAW conditioning by simply concatenating the RAW image tokens with the text and HDR latent tokens [Zhang et al. (2025a); Tan et al. (2025)]. Empirically, this simple design converges fast and reliably: the model learns to recover coarse scene structure and texture early in training, while dark-region denoising and bright-region inpainting improve steadily with continued optimization.

    5 Experiments

    In this section, we benchmark X2HDR against previous HDR adaptation techniques that follow a bracket-and-merge paradigm (i.e., LEDiff [Wang et al. (2025)] and Bracket Diffusion [Bemana et al. (2025)]) and a dedicated RAW-to-HDR reconstruction method (i.e., RawHDR [Zou et al. (2023)]) using metrics that capture 1) perceptual image quality and text-image alignment, 2) effective dynamic range, and 3) HDR reconstruction fidelity.

    5.1 Evaluation Metrics

  • •

    Perceptual image quality and text-image alignment. We employ Q-Eval-100K [Zhang et al. (2025b)], which provides two finetuned vision and language models (VLMs) (based on Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct) that produce scalar scores in [0,1] for perceptual image quality and text-image alignment assessment for LDR images. To better match the VLMs’ expected input statistics, HDR images are first PU21-encoded prior to evaluation. A dedicated sanity check is reported in Supplemental Section F.12.

  • •

    Effective dynamic range. For each HDR image generated in text-to-HDR, we compute an effective dynamic-range estimate in exposure “stops.” We first apply Gaussian smoothing to suppress prediction noise, L̃=G_σ*L, using σ=3 pixels. We then remove extreme outliers by retaining only the [0.5,99.5] percentile range, and define the dynamic range (in stops) as

    DRₛₜₒₚₛ=\log₂(L̃_99.5/L̃_0.5),

    		(6)

    where L̃_0.5 and L̃_99.5 are the 0.5ᵗʰ and 99.5ᵗʰ percentiles of the filtered luminance, respectively.

  • •

    HDR reconstruction fidelity. For reconstruction evaluation, we use two complementary measures. We report JOD scores using ColorVideoVDP [Mantiuk et al. (2024)]. Meanwhile, we compute exposure-optimized variants of standard LDR metrics—PSNR, SSIM [Wang et al. (2004)], LPIPS [Zhang et al. (2018)], and DISTS [Ding et al. (2020)]—via an inverse display model [Cao et al. (2024)] that decomposes both the reconstruction and reference into aligned exposure stacks and evaluates each LDR metric at the best-matching exposures.

    • 5.2 Text-to-HDR Comparison

    We compare X2HDR instantiated with two backbones (FLUX.1-dev and SD-1.5) against LEDiff [Wang et al. (2025)] and Bracket Diffusion [Bemana et al. (2025)]. We evaluate on 100 text prompts generated by ChatGPT-5, spanning diverse lighting conditions (e.g., sunlight, candles, aurora, and fireworks). To match baseline constraints, all methods generate 512×512 outputs for this comparison, though X2HDR supports higher resolutions. The full set of prompts, additional details for the SD-1.5 variant, and results at higher resolutions are provided in Supplemental Sections C, F.5, and F.9.

    Quantitative Comparison

    Table 2 shows the quantitative results. X2HDR achieves the best perceptual image quality and text-image alignment, with the FLUX-based variant performing strongest. Even when controlling for backbone (i.e., SD-1.5), X2HDR remains competitive or better than competing methods while being much lighter at inference, owing to its parameter-efficient finetuning.

    Beyond Q-Eval-100K scores, X2HDR produces HDR outputs with a wide effective dynamic range (≈14 stops). In contrast, LEDiff yields significantly lower dynamic range (see also Figure 5). Bracket Diffusion reaches higher DRₛₜₒₚₛ than LEDiff, but does so at extreme computational cost (i.e., hundreds of seconds per image) and can exhibit luminance pathologies despite high DRₛₜₒₚₛ statistics. For example, Bracket Diffusion may collapse large regions toward near-zero values, i.e., a “shadow clipping” failure mode (see the palm tree in the second row of Figure 4), whereas X2HDR tends to maintain a more natural luminance distribution for each generation.

    Qualitative Comparison

    Figure 4 visualizes results at multi-exposure settings (in the sRGB color space). At EV -4, X2HDR better preserves distinct highlight emitters (e.g., lightning, bonfires, and the sun), indicating its capability of predicting sufficiently high peak luminance; LEDiff and Bracket Diffusion often appear dimmer with reduced highlight contrast. At EV +4, X2HDR reveals additional shadow structure, whereas LEDiff often washes out toward white and Bracket Diffusion tends to leave large regions nearly black due to shadow clipping. Overall, X2HDR better retains usable details across both highlights and shadows.

    5.3 RAW-to-HDR Comparison

    For RAW-to-HDR, we compare X2HDR to RawHDR [Zou et al. (2023)] and additionally include LEDiff and Bracket Diffusion, adapting them to the RAW setting by a RAW-to-sRGB conversion before applying their original pipelines. Evaluation uses 96 RAW images from the SI-HDR dataset [Hanji et al. (2022)] at 512×512 (see Supplemental Section F.2). For methods supporting text conditioning, we use an empty prompt (i.e., setting cₚ=∅) to ensure fairness. Text-guided hallucination results are deferred to Supplemental Section F.10.

    Quantitative Comparison

    Table 3 reports the JOD scores by ColorVideoVDP [Mantiuk et al. (2024)] and exposure-optimized Q^⋆ metrics [Cao et al. (2024)]. X2HDR achieves the best performance across all reported measures, outperforming RawHDR as well as the LDR-to-HDR counterparts in this RAW setting. These trends are consistent with the methodological differences: RawHDR trains a small U-Net from scratch, limiting its ability to plausibly inpaint missing content, while LEDiff and Bracket Diffusion operate with weaker priors and face a larger domain gap when driven by sRGB-converted RAW inputs.

    Qualitative Comparison

    Figure 6 shows representative results on four test RAW images. For underexposed inputs, RawHDR is inclined to introduce noticeable chromatic noise (e.g., in the tree of the first row). For overexposed scenes, RawHDR often suffers from color shifts (e.g., green cast) and struggles to inpaint coherent sky texture. LEDiff and Bracket Diffusion likewise fail to hallucinate plausible bright-region content. When conditioned on image inputs, Bracket Diffusion is further constrained by a lower operating resolution (256×256), leading to blur after upsampling. In contrast, X2HDR suppresses noise in dark regions and performs more spatially consistent inpainting in saturated areas, yielding cleaner and more realistic HDR reconstructions overall.

    5.4 Ablation Studies

    Necessity for Perceptually Uniform Representation

    To isolate the role of HDR representation, we replace the default PU21 encoding with linear encoding (normalized to [0,1]), gamma encoding (γ=2.2), log encoding (μ=500), and PQ encoding [Miller et al. (2013)]. As shown in Table 4 and Figures 7 and 8, all non-perceptually-uniform alternatives substantially degrade HDR behavior: in text-to-HDR, linear encoding yields severely limited dynamic range (i.e., DRₛₜₒₚₛ=5.5), and in RAW-to-HDR, it introduces strong artifacts (e.g., quantization), causing large drops across reconstruction metrics. Gamma and log encodings mitigate these issues to some extent, but both still exhibit reduced dynamic range and noticeable quantization artifacts. This arises because these representations assign an excessive portion of the available output range to highlights, resulting in a significant mismatch with sRGB statistics and lower image quality and text-image alignment scores under Q-Eval-100K. PQ, as expected, performs comparably to PU21 on both tasks, supporting the central claim that perceptually uniform HDR representation is critical for adapting LDR-pretrained T2I models to HDR synthesis and reconstruction.

    Necessity for Finetuning

    We also test whether HDR outputs can be obtained without any finetuning by directly decoding and rescaling pretrained T2I latents, followed by the inverse PU21 transform. This text-to-HDR configuration frequently over-stretches the tonal and chromatic range, leading to two characteristic failure modes: 1) exaggerated global contrast and saturation caused by over-expanding LDR latents (see the third row of Figure 7) and 2) widespread clipping that removes recoverable details (e.g., the grassland remains dark even at EV +4). We direct the readers to more visual examples in the HTML supplementary and the discussion in Supplemental Section F.12.

    6 Conclusion

    We have presented X2HDR, a simple and effective adaptation method that enables pretrained T2I diffusion models to operate in HDR for both text-to-HDR generation and RAW-to-HDR reconstruction. The key idea is to mitigate the distribution gap between linear-light HDR/RAW data and LDR-pretrained models by mapping HDR values into a perceptually uniform space. This simple preprocessing allows an off-the-shelf LDR-pretrained VAE to represent HDR content faithfully, so HDR capability can be acquired by parameter-efficient LoRA finetuning of the denoiser while keeping the rest of the computational structure unchanged. The resulting X2HDR is unified and deployment-friendly, and it yields reliable HDR generation and reconstruction results with improved perceptual fidelity and usable dynamic range.

    This work was supported in part by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the Research Grants Council of Hong Kong under the Collaborative Research Scheme (Project No. CRS_HKUST605/25), and by the Innovation and Technology Fund of the Hong Kong Innovation and Technology Commission (Project Nos. 9440379 and 9440390).

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Overview

    This appendix provides supplementary results and implementation details that support and extend the findings of the main paper. Specifically, it includes:

  • •

    Prior HDR generation and reconstruction methods (Section B);

  • •

    Complete HDR results for text-to-HDR generation and RAW-to-HDR reconstruction, including comparisons, ablations, and perceptual experiments, as well as HDR outputs at multiple resolutions and for synthetic stimuli (Sections C, F.5, F.6, and F.9);

  • •

    Detailed analysis of PU21 perceptually uniform encoding (Section D);

  • •

    HDR encoding function visualization (Section E);

  • •

    Dataset and reproducibility details for training and evaluation (Sections F.1 and F.3);

  • •

    Extended VAE analysis, including failure characterization, VAE finetuning, and latent distribution visualization (Section F.4);

  • •

    LDR-to-HDR reconstruction experiments (Section F.7);

  • •

    Perceptual study details (Section F.8);

  • •

    Applications to text-guided hallucination (Section F.10);

  • •

    Limitations (Section G) and future research directions (Section H).

    • Appendix B Related Work

    Our work connects three lines of research: T2I diffusion models in LDR, efforts to extend such models to HDR, and HDR reconstruction from a single image or multi-exposure brackets.

    B.1 T2I Diffusion Models in LDR

    Diffusion models have become a dominant paradigm for text-guided image synthesis, producing high-quality results across diverse scene types, semantic compositions, and visual styles [Chen et al. (2023a); Rombach et al. (2022); Saharia et al. (2022); Nichol et al. (2021)]. Latent diffusion models [Rombach et al. (2022)] improve scalability by learning the generative process in a compressed latent space: a VAE maps high-dimensional images into low-dimensional latents, and a denoiser learns to invert progressive corruption in this space. More recent work integrates Transformer backbones [Vaswani et al. (2017)] into diffusion processes, giving rise to diffusion Transformers (DiT) [Peebles and Xie (2023)]. Building on these developments, FLUX[Labs (2024)] combines Transformer-based architectures with flow matching objectives [Lipman et al. (2022); Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden (2022); Liu et al. (2022a)], achieving state-of-the-art T2I generation performance. Here we mainly adopt FLUX.1-dev as the backbone and investigate how to extend it to HDR tasks with minimal changes.

    B.2 HDR Image Generation

    Compared with LDR generation, text-guided HDR image synthesis remains relatively underexplored. Two closely related methods are LEDiff [Wang et al. (2025)] and Bracket Diffusion [Bemana et al. (2025)]. Both emulate the classical HDR workflow by generating multi-exposure “brackets” and subsequently merging them into a single HDR output [Debevec and Malik (1997)]. LEDiff finetunes specialized denoisers for highlight hallucination and shadow recovery, and adapts the VAE decoder to produce linear RGB values. Bracket Diffusion instead jointly denoises over multiple exposures, incorporating constraints that preserve exposure diversity while enforcing semantic consistency across the exposure stack. While effective, these bracket-and-merge designs add architectural and algorithmic complexity, increase inference-time and memory requirements, and can introduce unwanted fusion artifacts—factors that hinder portability to newer, more memory-intensive T2I backbones. In contrast, X2HDR adapts pretrained T2I models by operating directly in a perceptually uniform space, avoiding explicit bracket generation and fusion while remaining compatible with modern architectures.

    B.3 HDR Image Reconstruction

    Most HDR imaging techniques rely on multi-exposure bracketing: capturing several LDR exposures and merging them into HDR radiance maps [Debevec and Malik (1997)]. For dynamic scenes, however, camera/scene motion causes misalignment and ghosting, motivating an extensive body of work on motion-aware HDR reconstruction [Sen et al. (2012)]. Recent methods integrate stronger alignment and deghosting modules [Kalantari and Ramamoorthi (2017); Yan et al. (2019); Yan et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2025); Kong et al. (2024); Ye et al. (2021)] with powerful backbones such as U-Nets [Wu et al. (2018)] and Transformers [Chen et al. (2023b); Liu et al. (2022b); Song et al. (2022); Tel et al. (2023)]. Nevertheless, robust reconstruction under large motion and severe saturation remains challenging.

    A complementary line of research considers single-image LDR-to-HDR reconstruction (also referred to as inverse tone-mapping). Classical inverse methods expand dynamic range via heuristic linearization and optional detail hallucination [Akyüz et al. (2007); Banterle et al. (2008); Banterle et al. (2009); Didyk et al. (2008); Masia et al. (2009); Masia et al. (2017)]. Learning-based methods either approximately invert the ISP end-to-end [Eilertsen et al. (2017); Liu et al. (2020); Marnerides et al. (2018); Santos et al. (2020); Yu et al. (2021); Dille et al. (2024)], or synthesize multi-exposures from a single image and then apply conventional HDR merging [Endo et al. (2017); Lee et al. (2018); Zhang et al. (2023b); Wang et al. (2025); Bemana et al. (2025)]. However, limited training data can reduce generalization, and bracket-synthesis approaches tend to introduce inter-exposure inconsistencies, especially under extreme dark and bright regions.

    In this paper, we depart from the prevailing LDR-to-HDR paradigm and study HDR reconstruction from a single RAW capture, a setting that has received comparatively little attention. Zou et al.[Zou et al. (2023)] explored a related setting with a rather elaborate workflow. In contrast, we propose a simple approach that leverages powerful generative priors to denoise and inpaint effectively during HDR reconstruction, yielding superior performance.

    Appendix C Complete HDR Results

    Because HDR content is difficult to reproduce faithfully in a static PDF, we provide extended results on the project website https://X2HDR.github.io/, including 1) 100 text-to-HDR images, 2) 96 RAW-to-HDR reconstructions, 3) ablation results under linear encoding, PQ encoding, and without finetuning for both text-to-HDR and RAW-to-HDR tasks, and 4) visual stimuli selected in the perceptual study with their corresponding JOD scores.

    To ensure comparable perceived brightness, we normalize all HDR images by mapping the median luminance to 0.5~cd/m². For efficient browser-based viewing, EXR files are converted to a compact JPEG gain-map representation using gainmap-js111https://github.com/MONOGRID/gainmap-js. Note that a correct HDR viewing experience requires an HDR-capable display; on LDR monitors, appearance may deviate from true HDR content, and perceived quality depends on the specific HDR hardware.

    Appendix D PU21 Perceptually Uniform Encoding

    PU21 [Mantiuk and Azimi (2021)] is a scalar encoding that maps absolute HDR luminance values from 0.005 to 10,000 cd/m2 into an approximately perceptually uniform domain. In this domain, Euclidean distances correspond more closely to visible differences, allowing metrics such as PSNR and SSIM to be applied meaningfully to HDR images. The encoding is derived by numerically integrating contrast sensitivity, defined as the inverse of the detection threshold, over log-luminance. An analytic, invertible curve is then fitted and scaled to map the luminance range to [0,1].

    Whereas PU08 [Aydın et al. (2008)] and PQ [Miller et al. (2013)] are derived from peak contrast sensitivity, PU21 models the detection of banding artifacts caused by fixed-bit-depth quantization. It also accounts for the reduced visibility of differences in dark image regions due to disability glare—the scattering of light within the optics of the eye.

    Appendix E Encoding Function Visualization

    Figure 9 compares five encodings used to map linear RGB luminance to display-encoded values: linear encoding, gamma encoding (γ=2.2), log encoding (μ=500), PQ [Miller et al. (2013)], and PU21 [Mantiuk and Azimi (2021)]. Linear mapping assigns a disproportionately large range to highlights, heavily compressing low-luminance values. Gamma and log encodings partially rebalance this allocation, but they still do not achieve the same degree of perceptual uniformity as PQ and PU21. In contrast, PQ and PU21 nonlinearly compress extreme highlights while allocating more resolution to shadows and midtones, spreading low-luminance differences in the encoded domain. Although PQ and PU21 differ in functional form, both reshape HDR statistics toward distributions that better match LDR-pretrained models. We further visualize the RGB value distributions in Figure 10 using the histogram procedure described in Section 2.2. Gamma and log encodings produce distributions closer to that of LDR data than PQ and PU21 do. However, the ablation study in Section 5.4 shows that they underperform perceptually uniform encodings after finetuning, suggesting that LDR-like statistics alone are insufficient for HDR adaptation. One possible explanation lies in the inverse transformation applied after generation: the decoded image must be mapped back to linear RGB values, and this mapping can amplify errors introduced in the encoded domain. Although generic concave mappings such as gamma and log improve histogram alignment, they do not allocate encoded values according to perceptual sensitivity across the HDR luminance range. Consequently, small errors in the encoded domain can produce visible errors after inversion.

    Appendix F More Experimental Details and Results

    F.1 Training Dataset

    Text-to-HDR

    We build the training set (3,278 HDR images) primarily from publicly available HDR datasets used in prior work [Poly Haven (2025); Bolduc et al. (2023); Fairchild (2007); Gardner et al. (2017); Kalantari and Ramamoorthi (2017); Liu et al. (2020); Panetta et al. (2021); Tel et al. (2023)]. From each HDR image, we randomly extract 512×512 and 1,024×1,024 crops, retaining only those with an effective dynamic range of DRₛₜₒₚₛ≥5. For HDR panoramas, random perspective projections are applied before cropping. To better exploit high-resolution sources, we use an adaptive sampling scheme that draws proportionally more crops from larger images, producing 32,200 patches at 512×512 and 6,714 patches at 1,024×1,024. Text prompts are obtained by tone-mapping HDR crops [Drago et al. (2003)] and captioning them with a VLM (i.e., Gemini-2.0-Flash) using the following instruction:

    ⬇Youareaprofessionalimage-captioningassistant.Generateobjective,accurate,anddetailedcaptionsbasedontheprovidedimage.Producetwooutputs:(i)ashortcaption(1--3sentences)thatsummarizesthemaincontent,and(ii)alongcaption(oneparagraph)thatdescribesallsalientdetails.Useprecise,descriptivelanguage;remainfactualandavoidsubjectiveinterpretation.Outputonlythecaptions,formattedexactlyas:’###Short:’and’###Long:’.

    During training, we randomly select either the short or long caption at each iteration.

    RAW-to-HDR

    The RAW-to-HDR training data are drawn from prior HDR datasets [Fairchild (2007); Zou et al. (2023)], comprising 517 scenes with multiple RAW exposures. For each scene, bracketed RAW images are merged into a reference HDR image using HDRUtils222https://github.com/gfxdisp/HDRUtils, with exposure estimation and alignment [Hanji et al. (2020); Hanji and Mantiuk (2023)]. Paired (RAW, HDR) samples are formed by cropping spatially co-located regions. We extract 10 crops per RAW exposure, resulting in a total of 22,160 pairs at 512×512. HDR targets are tone-mapped and captioned with the same VLM.

    F.2 RAW-to-HDR Test Dataset

    Instead of splitting the collected training data, evaluation is performed on an independent SI-HDR dataset [Hanji et al. (2022)], consisting of 183 scenes with up to 7 RAW exposures and merged HDR references. It provides a clear domain gap and is well-suited for assessing the generalizability of RAW-to-HDR reconstruction methods. We randomly sample 96 scenes; for each scene, we discard the darkest and brightest exposures and then randomly choose one RAW image from the remaining. Each selected RAW image is cropped and resized to ensure pixel-alignment with the HDR reference at 1,888×1,280, and then further cropped and downsampled to 512×512 for evaluation.

    F.3 Implementation Details

    We use FLUX.1-dev as the default T2I backbone. For text-to-HDR, we set the LoRA rank to 32, with a learning rate of 1×10⁻⁴ and a dedicated LoRA trigger token, [PU21]. The per-GPU batch size is 8 for 512×512 and 2 for 1,024×1,024, with 4 gradient accumulation steps. Training converges after approximately 3,000 steps on 4 GPUs. For RAW-to-HDR, we adopt EasyControl [Zhang et al. (2025a)] for conditional generation, which enhances the DiT backbone by introducing attention masking, position-encoding cloning, and conditional LoRA injection. We set the LoRA rank to 128 with learning rate 1×10⁻⁴. During training, we randomly drop text prompts (i.e., setting cₚ=∅) with 50% probability to implement RAW-only reconstruction. Training runs for 8 epochs on 512×512 images with batch size 2 on 4 GPUs. For both tasks, the LoRA scaling factor α is set equal to the LoRA rank.

    F.4 Additional VAE Analysis

    By default, X2HDR freezes the pretrained VAE and adapts only the denoiser of the T2I model. We further analyze when the frozen VAE fails on PU21-encoded HDR data and whether HDR-specific VAE finetuning provides additional benefits.

    Failure characterization

    While PU21 generally induces high-fidelity reconstruction, the pretrained VAE occasionally under-reconstructs highlight regions (see Figure 11).

    VAE finetuning

    To improve highlight reconstruction, we finetune the pretrained FLUX.1-dev VAE on PU21-encoded HDR data. Dataset preparation largely follows the text-to-HDR training pipeline (see Section F.1), but omits VLM captioning and fixes crop resolution to 768×768. This yields a total of 60,399 HDR images. Training uses learning rate 1×10⁻⁵, batch size 1, 8 gradient accumulation steps, 2 epochs, and 4 GPUs. Several reconstruction losses are tested, including the mean absolute error (MAE), locally adaptive DISTS (ADISTS) metric [Ding et al. (2021)], a differentiable histogram matching loss [Mustafa et al. (2022)], and their variants combined with an inverse display model [Mantiuk and Heidrich (2009)]. MAE is found sufficient.

    After finetuning, average JOD on 512 test HDR images rises from 9.44 to 9.72, with visible improvements in some highlight cases (see the last column of Figure 11). However, gains are not consistent across content, and the finetuned VAE remains below the LDR reconstruction counterpart. The remaining gap may be due to limited HDR data scale and diversity (with many crops originating from relatively few scenes).

    Latent distribution visualization

    Using 512 (LDR, HDR) pairs, we compare the VAE latent distributions for 1) LDR inputs, 2) linear HDR inputs, 3) PU21-encoded HDR inputs with the pretrained VAE, and 4) PU21-encoded HDR inputs with the finetuned VAE. A t-SNE projection with 2σ confidence ellipses in Figure 12 shows that PU21 significantly reduces the LDR-HDR mismatch relative to linear HDR, while VAE finetuning produces only marginal latent changes.

    Effect of VAE finetuning on RAW-to-HDR

    Training a RAW-to-HDR model with the finetuned VAE (all else unchanged) does not yield consistent improvements. As shown in Table 5, aside from a modest gain in Q^⋆_SSIM, other measures slightly degrade, plausibly due to mild latent distribution shift that affects denoising and inpainting during reverse diffusion.

    Summary

    Perceptually uniform encoding (e.g., PU21) is the dominant factor facilitating alignment between LDR and HDR latent representations. Under the current data scale, VAE finetuning adds limited benefits, though it may be more valuable with larger and more diverse HDR datasets.

    F.5 Text-to-HDR with SD-1.5

    To verify backbone generality (and support fair comparison with LEDiff and Bracket Diffusion), X2HDR is also instantiated with SD-1.5, using the same PU21 encoding and LoRA strategy. The SD-1.5 setup uses LoRA rank 8, learning rate 1×10⁻⁵, and batch size 32. Training is limited to 1,000 steps to avoid overfitting, and the trigger token [PU21] is prepended.

    Additional visual results in Figure 13 show that highlights remain well separated at EV -4 and shadow details emerge at EV +4. Figure 14 further indicates that the SD-based variant achieves dynamic range comparable to the FLUX-based model, supporting the reliability of PU21-based adaptation across backbones.

    F.6 RAW-to-HDR on Synthetic Data

    To probe RAW-to-HDR behavior under controlled degradation, we construct a synthetic dataset using 512×512 HDR images with radial luminance gradients that decrease logarithmically from 4,000 cd/m2 at the center to 0.005 cd/m2 at the corners, instantiated across multiple chromatic channels (e.g., yellow and red). Synthetic RAW inputs are simulated by applying a virtual exposure that clips values above 100 cd/m2 and adding Poisson-Gaussian noise calibrated to Sony A7R III.

    Reconstructions in Figure 15 indicate that X2HDR effectively suppresses sensor noise, while competing techniques introduce structured artifacts. However, all methods struggle to recover ideal smooth gradients in heavily clipped regions, reflecting limited generalization to synthetic patterns absent from training. RawHDR [Zou et al. (2023)] is excluded because it requires camera-specific metadata (e.g., Bayer pattern and camera-to-RGB transformations) not defined in this synthetic setup.

    F.7 LDR-to-HDR Image Reconstruction

item.title: 用代码改 3D 比重新生成更实用：3DCodeEdit 建了 2592 个编辑任务，17 个模型平均只有 37% 成功率 ｜ 3DCodeEdit: Benchmarking Instruction-Guided 3D Program Editing
item.description:
一句话：改已有程序比重新生成快且可控，但模型普遍不会「预见改动会怎么改写结构」。

要点：

  • 问题定位准确：语言模型越来越多通过代码造 3D 内容，而实际工作流常是**编辑已有程序**（更快、可控），这要求模型既懂「这段程序会造出什么」，又能预见「改动会怎样重塑它」
  • 3DCodeEdit 提供 2592 个指令引导的编辑任务，覆盖 108 个纯代码构建物体的 Blender 程序；编辑类型从参数改动到结构修改、风格重设计、场景组合
  • 判分基于渲染结果 + 人工复核的检查清单；17 个模型的平均成功率只有 37%

为什么值得看：「AI 造资产」的真实工作是改而不是造。这个 benchmark 把「程序化资产的增量编辑」单独衡量，并把判据放在渲染与人工清单上——对做 agent + 程序化内容管线的团队，这是目前最贴近工作流的评测口径。

中文摘要：语言模型越来越多地通过写代码来造 3D 内容，而实际工作流往往不是重新生成，而是**编辑已有程序**——这样更快、控制更精确。这类编辑要求模型同时理解「这段程序会构建出什么」与「一处改动会如何重塑结构」，而此前的基准多只评测生成或对着参考做简单编辑。3DCodeEdit 因此提出一个面向指令引导的程序化编辑基准：2592 个编辑任务分布在 108 个完全用代码构建物体的 Blender 程序上，编辑类型覆盖参数调整、结构性修改、风格重设计与场景组合，并按渲染结果对照人工复核的检查清单判分。横评 17 个模型，平均成功率仅 37%，说明「看懂程序再改对」远未被解决。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-30

本期推送：2026-10-31

3DCodeEdit: Benchmarking Instruction-Guided 3D Program Editing

Abstract

Language models increasingly create 3D content through code, with practical workflows often relying on editing existing programs rather than regenerating them, for speed and precise control. Such edits require understanding what a program builds and foreseeing how a change reshapes it, yet prior benchmarks mostly evaluate generation or simple edits against a reference. In this paper, we introduce 3DCodeEdit, a benchmark of 2,592 instruction-guided editing tasks over 108 Blender programs that construct objects entirely in code. Its edits range from parameter to structural changes, style redesign, and scene composition, and are judged from renders against human-reviewed checklists. Across 17 models, the average success rate is only 37%, and even the strongest models complete fewer than 60% of structural and style edits. As models become more capable, their failures shift to geometric foresight, where the code runs but builds the wrong shape. We therefore study whether multi-turn feedback can compensate for this missing foresight. Feedback from a separate reviewer model that describes how the renders differ from the request helps most, more than maximum reasoning effort or an agent harness, and can let a 27B model surpass the single-shot rate of a 2.8T-parameter model.

1 Introduction

Code is becoming a common way to represent 3D assets. Procedural generators define objects as programs [(Raistrick et al., 2023)], game engines define reusable assets as parametric classes [(Epic Games, 2026)], and frontier models now build objects by writing Blender programs [(Anthropic, 2026a; OpenAI, 2026b)]. Once written, such a program is revised many times, as users refine the asset, adapt it into variants, or update it to new requirements. A user who has generated an armchair, for example, may later want a taller backrest, or want to turn it into a rocking chair (Figure 1c). Editing the program is faster than regenerating the chair, and it changes only the requested parts while keeping the rest intact.

Such an edit is demanding because the instruction describes how the object should look, while the model can only change the code. The model must work out from the code what shape it builds, foresee how a change will reshape it, and write renderable code that makes exactly this change. The task therefore requires multimodal understanding and foresight that link code to 3D geometry, on top of code editing. Even as code generation improves rapidly [(Chen et al., 2021; Jimenez et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2026; Merrill et al., 2026)], frontier models still struggle with instructed code editing [(Cassano et al., 2024; Chi et al., 2026)] and with spatial reasoning [(Fu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a)]. For example, a model may break the structure of the existing program so that it no longer runs, or, failing to foresee the result of its change, write code that runs but builds the wrong shape, such as a new part floating in the air, disconnected from the object [(Gao et al., 2026)].

A benchmark for this kind of editing should meet three requirements. First, the program should build the entire object in code, exposing its parameters and parts to the edit. An object stored in a pre-built scene file or as raw mesh data leaves nothing meaningful to edit. Ideally, the programs are also larger, more complex, and diverse, so that the shape cannot be read off at a glance. Second, the edits should range from local changes to structural and open-ended ones, which capture more edit types in practice and also require foreseeing more of the geometry. Third, each edit should be judged from renders on whether the requested change is made and the rest preserved, without relying on a reference output. An instruction rarely fixes a single outcome. Even “make the backrest taller” can be met at many heights, and open-ended edits, common in real-world editing, admit far more. However, existing benchmarks either evaluate generation from scratch [(Du et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Noor et al., 2026)] or edit objects in pre-built scenes against a reference output [(Gu et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2026)] (Table 1).

To fill this gap, we introduce 3DCodeEdit, a benchmark of 2,592 instruction-guided editing tasks over 108 Blender programs (Figures 1 and 2). Each program builds its object entirely in code. Besides procedurally generated objects, the programs include designs of buildings, furniture, and mechanical parts shared by designers online, which we reconstruct as editable Blender programs through an agent loop grounded in renders. Building on these programs, we design six edit types: four geometric types graded by scope, from a single parameter to the structure of the whole object, and two open-ended types, style redesign and scene composition. The editor sees only the program and the instruction. An edit succeeds only if its code runs and renders, and it passes a human-reviewed checklist, with one item per requested change and one for preserving the rest, as judged by a multimodal verifier that compares renders of the original and edited objects.

We evaluate 17 models and find that editing remains hard, and gets harder with scope. The average success rate is only 37%, falling from 82.9% on single-parameter edits to 24.6% on structural edits, and even strong models, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1-sol, complete fewer than 60% of structural and style edits. Moreover, as models get stronger, their failures shift from misreading the instruction or the program, or writing code that does not run, to geometric foresight, where the code runs but builds the wrong shape. Since the editor cannot foresee its result, we further study multi-turn editing, in which a reviewer inspects the renders and returns feedback, as a user would. We investigate which kinds of feedback compensate for the missing foresight and who should provide them. Seeing its own renders helps the editor, but models rarely revise their own edits. Feedback from a separate reviewer helps far more, especially when it describes how the renders differ from the request, and beats both maximum reasoning effort and an agent harness. The reviewer needs to judge well rather than edit well, and with a stronger reviewer, even Qwen3.8-27B surpasses the single-shot rate of the 2.8T-parameter Kimi K3 (50.3% vs. 46.8%). Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We present 3DCodeEdit, a novel benchmark that captures edits to how an object is built in code, graded from a single parameter to the whole structure, as well as open-ended style redesign and scene composition, which previous benchmarks do not test.

  • •

    We design a reference-free evaluation that makes open-ended edits measurable, judging each edit from renders against an instance-specific checklist of the requested changes and the preservation of the rest, with 90.4% agreement with human labels.

  • •

    We evaluate 17 models and track 44 over time, revealing that as models improve, their failures shift from comprehension and coding to geometric foresight.

  • •

    We show that feedback from a separate reviewer, especially a description of how the renders differ from the request, compensates for this missing foresight far better than self-checking, more reasoning, or an agent harness, even when the reviewer edits worse than the editor.

    • 2 Related Work

    Generating and editing 3D with code.

    Neural 3D generators now produce high-fidelity assets [(Poole et al., 2023; Xiang et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025)], but they represent an asset without explicit parts or parameters, so precise and controllable edits remain difficult [(Zhang et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025c; Sella et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2025)]. Code instead exposes parameters and construction logic. Language models first generated 3D programs by calling procedural generators such as Infinigen [(Raistrick et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2025)] or simplified APIs [(Yamada et al., 2025)], and now write Blender programs directly, building complex, part-structured objects and scenes [(Hu et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2025; Dai et al., 2025; Noor et al., 2026; Yin et al., 2026)]. Editing has received less attention. BlenderAlchemy searches over edits to materials, geometry, and lighting [(Huang et al., 2024)], and LL3M, MeshCoder, and Nova3D demonstrate edits through code changes [(Lu et al., 2025; Dai et al., 2025; Noor et al., 2026)], but these works evaluate editing only qualitatively or on small, narrow sets.

    Benchmarks for 3D code.

    Most benchmarks for Blender code evaluate generation from scratch, from text, images, target geometry, or videos [(Du et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Noor et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026)]. Only two benchmarks evaluate editing, both at a small scale. BlenderGym defines each of its 245 instances by a start and a goal scene and scores an edit by its distance to the goal [(Gu et al., 2025)], and BlenderBench specifies 27 tasks by target images [(Yin et al., 2026)]. Both run short scripts on pre-built scene files, and their edits tune placement, materials, lighting, the camera, shape keys, or the parameters of an existing generator, without restructuring how an object is built. Their reference outputs also penalize valid edits that differ from the target, which rules out open-ended edits. 3DCodeEdit instead edits programs that build the whole object, at scopes up to its overall structure and including open-ended edits, which it judges with instance-specific checklists (Table 1).

    3 The 3DCodeEdit Benchmark

    3DCodeEdit pairs Blender programs that build entire objects with instructed edits of graded scope, and judges each edit from renders against a checklist (Figure 2). After defining the task (§3.1), we describe the programs (§3.2), the edits (§3.3), and the checklists that judge them (§3.4).

    3.1 Task Definition

    Given a Blender program that builds an object and an edit prompt, the editor returns the edited program. The edit succeeds if the edited program runs and renders, and its renders satisfy every item of a checklist paired with the prompt.

    Formally, a task is a tuple (P,q,L). P is a Blender Python program, and R(P) denotes its renders from six fixed views. The edit prompt q=(q₀,q₁,…,qₖ) consists of a preservation instruction q₀, which asks to keep the object’s identity and the parts outside the requested edits, and edit instructions q₁,…,qₖ. The checklist L=(ℓ₀,…,ℓₖ) pairs each instruction qᵢ with a binary item ℓᵢ. The editor receives only (P,q) and returns an edited program P^′. A verifier receives R(P), R(P^′), q, and one item ℓᵢ, but neither program, and returns vᵢ∈{0,1}. The edit succeeds if

    y=1[R(P^′)≠∅]·∏_i∉Avᵢ,

    		(1)

    where R(P^′)=∅ if P^′ fails to execute or render, and A is a small set of items excluded as ambiguous (§3.4). We report the all-pass rate, the mean of y over tasks. Both objects are rendered with the same cameras, so the verifier can judge comparative items such as “taller than before” and detect unintended changes (Appendix C).

    3.2 Programs That Build Entire Objects

    Our 108 programs cover six object categories (Figure 3a), with 53 reconstructed from OpenSCAD111https://openscad.org models and 55 from 3DCodeBench [(Gao et al., 2026)]. From 3DCodeBench, we keep 55 of 76 executed candidates that have sound geometry and offer visible structure to edit. Since these programs include no buildings or mechanical parts, we reconstruct the other 53 from parametric OpenSCAD models of architecture, furniture, and manufacturing objects shared by designers online.

    Converting these models directly loses either the parameters or the shape. Translating the constructive solid geometry keeps the shape but flattens modules and parameters into raw vertices and Boolean operations, whereas asking a model to rewrite the design in one pass keeps the structure but loses fidelity on complex objects (Appendix A.1). We instead reconstruct each model in a loop grounded in renders (Figure 2). A generator agent writes and renders a Blender program, and an independent evaluator agent compares its renders with those of the source and either accepts it or returns feedback for the next round. Mirroring how designers write parametric models, the generator separates low-level geometry helpers from a high-level, parameterized assembly of the parts, so that edits of growing scope touch a parameter, a part, or the assembly itself. Reconstructions take 5.5 rounds on average and run without human intervention (example trajectory in Appendix Figure 5). From 127 reconstructions, we keep 53 after removing simple objects, duplicate object types, and models whose license does not clearly permit redistribution. The resulting programs (examples in Appendix Figure 7) have a median of 440 lines, an order of magnitude longer than the BlendNet programs used by CADBench (Appendix B).

    3.3 Edits of Graded Scope

    The scope of an edit determines how much of the existing geometry the model must work out and foresee. We therefore grade edits by scope, following the SOLO taxonomy of learning outcomes [(Biggs and Collis, 1982)], and add open-ended edits that go beyond the existing structure, as users often request in practice (Table 2). The four geometric edit types grow in scope. G1 changes one attribute of a part, G2 and G3 rebuild one or two parts, and G4 reorganizes how parts relate to one another. Style redesign (S) gives the whole object a different style, and scene composition (C) builds a functional scene around it. Each program receives four prompts per edit type, giving 2,592 tasks (Figure 3c).

    3.4 Checklists Judged from Renders

    Since an instruction admits many valid results, we score no edit against a reference output. Instead, every instruction qᵢ is paired with a checklist item ℓᵢ that verifies it, so each item must be decidable from the renders and admit a single reading. Appendix D shows eight tasks with edits from six models.

    Writing and filtering prompts.

    For each program and edit type, GPT-5.6-sol reads the program, its description, and four renders, and writes eight candidate prompts, pairing each instruction with a checklist item. Each task also receives a preservation instruction q₀, whose item ℓ₀ checks that the object stays identifiable outside the edit. We then filter the candidates in three steps. (1) GPT-5.6-sol rejects candidates whose outcome would not be visible or that violate the edit-type definition. (2) Human annotators reject candidates that are ambiguous, not visually verifiable, or unreasonable. Together, these two steps admit 73.4% of 5,620 candidates, and we keep four per program and edit type, giving 2,592 prompts with 12,528 checklist items. (3) Claude Opus 5.5 screens every item for multiple readings, such as whether “about 50% larger” refers to diameter or area, and flagged instructions are rewritten under human supervision. This revises 787 prompts, and the 51 items (0.4%) that remain ambiguous are excluded from scoring as the set A. Details are in Appendices A.2 and A.3.

    Verifier.

    Among 16 multimodal models compared against human judgments, we choose Gemini 3.8 Flash as the verifier to balance accuracy and cost (Appendix E). On 210 items that a human annotator labels from the same renders, it agrees with the human label on 90.4% of items (Cohen’s κ=0.80). Judging from the programs instead lowers agreement for every verifier we test, because code that reads as correct can still build the wrong shape, such as a part tilted the wrong way or left floating, which is hard to see in the code but obvious in the renders (Appendix E).

    4 How Well Do Models Edit 3D Programs?

    Setup.

    We evaluate 17 models, 9 proprietary and 8 open-weight, in a single-shot setting: each model receives the task once and returns the complete edited program. We report the all-pass rate (§3.1): the percentage of tasks whose edit renders and passes every checklist item under the verifier of §3.4. Model references and decoding settings are in Appendix C. Analyses that need many runs use an analysis subset of 312 tasks from 13 randomly chosen source programs (§4.2, §4.3, and §4.4).

    4.1 Main Results

    Table 3 reveals three patterns. First, a steep scope gap. The average all-pass rate is 37.1%, and even the strongest editors, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1-sol, reach only about 70% overall and fewer than 60% on structural (G4) and style (S) edits. The average rate drops most from parameter edits (G1, 82.9%) to component edits (G2, 43.5%) and falls to 24.6% on structural edits (G4). Second, open-ended edits distinguish strong models. All six types order the 17 models almost the same way (mean Spearman ρ=0.97), but the gaps between models are not the same. Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1-sol, and Gemini 3.8 Flash are within about 8 points of each other on G2–G4, yet 23 points apart on S and 35 points apart on C. Third, the two best models solve different tasks. Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1-sol each solve about 70% of the tasks, but 82.6% are solved by at least one of them. Their successes overlap least on S and C (task-level correlation 0.23 and 0.18, against about 0.4 on G2–G4; Appendix Table 15).

    4.2 Editing Ability over Time

    To measure how fast this ability improves, we evaluate 44 models released since November 2024 on the analysis subset (Figure 4; models listed in Appendix Table 14). First, progress has accelerated. The best all-pass rate took 16 months to rise from 9.0% to 40.1% (November 2024 to March 2026) and only six more months to reach 67.6%. The same holds within families: Claude Opus gained 9 points in the six months up to Opus 4.8 and 28 points in the four months after it. Second, mid-sized open-weight models fall behind. The 27–32B Qwen models trail the best model available at their release by 20 points (Qwen3.5, February 2026) and 27 points (Qwen3.8, August 2026). Third, recent gains appear on open-ended edits. Earlier models could already handle simple edits but rarely open-ended ones. Claude Opus 4.5 (November 2025), for example, passes 88.5% of parameter edits but under 4% of style and composition edits. Ten months later, Claude Opus 5.5 passes 51.9% of style and 76.9% of composition edits, matching or exceeding its 51.9% on structural edits, which were once easier for models (Appendix Table 14). Structural edits, in contrast, must foresee how several tightly coupled parts interact, which remains a bottleneck (§4.3).

    4.3 Why Do Models Fail?

    We code every failure of all 76 configurations on the analysis subset (the 44 models of Figure 4 and 32 further effort levels of nine models) with a two-level taxonomy: the stage at which the edit first diverges from the instruction, and a mechanism within that stage (Appendix Table 16; details in Appendix H). Edits that fail to run or render are classified from their error logs, and the others by Gemini 3.8 Flash from the instruction, both programs, and both sets of renders (Cohen’s κ=0.71 against human labels on 150 failures; Appendix H). Table 4 summarizes the result.

    As models improve, failures shift from comprehension and coding to geometric foresight.

    Most failures of weak models happen before the shape is built, as the model misreads the instruction or the program, or writes code that does not run (82% of failures in the weakest band; Table 4). Strong models make these mistakes less often, and their failures move to geometric foresight. Their code runs and changes the intended parts, but builds the wrong shape. Avoiding them requires 3D understanding and spatial reasoning rather than coding skill. Therefore, such failures are hard to detect by running or reading the code, and show up only in the renders. The shift follows capability. From the weakest band to the two strongest, comprehension and coding fall to under 60% of failures, while geometric foresight doubles from 18% to about 40% and becomes the most common stage (Table 4).

    Geometric foresight fails most where parts meet.

    Looking further into geometric foresight (G) across all models, we find that the most common mechanism is an unforeseen interaction between parts (G-INTERACT, 9.2% of all failures), where a new or changed part collides with or is swallowed by the existing geometry, or leaves an unintended gap. Next come generator parameters that reshape the object in unintended ways (G-PARAM, 7.3%) and parts that float or detach (G-SUPPORT, 5.3%). Edits of the wrong size, too small or too large, are less than half as frequent as interactions (G-TIMID and G-OVER, 4.3% together; Appendix Table 16). Models thus usually make the requested change but misjudge how it fits with the rest of the object.

    4.4 Multi-Turn Editing: Supplying What the Editor Cannot Foresee

    §4.3 suggests that strong models most often fail to foresee what their code builds. If foresight is the main bottleneck, supplying the result should help more than additional reasoning or attempts without it. We test this through multi-turn editing, which mirrors how a user inspects the result and asks for corrections. After each edit, the editor may receive feedback and revise its program, for up to 8 rounds on the analysis subset (details in Appendix F). Our settings compensate for the missing foresight in different ways, each supplying a different amount of information about the result (Table 5):

  • 1.

    Self-check (code): no new information. The editor rereads its own code and decides whether to revise, which controls for the extra rounds alone.

  • 2.

    Self-check (renders): the result itself. The editor sees its renders but judges them on its own.

  • 3.

    Reviewer, P/F: which requirements the result misses. A separate reviewer, GPT-6-luna, writes its own checklist from the instruction and the original renders, inspects the edited renders as a user would, and reports only which items pass.

  • 4.

    Reviewer, full: how the result misses them. The reviewer also describes how the renders differ from what each item requires.

  • 5.

    Self-review: the same full feedback, from the editor’s own model in a separate conversation.

    • Seeing the result helps.

    When the editor checks its own work, seeing its renders beats rereading the code for every editor that can see images, by up to 7.1 points for GPT-6-luna (Table 5). This gain comes from seeing the result itself, consistent with foresight being a bottleneck.

    A reviewer’s description of the renders helps most.

    However, strong models rarely revise after checking their own renders, in at most 0.6 rounds on average, against 2.7 or more with a reviewer (Appendix Table 10). The more a reviewer tells the editor, the better it edits. Reporting only which items pass already beats self-check with renders for most editors, and describing how the renders differ from each requirement adds up to 10 more points, as for GPT-6.1-sol (75.6% to 85.6%). A description states exactly what the editor fails to foresee, whereas renders alone leave it to find the difference itself. For text-only editors, a reviewer’s feedback is even the only way to learn what their code builds, and full feedback raises gpt-oss-120b from 14.4% to 22.8%.

    Feedback beats more reasoning and an agent harness.

    Feedback also helps more than additional reasoning. Full feedback lifts GPT-6.1-sol from 64.7% to 85.6%, whereas its best reasoning effort reaches only 74.7% in a single shot (Appendix Table 13). Similarly, an agent harness that renders its own result and decides when to stop falls short, unless a reviewer provides feedback and decides when the edit is done (Appendix F). The gains thus come from a review of the result rather than from additional computation or the renders alone, consistent with foresight, rather than writing the code, being the main bottleneck.

    A reviewer needs to judge well, not necessarily edit well.

    Who, then, should provide the feedback? For strong editors, a weaker model is enough. Although GPT-6-luna edits worse, it reviews the three strongest editors about as well as self-review does, so judging an edit is easier than producing it. Weak editors, however, cannot judge their own edits. With GPT-6-luna instead of self-review, Qwen3.8-27B rises from 37.2% to 50.3%, surpassing the single-shot rate of Kimi K3 (46.8%).

    5 Conclusion

    We introduced 3DCodeEdit, a benchmark for editing Blender programs that build entire objects. Its edits range from geometric changes graded by scope to open-ended style redesign and scene composition, and each edit is judged from renders against a checklist. Editing remains hard, especially for structural and open-ended edits, and as models improve, their failures shift from comprehension and coding to geometric foresight. Supplying the result through multi-turn feedback closes much of this gap. A reviewer’s description of the renders helps most, more than self-checking, maximum reasoning effort, or an agent harness. These results point to geometric foresight as an important capability to improve, and 3DCodeEdit provides a testbed for measuring it.

    Limitations

    3DCodeEdit covers Blender programs that build single objects. Other 3D tools, such as CAD scripts, game-engine blueprints, and shader code, as well as larger scenes, animation, and articulated objects, are natural extensions of the same construction and evaluation pipeline. Our multi-turn study examines feedback in natural language, and other forms of feedback, such as sketches or reference images, remain to be explored. Finally, the checklists target the requested changes and the preservation of the object, so they do not capture every aspect of quality that a 3D artist would assess, such as aesthetic appeal. We release our code and data so that future work can extend these dimensions.

    Ethical Considerations

    All source programs are derived from publicly available models whose licenses permit redistribution, and we release the benchmark under the original licenses with attribution. Edit prompts, checklists, and reconstructions were produced with language models. Human annotators reviewed the prompts and checklists. The benchmark consists of everyday objects such as furniture, buildings, and mechanical parts, and we do not foresee risks beyond those of general-purpose code generation. We used AI assistants for coding and for editing the writing of this paper, and the authors take full responsibility for all content.

    Appendix A Benchmark Construction Details

    A.1 Source Programs

    3DCodeBench.

    We execute and render 76 candidate programs from 3DCodeBench and keep the 55 that run, have sound geometry, do not duplicate another selected object, and offer visible structure to edit. The retained programs are used without modification.

    OpenSCAD reconstruction.

    Converting OpenSCAD directly to Blender does not yield editable programs. Translating the constructive solid geometry keeps the shape but flattens modules and parameters into raw vertices, transformation matrices, and Boolean operations, so the program no longer exposes concepts such as a part count or a structural parameter. Prompting a frontier model once to rewrite the design keeps the structure but loses fidelity on complex objects. We therefore reconstruct each model with Codex CLI agents backed by GPT-5.5. In each round, a generator writes a Blender program, renders it, and compares the renders with those of the OpenSCAD source. An evaluator, which does not see the generator’s reasoning, then returns concrete revision feedback. A coordinator agent alternates the two and stops when the evaluator reports that no meaningful geometric or structural defect remains, or when the round budget is exhausted. Reconstructions take 5.5 rounds on average. Prompts A.1 and A.1 abbreviate the generator and evaluator briefs, and Figure 5 shows one of the longest trajectories.

    Curation.

    From the 127 reconstructions, we remove relatively simple objects and objects whose type duplicates another reconstruction, and we exclude every model whose upstream license does not clearly permit redistributing a derived program. The 53 retained programs comprise 16 architecture, 19 furniture, and 18 manufacturing objects. Figure 6 shows one source object per category.

    Licenses and intended use.

    The 55 3DCodeBench programs are distributed under BSD-3-Clause and MIT, as derived from Infinigen. The 53 reconstructed programs derive from OpenSCAD models released under CC BY 4.0 (16), CC BY-SA 4.0 (13), CC BY-NC 4.0 (7), GPL-3.0 (4), CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (3), CC0 1.0 (3), MIT (3), and other open licenses (4). We release each program under its upstream license with attribution to its creator, our prompts and checklists under CC BY 4.0, and our code under the MIT license. 3DCodeEdit is intended for research on evaluating code editing, and programs under non-commercial licenses may be used only for non-commercial purposes.

    A.2 Prompt Generation

    Generation.

    For each program and edit type, GPT-5.6-sol receives the object’s name and one-line description, the program, and four renders from the corners of the object (512×512), together with the definition of the edit type and one worked example. It returns eight candidates, each an edit-only prompt with one checklist item per instruction. Prompt A.2 shows the system prompt, the user template, and the definition of G4. The prompts number the edit types as Levels 1–6 (G1–G4, S, C). All edit prompts and checklists are in English.

    Admission and human review.

    The admission model rejects a candidate whose evidence depends on names, metadata, implementation method, topology or connectivity, hidden or internal geometry, subtle surface appearance, or details below reliable image scale; whose baseline is unsupported by the source; whose target is ambiguous among repeated parts; whose outcomes are bundled or duplicated; whose checklist drifts from its instructions; that violates the edit-type definition; or that refers to image position, a named view, or the camera. Human annotators then review the admitted candidates and reject those that are ambiguous, not visually verifiable, or unreasonable. All human review and annotation in this paper, including this review and the labels used to validate the verifier (Appendix E) and the error analysis (Appendix H), were done by the authors. Of 5,620 candidates for the 108 programs, 4,123 (73.4%) pass both filters. Prompt A.2 gives the admission rubric. If fewer than four candidates of a program and edit type pass, more are generated.

    Selection.

    GPT-5.6-sol then keeps four candidates per program and edit type (Prompt A.2). It ranks them by how clearly the results would be visible, how natural and well aligned the requests are, and how diverse their targets are, without seeing any editor output.

    A.3 Ambiguity Screening

    We screen each checklist item with Claude Opus 5.5 in two separate calls, one given the prompt and checklist only and one also given the source program, and flag the item if either call does. For each flagged task, a resolver call decides for each flagged item whether to keep it, revise it, or drop it. A rewriter then revises only the flagged instructions and their partners, keeping the requested difficulty, and the revised task is screened again, with up to two rewriting rounds. All rewrites are made under human supervision. The process revises 787 of the 2,592 tasks, and the 51 items (of 12,528) that remain ambiguous are excluded from scoring. Prompt A.3 is the screening prompt, and Prompts A.3 and A.3 abbreviate the resolver and the rewriter. Table 6 shows two rewritten instructions: “about 50% larger” can refer to the diameter or the area of each opening, and a pedestal-mounted arm conflicts with a gantry that carries it.

    Appendix B Program Length of Blender Code Benchmarks

    Table 7 reports the program length behind the “Complex code” column of Table 1; a benchmark is marked complex when its programs average more than 200 lines. Length is the number of physical lines in each Python file, including comments and blank lines. For editing benchmarks we measure the program given to the model; for generation benchmarks we measure the reference program when one exists.

    Appendix C Evaluation Protocol Details

    Each editor receives the task once, with reasoning effort medium (or an equivalent thinking budget for models without effort levels) and at most 64k output tokens, and a truncated or refused reply counts as a failed edit. We extract the edited program from each reply as the longest complete fenced code block that compiles, or otherwise as the reply with leading and trailing prose removed. Edited programs run in Blender [(Blender Online Community, 2026)] 5.1.0 with a 480-second limit for execution and rendering. Each artifact is rendered from six canonical views at 512×512 with Cycles, and the original and edited artifacts share one camera framing, so that changes in size and position remain visible. A program fails if it raises an error, produces an empty scene, or exceeds the time limit. The verifier receives the six original and six edited views, the full prompt, and one checklist item per call, and answers yes or no; it does not see either program. Prompt C is the single-shot editor prompt, and Prompt C is the verifier prompt. Gemini 3.8 Flash is called once per item with thinking level high.
